VCS Distributed Simulation
This chapter explains how to use VCS Distributed Simulation in the following sections:
• Distributed Simulation Setup
• Synchronization Among Client Simvs
• Finish Behavior
• DUT Synchronization
• Testbench Synchronization
• Debugging Distributed Simulation
• Quick Reference: VCS Distributed Simulation Options
Subsystems compile and simulate individually as separate blocks developed for multi-
die verification. However, integrating these subsystems in a top-level SoC poses various
challenges including the resolution of modules with the same names and class/package
name collision. This process needs to be repeated with every new revision of subsystems.
Also, the high-memory consumption of huge designs and ever-increasing memory
requirement of simulation require high-capacity machines to simulate entire designs.
VCS Distributed Simulation solution allows you to perform the following simulations:
• Homogeneous Simulation
• Heterogeneous Simulation
Homogeneous Simulation
In this mode, a simulation executable (simv) is duplicated as multiple runs on the same
or different machines representing multiple instances of the same module. All the data
transfers across subsystems get synchronized based on the synchronization settings
defined in the configuration file.

In the following figure, simv run1 and simv run2 are the same simv processes executed
on two different machines.
Figure 122 Homogeneous Simulation
Heterogeneous Simulation
In this mode, multiple simulation executables (simvs) are created for different modules
with their own testbenches running on different machines in parallel. Communication
across the simvs for data transfers is based on the synchronization settings defined in the
Figure 123 Heterogeneous Simulation
The Distributed Simulation solution allows you to overcome synchronization issues,
maintain deterministic simulation behavior during a rerun of the simulation, and achieve
better runtime performance along with a reduction in memory footprint, thereby reducing
the need for large-capacity machines.

A Distributed Simulation (Distsim) setup consists of individually-developed multiple
subsystems which are to be verified together. In a Distsim setup, you can run multiple
subsystems on different machines, or all the subsystems on the same machine, as
required.
A simv corresponding to a subsystem which is a part of a Distsim setup is called a client
simv. To run all the simvs in a distributed fashion using the Distsim setup, all the simvs
must be compiled using the -distsim compile option, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 124 Distributed Simulation Setup
You can use the -distsim=help compile option to view all the supported -distsim
options along with the purpose.
• Default Setup Using TCP/IP
• User-Defined TCP Port for Server Launch
• Distsim Flow Without Shared File System
• Server Launch as Independent Process
• Include Syntax in Configuration File
• Support for Version Compatibility Across VCS Releases

section: 1.10 Interface definition to be passed before the virtual interface is created to the vlogan
title: 1.10 Interface definition to be passed before the virtual interface is created to the vlogan
text:
Default Setup Using TCP/IP
You must specify the following options in the Distsim setup:
• -distsim=num_sockets:<total_Clients>: Specify the total number of clients in the
setup using the -distsim=num_sockets:<total_Clients> option. The simulation
can only proceed when all the clients are connected as they are mutually dependent.
The maximum number of clients cannot exceed 16.
• -distsim=client_id:<id>: Specify the client ID using the
-distsim=client_id:<id> option. All the clients are distinguished based on their id
to parse the configuration file.
• -distsim=server_info:<file_path>: Specify a file to dump the server information.
It allows you to establish TCP connection among all the clients through a server. If the
common file system is not available to provide the server_info file, the Distsim Flow
Without Shared File System feature is used to run the Distsim flow.
• -distsim=launch_server: To designate one of the simvs to launch the server process
internally, use the -distsim=launch_server option.
To define a specific TCP port for the server launch, refer to the User-Defined TCP Port
for Server Launch feature.
To launch the server process as an independent process, refer to the Server Launch as
Independent Process feature.
• -distsim=config_file:<file_path>: Specify the Distsim configuration file using
the -distsim=config_file:<file_path> option. The configuration file defines
connections of the DUT and testbench of simvs. To specify the configuration file with
the full or relative file path with respect to the top-level connectivity file, refer to the
Include Syntax in Configuration File feature.
Based on the Distsim configuration file, debug capabilities are required to be enabled
during compilation. For DUT connection, you can enable force capabilities using the
-debug_acc+f compile-time option. However, for enhanced performance, refer to the
Compile Time Configuration File Support section. For details on DUT, refer to the DUT
Synchronization section.
For Testbench, refer to the Testbench Phase Synchronization and Testbench Data
Transfer of Class Objects sections.
For details related to the Bidirect support and the HDL access across simvs features,
refer to the Bidirect Support and HDL Access Across Simvs sections.
For information related to the synchronization of client simvs, refer to the
Synchronization Among Client Simvs section.

User-Defined TCP Port for Server Launch
All the ports in a network might not be open to establish a TCP/IP connection due to
network security reasons. The User-Defined TCP Port feature passes the required port in
the command line to the master simv.
The User-Defined TCP port feature is required only for the Server, when
launched separately, or for the master simv to launch the server. It is ignored for
rest of the Clients.
The following is the runtime option:
-distsim=port:<TCP port number>
• The configuration allows only single set of distributed simulation to run on a unique
port.
• You need to provide different unique port numbers during a regression or you need
to run multiple test cases simultaneously while using the -distsim=port:<TCP port
number> option.
Distsim Flow Without Shared File System
When the common file system is not available to provide the Server Info File, the Distsim
Flow Without Shared File System feature is used to run Distsim flow. Therefore, instead of
passing Server Info File in all the clients commands, you need to pass the IP address of
the Server and the TCP port through the runtime arguments. The IP address can be a host
name or an IPv4 address.
When the provided Server IP address is not correct, the client processes get timeout and
exit. The default timeout is 60 minutes and you can use the following option to specify time
in minutes:
-distsim=timeout:<time in minutes>
-distsim=ip:<ip_address> -distsim=port:<port_number>
• <ip_address> is the IPv4 address or the host name.
• <port_number> is the TCP port number.

section: 1.10 Interface definition to be passed before the virtual interface is created to the vlogan
title: 1.10 Interface definition to be passed before the virtual interface is created to the vlogan
text:
Using the -distsim=ip:<ip_address> and -distsim=port:<port_number> options,
you can establish connection between the client simvs and the server or the server
process.
In the following examples, instead of using the server_info runtime argument,
the -distsim=ip:<> option is used to pass the IP address of the server and
-distsim=port:<> option is used to pass the TCP port:
• Launching server using -distsim=launch_server
mkdir S0; cd S0
vcs ../w0.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:0
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 |& tee
vcs.log.distsim.0 & ; cd ..
mkdir S1; cd S1
vcs ../w1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:1
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 |& tee
vcs.log.distsim.1 &
./simv0
-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt -distsi
m=port:8080 -distsim=ip:10.192.194.52 -distsim=launch_server -l
sim0.log > client.log.0 &
./simv1
-distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt -distsi
m=port:8080
-distsim=ip:127.0.0.1 -l sim1.log > client.log.1 &
• Launching server manually
mkdir S0; cd S0
vcs ../w0.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:0
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 |& tee
vcs.log.distsim.0 & ; cd ..
mkdir S1; cd S1
vcs ../w1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:1
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 |& tee
vcs.log.distsim.1 &; cd ..
$VCS_HOME/bin/simv.distsim -full64 -distsim=num_sockets:2
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080
-distsim=ip:localhost > server.log &

./simv0 -distsim=client_id:0 -distsim=num_sockets:2
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080
-distsim=ip:localhost -l sim0.log > client.log.0 &; cd ..
./simv1 -distsim=client_id:1 -distsim=num_sockets:2
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -distsim=port:8080
-distsim=ip:localhost -l sim1.log > client.log.1 &; cd ..

In the example, localhost is the local computer with the loop back address,
127.0.0.1. You can get the IPv4 address or host name using the following UNIX
command: hostname -i
Server Launch as Independent Process
The Server Launch as Independent Process feature allows you to run the Distsim server
process as a standalone, independent process rather than having one of the client simvs
launch it. This approach is useful when you want to explicitly control the server process or
run it on a specific host.
You can launch the server process as an independent process using the following three
points:
• No -distsim=launch_server Clients
None of the client simvs should use the -distsim=launch_server option. This
ensures that the server process is not launched by any of the clients.
• Server Process Executable
The server process is launched using the executable located at $VCS_HOME/bin/
simv.distsim. This is a dedicated executable for running the Distsim server.
• Passing Runtime Flags
The server process must have all the -distsim runtime options that are passed to
Client 0 if it is launching the server. These options include configuration details such as
the number of sockets, configuration file, and server information.
You can use this feature to ensure that the server process is independent of all the client
simvs and provides a known and stable server endpoint for all clients to connect to.
$VCS_HOME/bin/simv.distsim
-distsim=num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info:../server.txt
> ../server.log &
simv0
-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info:
../server.txt -l ../sim.log0 > ../client.log0 &

simv1
-distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info:
../server.txt -l ../sim.log1 > ../client.log1 &
simv2
-distsim=client_id:2,num_sockets:3,config_file:../mapping,server_info:
../server.txt -l ../sim.log2 > ../client.log2 &
Include Syntax in Configuration File
The Include Syntax in Configuration File feature enables a top level connectivity file
to include lower level connectivity file. The top level connectivity file is passed with the
following option: -distsim=config_file:<top level connectivity file>
Configuration File Syntax
Use include or 'include identifier to specify the configuration file with the full or relative
file path with respect to the top level connectivity file. You must use double quotation
marks to specify the configuration file.
-distsim=config_file:top.connectivity.txt
> cat top.connectivity.txt
include "sub1.connectivity.txt"
//DUT connections

> cat sub1.connectivity.txt
//DUT connections
include "sub2.connectivity.txt"

and so on
Support for Version Compatibility Across VCS Releases
VCS Distributed Simulation (Distsim) enables you to run cosimulation across multiple
machines. The Distsim Version Compatibility feature allows you to cosimulate the
simulation executables (simvs) generated from different VCS releases, provided they
share a common Distsim version.
To use the common Distsim version, provide the common VCS_HOME directory that locates
the Distsim library.
A higher Distsim version includes all features from earlier versions, plus new features only
found in the higher version. To ensure compatibility and support co-simulation of the simvs
generated using different VCS release versions, you must use the same Distsim version.

To enable version compatibility across VCS releases, set the
-distsim=versionpath:<path_to_common_vcs_home> option at compile time. This
ensures that all simvs use the same Distsim version, regardless of their individual
VCS_HOME settings.
The following is the use model for the
-distsim=versionpath:<path_to_common_vcs_home> compile option:
% vcs ../w0.v -sverilog
-full64 -distsim=versionpath:<path_to_common_vcs_home> -o simv0
% vcs ../w1.v -sverilog
-full64 -distsim=versionpath:<path_to_common_vcs_home> -o simv1
• If you do not specify the
-distsim=versionpath:<path_to_common_vcs_home> option during
compile time, by default VCS uses the Distsim version or library from
VCS_HOME where simv is compiled.

Using different Distsim libraries might result in an unexpected behavior.
Synchronization is a process of communicating with multiple client simvs based on any
design signal or a periodic interval. The simulation time when the client simvs initiate two-
way communication with the server process to exchange the required data with other
clients is called the synchronization point or sync point. After all the clients reach their sync
point, the server provides the required data and all the simvs waiting at the sync point
continue.
You can synchronize client simvs using the following methods:
• Master-Sync Signal or Interval
• Multiple Synchronization Signals Using Multiple Groups

• Distsim Nsync: Synchronization After a Transport Delay
• Distsim Tsync: Synchronization After a Transport Delay
Master-Sync Signal or Interval
A master-sync signal or interval can be used to determine the sync point for the client
simv. A master-sync signal is a design signal for the simv and synchronization is triggered
each time the master_sync_signal changes its state.
A master-sync interval is the time period specified by the user, and the synchronization is
triggered periodically at the time interval defined by master_sync_interval.
It is mandatory to provide either a synchronization signal with master_sync_signal or a
time interval with master_sync_interval as follows:
• Sync Signal Specification
The following is the syntax:
<master_sync_signal>: s<Client ID>: <Edge Identifier> <Hierarchical
Path of Sync Signal>
<master_sync_signal>: A required field.
s<Client ID> : Optional field. Specifies client-specific synchronization signal.
<Edge Identifier> : Optional field. Use posedge/negedge.
• Time Interval-Based Synchronization
The following is the syntax:
<master_sync_interval>: s<Client ID>: <interval><time unit>
master_sync_interval: A required field.
s<Client ID> : Optional field. Specifies client-specific time interval.
<interval>: Specifies numeric time period in positive integers only.
<time unit> : Optional field. If not provided, the timescale of the design is used;
otherwise, you can use s/ms/us/ns/ps/fs.

Consider the following example with two simulation clients, client 0 and client 1:
master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0]
master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0]
• s0 and s1 refer to the simulation clients, client 0 and client 1.
• top.clk[0] is the hierarchical path to the clock signal to be used as the master-sync
signal.
This means that s0 and s1 get synchronized at every edge of top.clk[0].
To understand how a master-sync signal is used to synchronize DUT, refer to the DUT
Synchronization section.
Multiple Synchronization Signals Using Multiple Groups
To create a distributed simulation setup, the default use model identifies a master-sync
signal or master-sync interval. This master-sync signal or master-sync interval is used as
the primary synchronization mechanism across multiple simvs. However, it introduces an
additional complexity of adding a common clock or common time interval and managing
the synchronization points. Furthermore, it impacts the performance when you need to
synchronize the slower DUT connections with the faster master-sync signal or interval.
The Multiple-Synchronization Groups feature is introduced to synchronize simulations with
multiple clock domains, instead of using one master-sync signal or master-sync interval. It
allows grouping signals in a synchronization group based on different clocks of a client.
A synchronization group is a group that contains a set of synchronization signals and their
corresponding DUT connections. It is recognized by a group ID, which is a unique positive
integer assigned to each synchronization group. A distributed simulation configuration file
can contain multiple synchronization groups with unique group IDs for easy identification.
To enable the Multiple-Synchronization Groups feature, you must define synchronization
groups with appropriate synchronization signals in the distributed simulation configuration
file and run the following option:
-distsim=syncgrp
To define sync groups in the distributed simulation configuration file, use the following use
model:
//Sync group with <group ID>
sync_group:<group_id>

sync_signal:s0:<Sync Signal 0>
sync_signal:s1:<Sync Signal 1>
sync_signal:s2:<Sync Signal 2>
s0:<hier_path.signal0> = s1:<hier_path.signal1>

sync_group:0
sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk
sync_signal:s1:negedge top1.clk
sync_signal:s2:negedge top2.clk
s0:top0.a1 = s1:top1.a1
s0:top0.b2 = s2:top2.b2
s1:top1.a3 = s0:top0.b3
s2:top2.a4 = s1:top1.b4
tbtrans=CH0:s0::CH1:s1

sync_group:1
sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk2
sync_signal:s2:negedge top2.clk2
s0:top0.a2 = s2:top2.a2

sync_group:2
sync_signal:s0:negedge top0.clk4
sync_signal:s1:negedge top1.clk4
s0:top0.b1 = s1:top1.b1
You must define synchronization groups in the distributed simulation configuration file
using the following guidelines:
• You must use the sync_group identifier to define the set of synchronization
signals or intervals for the required clients. In the example, s0, s1, and s2 indicate
synchronization signals for client 0, client 1, and client 2, respectively.
• You must specify DUT connections corresponding to the synchronization group.

Distsim Nsync: Synchronization After a Transport Delay
The support for synchronizing after a transport delay allows you to optimize simulation
performance when connecting subsystems, such as those using high-speed interfaces
(UCIe), by reducing the frequency of synchronization (sync) events. This type of
synchronization is called the Distributed Simulation (Distsim) Nsync feature. The Distsim
Nsync feature synchronizes data exchange between clients after a specified number of
changes of the master-sync signal. This approach is particularly useful for designs that
can tolerate some delay between data transfers, resulting in improved performance.
The Distsim Nsync feature consists of the following three steps:
1. Sampling: Each client samples data at every master-sync signal change and stores it in
an internal buffer.
2. Data exchange: Clients exchange all the stored data packets at every nth change of the
master-sync signal. This is called the sync point.
3. Driving: After synchronization, each client drives the received data packets one by one
at every subsequent master-sync signal change until the next sync point.
To enable the Distsim Nsync feature, use the following runtime option during simulation in
all the clients:
-distsim=nsync:<n>
Where, <n> is a variable that depends on the delay tolerance of a design.

It means that,
• The synchronization happens on every n th change of the master-sync signal or interval.
• A transport delay of n*frequency of a master-sync signal or interval is
added in transferring data between the clients.
• It enhances performance due to the reduced number of synchronizations.
If you pass the -distsim=nsync:10 runtime option, the clients exchange all the stored
packets at every 10th change of the master-sync signal.
The Distsim Nsync feature has the following limitations:
• The feature is only suitable for designs that can tolerate the introduced delay.
• Multiple synchronization signals or intervals are not supported.
• Bidirect support through wired OR or AND is not supported.
• Multiple synchronization groups are not supported.
• Synchronization for the TB data transfer does not occur with every change of the
master sync signal or interval, but rather at the nth change.
Distsim Tsync: Synchronization After a Transport Delay
The Distsim Tsync feature helps optimize simulation performance when connecting
subsystems, such as those with high-speed interfaces like UCIe. It does this by reducing
how often synchronization events happen. With Distsim Tsync, simulation data is
synchronized at a specified master-sync time interval, which is slower than the default
Distsim synchronization interval.
With the default Distsim, only one value change can happen at the master-sync interval.
However, Distsim Tsync allows you to collect all value changes in the connectivity signals
within the master-sync interval (t) and synchronize them together. The Distsim Tsync
feature is useful for designs that can accept some delay, as it reduces the number of
synchronization events and speeds up simulation.

The Distsim Tsync feature consists of the following three steps:
1. Sampling: Each client stores all value changes of load signals with respect to the
simulation time in an internal buffer.
2. Data exchange: Clients exchange all stored data packets at every change of the
master-sync interval (t). This is called the sync point.
3. Driving: After the sync point, each client drives the received data packets one by one
using the simulation time provided by the sender clients.
To enable the Distsim Tsync feature, use the following runtime option during simulation in
all the clients:
-distsim=tsync
The simulation time is synchronized with the master-sync interval, t.
It means that
• The synchronization happens at the master-sync interval.
• A transport delay of t is added in transferring data between the clients.
• It enhances performance due to the reduced number of synchronizations.

master_sync_interval:10ns

Finish Behavior
The Distsim Tsync feature has the following limitations:
• This feature is only suitable for designs that can tolerate the introduced delay.
• Synchronization signals are not supported.
• Multiple synchronization intervals are not supported.
• Bidirect support through wired OR or AND is not supported.
• Multiple synchronization groups are not supported.
• In Distsim Tsync, the master-sync interval can be longer than the usual interval used in
normal Distsim. As a result of this change, you can expect the same delay in TB data
receive calls.
Finish Behavior
The finish behavior in VCS Distsim controls how the simulation ends across all the client
simvs. It determines what happens when one or more clients reach the end of their
simulation and call for $finish. Distsim supports the following finish behaviors:
• Safe finish: By default, VCS waits for all the clients to finish their simulation. The
simulation ends only when every client reached its own end-of-simulation point, or
when an error exit happens. When an error exit happens, all the client simvs exit with
an error.
• Finish order: With the -distsim=finish:first option, the simulation ends for all the
clients as soon as any one client finishes. When a client finishes, the rest of the clients
exit their simulation at the next synchronization point instead of continuing till the end of
their simulation.
simv
-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping,server_info
:../server.txt -distsim=finish:first
• Early finish: When a client finishes early, the -distsim=finish:freeze option allows
you to freeze the DUT signals to their last forced values in the remaining clients.
This prevents local drivers from taking over those signals after the original driver has
finished.
This option is used when a client finishes early, and you want to freeze the DUT signals
(that were being driven by the finished client) to their last forced values in the remaining
clients. This prevents local drivers from taking over those signals after the original
driver has finished.

DUT synchronization in Distsim is a process of ensuring that the Design Under Test
(DUT) instances running in different clients simvs operate in a coordinated and time-
aligned manner. DUT synchronization involves specifying the DUT signals that need to be
connected between client simvs. At each synchronization point, the values of these DUT
signals are transmitted to the appropriate client simvs.
• DUT Connections
• Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection
• DUT Connection with Constant Loads
• Bidirect Support
• Compile Time Configuration File Support
• HDL Access Across Simvs
DUT Connections
DUT connections establish seamless communication between signals in different client
simv processes. Specifically, a signal from one simv, referred to as the driver signal, can
be driven by a corresponding load signal in another simv. The default behavior ensures
synchronized operation. That is, the values of driver signals are sampled at designated
sync points, transmitted to the other simv at the same point, and subsequently driven in
the target simv at the sync point. For details on sync point, refer to the Synchronization
Among Client Simvs section.

For DUT connection, synchronization between signals is specified in the Distsim
configuration file at runtime.
Configuration file: The following is the configuration file syntax for DUT connection:
s<Destination Client ID>:<Hierarchical Path of Driver Signal> = s<source
Client ID>:<Hierarchical Path of Load Signal>
• s<Destination Client ID> : Specifies the client ID of the simv driven by the value.
• <Hierarchical Path of Driver Signal> : Specifies the full path of the driver signal
in the destination client.
• s<source Client ID> : Specifies the client ID of the simv that provides the value.
• <Hierarchical Path of Load Signal> : Specifies the full path of the load signal in
the source client.
Compile time: The load signal requires read capability and the driver signal requires force
capability. You can enable debug-read capability in the load signal using -debug_access
+r and debug-force capability in the driver signal using -debug_access+f. However, for
enhanced runtime performance, instead of using -debug_access+f, apply only selective
capabilities. For details on applying selective capabilities, refer to the Compile Time
Configuration File Support section.
Runtime: For simulation, no extra option is required.
The following example shows a configuration file where synchronization occurs when
value of the test.mid.clock_sig signal changes:
master_sync_signal: test.mid.clock_sig
s1:test.mid.clock_sig1 = s0:test.mid.clock_sig0
s2:test.mid.clock_sig2 = s1:test.mid.clock_sig1
s0:test.mid.clock_sig4 = s1:test.mid.clock_sig3
The s1:test.mid.clock_sig1 = s0:test.mid.clock_sig0 line indicates that
the client simv with client_id == 0 has signal test.mid.clock_sig0 that drives
test.mid.clock_sig1 of the client simv with client_id == 1 .
Similarly, the s2:test.mid.clock_sig2 = s1:test.mid.clock_sig1 line indicates
that the client simv with client_id == 1 has signal test.mid.clock_sig1 that drives
test.mid.clock_sig2 of the client simv with client_id == 2 .

Scalars and vectors of the following data types are supported for the
synchronization signal: reg, wire, logic, bit, enum, packed memory,
interface members, packed struct members, and packed struct (using the
-distsim=struct runtime option).
The following are the limitations of DUT connections:
• Interfaces are not supported; however, interface members of the specified data types
are supported.
• The unpacked memory, real, time, memword, interface, dynamic data type, and SV
data type are not supported.
• The unpacked structures are not supported.
Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection
The Sample Drive Signals for DUT Connection feature allows you to sample and
drive at two different signals. The sample and drive signals are different from the
synchronization signal. Therefore, they are used for sampling and driving the signal and
not for synchronization with other client simv.
Compile time and runtime: You must follow the same compile-time options used for DUT
Connections.
To specify different signals for sampling and driving signals across distributed simulation,
add the -distsim=drive_secondary_clk runtime option.
The following is the use model of the -distsim=drive_secondary_clk runtime option:
% simv -distsim=drive_secondary_clk <other_distsim_arguments>
<other_runtime_arguments>
Configuration file: You must use the identifier, master_sync_signal or
master_sync_interval, to designate the master-sync signal or master-sync interval,
respectively. Specify the connections that are to be sampled or driven with respect to a
different sampling and driving signal in the following format:
s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal>=s<Source_Client_ID>:<Load_Signal>
(Sample:<Sample_Signal>, Drive:<Drive_Signal>)
Where, in the source client, <Load_Signal> is sampled at the change of
<Sample_Signal> and transferred to the destination client when master sync signal

or interval changes. In the destination client, <Drive_Signal> is driven when
<Drive_Signal> changes after synchronization.
The configuration file format is limited to supporting only sample and drive
signals, and it does not allow for the specification of time intervals.
For the client-specific sample signal, add s<Client ID>: as the prefix in the configuration
The following is an example for the same configuration file with multiple synchronization
signals or intervals:
Configuration File:

// Define master sync signals for each client
master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0]
master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0]

// Specify sample and drive clocks for DUT connections

// Define master sync signals for each client

// Specify sample and drive clocks for DUT connections
s0:top.B1 = s1:top.b1.b (sample:top.clk[1], drive:top.clk[2])
s0:top.C1 = s1:top.c1.c (sample:top.clk[1])
s0:top.D1 = s1:top.d1.d (drive:top.clk[2])
In the example, top.b1.b is sampled on the sample clock top.clk[1]. The sampled
value is driven to top.B1 when the drive clock top.clk[2] switches value, following the
master-synchronization signal, top.clk[0].
Adding Delay in DUT Connection
You can introduce a delay in DUT connections that adds a transport delay in the driver
signal. Specify the delay in the Distsim mapping file in the following way:
s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal> = #<delay>
s<Source_Signal>:<Load_Signal>
or
s<Destination_Client_ID>:<Driver_Signal> = #<delay><timeunits> s<Source
Signal>:<Load Signal>
The #delay supports only positive integers, with or without timescale. To enable this
feature, no additional compile or runtime options are required. For example,
// Define master sync signals for each client
master_sync_signal:s0: top.clk[0]
master_sync_signal:s1: top.clk[0]

// Introduce a drive delay
s0:top.E1 = #5ns s1:top.e1.e
In the example, s0:top.E1 is driven with a delay of 5ns with respect to the last
synchronization.

DUT Connection with Constant Loads
The DUT Connection with Constant Loads feature drives any supported DUT signal using
the Verilog constants. It supports hexadecimal, binary, and decimal constants.
s0:top.a = 1'b1
s1:top.b = 8'hzx
s2:top.c = 2'd10
s3:top.d = 25

Bidirect Support With Distsim Master Sync
The Bidirect Support feature connects signals across different clients through the wired
gates behavior. This feature requires drivers capability on the design.
Compile time: The Bidirect Support feature requires driver capabilities. To add drivers
capability during compile time, use the -debug_acc+drivers compile-time option or the
The following is the use model for the -debug_acc+drivers compile-time option:
vcs -distsim -distsim=config_file:<config_file_name> -debug_acc+drivers
Runtime: Additional Distsim switches are not required to enable it during simulation,
except for adding the required connections in the configuration file in the specified format.

Configuration file: You must add the required connections in the configuration file in the
specified format. The following is the use model of the configuration file:
vcs -distsim -distsim=config_file:<configuration_file_name>
The following is the configuration file syntax:
<Gate Identifier> s<Client_ID>:<Signal> <=> s<Client_ID>:<Signal> <=>
s<Client_ID>:<Signal>
• <Gate Identifier> refers to the type of logical connection (specifically, a wired OR, a
wired AND, or an INOUT) used to connect signals across different simulation clients.
• <Client ID> refers to the unique integer identifier for each simulation process (simv).
• <Signal> refers to a specific variable in the design hierarchy of a client that is to be
connected via a bidirectional (WOR/WAND/INOUT) connection.
The following is an example showing the Bidirect Support feature:
WOR s0:top.b1.c <=> s1:top.b2.c <=> s2:top.c3
WAND s1:top.a1 <=> s3:top.a3
The following are the expected behaviors:
• The signals connected through a gate are to be resolved based on the gate type
specified in the configuration file in the server process.
◦ WOR: If any signal is 1, all the connections become 1.
◦ WAND: If any signal is 0, all the connections become 0.
◦ INOUT
▪ If both signals are the same, the output is the same signal.
▪ If the signals are different, the output is X.
▪ If one of the signals is Z, the output is the other signal.
The WOR, WAND, and INOUT gate behavior is shown in the following truth table:
A B WOR WAND INOUT

title: 1 Z 1 X 1
text:
• The signals on the client side are forced with the resolved value sent by the server.
wire [1:0] a;
reg [1:0] b;
reg [1:0] c;
reg [1:0] d;

WOR s0:top.a <=> s1:top.b <=> s2:top.c
The top.a signal in Client 0, the top.b signal in Client 1, and the top.c signal in Client
2 are connected to the Bidirect WOR gate.
The values of these signals are sent to the server, where they are resolved using the
WOR gate. The final resolved value is sent back to all the clients and the signals are
forced with the resolved value.
Bidirect Support With Distsim Tsync
The Distsim Tsync feature supports bidirectional connections (WOR, WAND, and INOUT)
defined in the configuration file. Apart from -distsim=tsync, no additional runtime option
is required.
For DUT connections, Distsim Tsync collects all value changes within the master-sync
interval and synchronizes them. However, bidirectional signals require value resolution

from all connected clients to determine the final value. Therefore, bidirectional signals in
Distsim Tsync are handled differently as follows:
• Only the current value at the sync point is considered. All intermediate value changes
within the master-sync interval are ignored.
• The current values from all clients are sent to the server process, where they
are resolved based on the gate type (WOR, WAND, or INOUT) specified in the
• The resolved value is driven back to all bidirectional connections.
The following example shows a bidirectional connection in Distsim Tsync mode with the
master-sync interval set to 10 ns :
master_sync_interval:10ns
WOR s0:top.a <=> s1:top.b
Consider that s0:top.a changes values at 4 ns , 8 ns , 12 ns , and 16 ns . Similarly,
s1:top.b changes values at 3 ns , 6 ns , 9 ns , 12 ns , and 15 ns .
At the sync point (10 ns ), only the current values of s0:top.a and s1:top.b at 10 ns are
considered. All intermediate value changes (that is, at 3 ns , 4 ns , 6 ns , 8 ns , 9 ns ) are
discarded.
The current values are resolved in the server process using the WOR gate, and the
resolved value is driven to both connections:
Resolved Value: WOR(s0:top.a at 10 ns, s1:top.b at 10 ns)
If the value of a bidirectional signal changes multiple times within one sync interval, only
the last value is honored.
The following are the limitations of the Bidirect Support feature:
• The feature supports only WOR and WAND gates.
• The feature supports wires and logic used as wire.
• The feature supports only scalar and full vectors.
• The Bidirect Support feature does not support registers, memories, bit select, part
select, and memory word.
• Distsim does not support tran gate drivers for the Bidirect connections. VCS displays a
warning message on the first occurrence of an active tran gate driver.
• The strength resolution is not supported for supply0, supply1, tri0, tri1, triand, trior,
WAND, and WOR data types.

Compile Time Configuration File Support
Using the Compile Time Configuration File Support feature for the limited debug
capabilities, you can avoid adding the global debug_access debug capabilities for Distsim.
Instead, you can pass the Distsim configuration file at compile time which enables
the required debug capabilities, such as deposit/force/release, only on the relevant
connectivity signals.
Compile time: The following is the compile option:
-distsim=config_file:<Distsim_Config_File_Path>
-distsim=client_id:<Client ID> // For Heterogeneous systems. For Homogeneous
systems, you can avoid this option.
#!/bin/csh -fx

rm -rf simv* csrc* S*

vcs w0.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0
-distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -distsim=client_id:0 | & tee
vcs.log0
vcs w1.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1
-distsim -distsim=config_file:mapping.txt -distsim=client_id:1 | & tee
vcs.log1

mkdir S0
mkdir S1

../simv0
-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf
o:../server.txt -l ../sim.log0 -distsim=launch_server > ../client.log0 &

../simv1 -distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,
config_file:../mapping.txt,server_info:../server.txt -l ../sim.log1
> ../client.log1 &
The above example is of a Heterogeneous system which consists of the distsim
configuration file, (-distsim=config_file:mapping.txt), and the client ID,
(-distsim=client_id:0 or 1) , options to enable the required debug capabilities for the
design and save runtime.

The following is the limitation of the Compile Time Configuration File Support feature:
• This feature is supported only for the DUT connections, bidirectional connections,
Testbench Phase Synchronization, and Testbench Data Transfer. Therefore, you can
avoid adding the -debug_access option for these features.
HDL Access Across Simvs
The HDL Access Across Simvs feature enables you to perform operations such as forcing
or depositing a DUT signal to a specific value, or releasing a signal which is present in a
different client simv. This is typically used in testbenches to override signal values in the
DUT for controlling and monitoring purposes.
The HDL Access Across Simvs feature provides access to signals across multiple simvs in
distributed simulation using the following two sources:
• Verilog source
• PLI source
HDL Access Across Simvs Using Verilog Source
Using this feature, you can deposit/force/release from other simvs in distributed simulation.
It supports scalars, vectors, and selects. The HDL access across simvs from the Verilog
Source supports the following operations:
• Force and Deposit
• Release
• Checking HDL Signal Paths
• Reading HDL Signal Paths
Force and Deposit
To force a signal from any other client simv, use the following macro in the Verilog source:
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE(<Label String>, <signal Name>, <value Expr>,
<isForce>)
• <Label String> is the unique string label for the destination client.
• <signal Name> is the hierarchical path for the destination signal. It requires debug-
force capability. To enable debug-force capability, use the selective capability using PLI
tab, or use the -debug_acc+f compile-time option.

• <value Expr> is any valid Verilog expression. It requires debug-read capability and
you can enable it using the -debug_acc+r compile-time option.
• <isForce> is 1 for force freeze and 0 for deposit.
For example, consider label string mapping as follows:
hdl_label:CH2:2
hdl_label:CH3:3
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("CH2","socket2.a2", a1, 0);
Release
To release a signal from any other client simv, use the following macro in the Verilog
source:
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE(<Label String> , <signal Name>)
• <Label String> is the unique string label for the destination client.
• <signal Name> is the hierarchical path for the destination signal. It requires debug-
force capability. To enable debug-force capability, use the selective capability using PLI
tab, or use the -debug_acc+f compile-time option.
For example, consider label string mapping as follows:
hdl_label:CH2:2
hdl_label:CH3:3
#10 `VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE("CH3", socket3.a2");
Checking HDL Signal Paths
The vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path API checks hierarchical path of HDL signals across
client simvs. This behavior is similar to the behavior of uvm_hdl_check_path in the UVM
testbench. However, the API call returns only after reaching the synchronization point in
the client simvs.
To check HDL signal paths in UVM designs running with Distributed Simulation, use the
following functions:
vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path(<Client Label>, <Target Signal Name>, <Status
Bit>)

• <Client Label> : A unique string that identifies the destination client.
• <Target Signal Name> : The full hierarchical path to the destination signal.
• <Status Bit> : A signal from the user design. It is set to ‘1’ when the target signal is
found in the destination client.
The vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path API is called from the test case to check if a signal
exists in your design.
Reading HDL Signal Paths
The vcsdistsim_hdl_read API reads HDL signal paths across client simvs. This
behavior is similar to the behavior of uvm_hdl_read in the UVM testbench. However, the
API call returns only after reaching the synchronization point in the client simvs.
To read HDL signal paths in UVM designs running with Distributed Simulation, use the
following functions:
vcsdistsim_hdl_read(<Client Label>, <Target Signal Name>, <Status Bit>,
<Read Buffer>)
• <Client Label> : A unique string that identifies the destination client.
• <Target Signal Name> : The full hierarchical path to the destination signal.
• <Status Bit> : A signal from the user design. It is set to ‘1’ when the target signal is
found in the destination client.
• <Read Buffer> : Buffer provided by the user design. If the target signal exists in the
destination client, this buffer is filled with the value of that signal. The Read Buffer uses
a logic data type, such as uvm_hdl_data_t. By default, its size is 1024 bits.
The key behavior of vcsdistsim_hdl_read is as follows:
• The vcsdistsim_hdl_read API is called from the test case to check if a signal exists
and read its value.
• The default read size for reading a signal using vcsdistsim_hdl_read is 1024 bits.
You need to define <Read Buffer> as logic [1023:0] Read_Buffer .
• If the target signal is bigger than 1024 bits, only the least significant 1024 bits are read
(same as uvm_hdl_read).
• To read larger signals, define read buffer with a size greater than 1024 bits. Use the
VCSDISTSIM_READ_ARRAY_SIZE macro to set the size. You can set this macro with the
+define option at compile time.

When you call these APIs, the source client gets the status of the target signal (and
its value, if you use the read API) at the next synchronization point. For example, if
synchronization happens every 5 time units and Client0 calls the API at time 7, the
server processes the request at time 10 and sends the response at time 15.
Compile time: You need to ensure that the correct debug capabilities are enabled for the
signals involved in distributed calls. You must pass the -distsim option in your vlogan
command to activate distributed simulation support. During compilation, include both
-distsim and -distsim=config_file:<path> options. The configuration file specifies
which signals require debug capabilities such as force or read.
For specific HDL operations,
• HDL force: Signals used in force operations must have the force capability enabled.
• HDL read or path check: Signals used in read or path check operations require read
capability.
To enable these capabilities, use one of the following ways:
• Pass an appropriate tab file during compilation, which selectively assigns the required
debug capabilities to the relevant signals or modules.
• Use the -debug_access+f option when force macros are used, or -debug_access+r
when only read or path check calls are needed.
To enable the HDL access across simvs, use the selective capability using PLI tab or use
the -debug_access+f compile-time option. It does not require configuration file support.
Runtime: For this feature, no extra option is required.
Configuration file: The following is the syntax for the configuration file:
hdl_label:<label>:clientID
Where, <label> is specified in the macro call to map it to the destination client ID.
The following example displays a Verilog source demonstrating the usage of HDL access:
#1;
a22 = 100;
b22[31:0] = 32'h33;
b22[63:32] = 32'h77;
c22 = 1;
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("mysim0", "cpu_1.a11", a22, 1);
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("mysim0", "cpu_1.b11", b22, 0);

#5;
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE("mysim0", "cpu_1.a11");
end
The label string mapping for client 0 and client 1 are as follows:
master_sync_signal: s0:cpu_1.clk_1
master_sync_signal: s1:cpu_2.clk_1
hdl_label:mysim0:0
hdl_label:mysim1:1
Where, s0 and s1 are client IDs 0 and 1 respectively. HDL label mysim0 is linked to client
ID 0 and mysim1 is linked to client ID 1.
The example run script for two client IDs (0 and 1) is as follows:
#!/bin/csh -fx

rm -rf simv* csrc* S*
vcs cpu_1.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 -distsim
-P ../mypli.tab | & tee vcs.log0 &
vcs cpu_2.v -sverilog -full64 -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1 -distsim
-P ../mypli.tab | & tee vcs.log1 &

mkdir S0
mkdir S1

$VCS_HOME/bin/simv.distsim
-distsim=num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping,server_info:../server.txt
../server.log &

../simv0
- distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping,server_info:
../server.txt -l ../sim.log0 > ../client.log0 &

../simv1
- distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping,server_info:
../server.txt -l ../sim.log1 > ../client.log1 &

The script launches the server process for client ID 0 and 1. In the example,
• `VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE forces the value of signal a22 at current time to signal a11 of
mysim0 simv which has client id 0 at the coming nearest distsim sync point.
• `VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE deposits the value of signal b22 at current time to signal b11
of mysim0 simv which has client id 0 at the coming nearest distsim sync point.
• `VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE releases the signal cpu_1.a11 of client id 0 at the
coming nearest distsim sync point.
The following example displays a Verilog source (cpu_1.v) where it tries to read the
cpu_2.big_signal signal from simv2 (cpu2.v):
include "vcsdistsim_pkg.sv"
import vcsdistsim_pkg::*;

typedef logic [1023:0] uvm_hdl_data_t;

module cpu_1(
I_1_1,
O_1_1);

input wire [76:0][3:0] I_1_1;
output logic [76:0][3:0] O_1_1;

bit status_cpu_1;
uvm_hdl_data_t value;

#5;
vcsdistsim_hdl_read("S1", "cpu_2.big_signal", status_cpu_1, value);
$display("Value after taskcall at time: %0t is: %h", $time, value);
//rest of the source file.
The following displays the cpu_2.v Verilog source:
`include "vcsdistsim_pkg.sv"
import vcsdistsim_pkg::*;

module cpu_2(
I_1_1,
O_1_1);

input wire [76:0][3:0] I_1_1;
output logic [76:0][3:0] O_1_1;

#5;

big_signal[1023:0] = 1024'h DEADBEEFDEADBEEFDEADBEEFDEADBEEF; // Assign
a pattern to the lower 1024 bits
big_signal[2047:1024] = 1024'hCAFEBABECAFEBABECAFEBABECAFEBABE; //
Assign a pattern to the upper 1024 bits
//rest of the source file.
Run the following commands:
mkdir s0
cd s0
vcs ../cpu_1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:0
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -o simv0 -Mdir=csrc0 |& tee
vcs.log.0
./simv0
-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf
o:../server.txt -l sim0.log -distsim=launch_server |& tee client.log.0 &

mkdir s1
cd s1
vcs ../cpu_2.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -distsim=client_id:1
-distsim=config_file:../mapping.txt -P ../pli.tab -o simv1 -Mdir=csrc1
|& tee vcs.log.1
./simv1
-distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf
o:../server.txt -l sim1.log |& tee client.log.1 &
The cpu_2.big_signal signal is defined in cpu2.v. At 5 time units,
vcsdistsim_hdl_read asks the client S1 to read the signal named cpu_2.big_signal.

• <value Expr> is any valid Verilog expression. It requires debug-read capability and
you can enable it using the -debug_acc+r compile-time option.
• <isForce> is 1 for force freeze and 0 for deposit.
For example, consider label string mapping as follows:
hdl_label:CH2:2
hdl_label:CH3:3
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("CH2","socket2.a2", a1, 0);
Release
To release a signal from any other client simv, use the following macro in the Verilog
source:
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE(<Label String> , <signal Name>)
• <Label String> is the unique string label for the destination client.
• <signal Name> is the hierarchical path for the destination signal. It requires debug-
force capability. To enable debug-force capability, use the selective capability using PLI
tab, or use the -debug_acc+f compile-time option.
For example, consider label string mapping as follows:
hdl_label:CH2:2
hdl_label:CH3:3
#10 `VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE("CH3", socket3.a2");
Checking HDL Signal Paths
The vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path API checks hierarchical path of HDL signals across
client simvs. This behavior is similar to the behavior of uvm_hdl_check_path in the UVM
testbench. However, the API call returns only after reaching the synchronization point in
the client simvs.
To check HDL signal paths in UVM designs running with Distributed Simulation, use the
following functions:
vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path(<Client Label>, <Target Signal Name>, <Status
Bit>)

• <Client Label> : A unique string that identifies the destination client.
• <Target Signal Name> : The full hierarchical path to the destination signal.
• <Status Bit> : A signal from the user design. It is set to ‘1’ when the target signal is
found in the destination client.
The vcsdistsim_hdl_check_path API is called from the test case to check if a signal
exists in your design.
Reading HDL Signal Paths
The vcsdistsim_hdl_read API reads HDL signal paths across client simvs. This
behavior is similar to the behavior of uvm_hdl_read in the UVM testbench. However, the
API call returns only after reaching the synchronization point in the client simvs.
To read HDL signal paths in UVM designs running with Distributed Simulation, use the
following functions:
vcsdistsim_hdl_read(<Client Label>, <Target Signal Name>, <Status Bit>,
<Read Buffer>)
• <Client Label> : A unique string that identifies the destination client.
• <Target Signal Name> : The full hierarchical path to the destination signal.
• <Status Bit> : A signal from the user design. It is set to ‘1’ when the target signal is
found in the destination client.
• <Read Buffer> : Buffer provided by the user design. If the target signal exists in the
destination client, this buffer is filled with the value of that signal. The Read Buffer uses
a logic data type, such as uvm_hdl_data_t. By default, its size is 1024 bits.
The key behavior of vcsdistsim_hdl_read is as follows:
• The vcsdistsim_hdl_read API is called from the test case to check if a signal exists
and read its value.
• The default read size for reading a signal using vcsdistsim_hdl_read is 1024 bits.
You need to define <Read Buffer> as logic [1023:0] Read_Buffer .
• If the target signal is bigger than 1024 bits, only the least significant 1024 bits are read
(same as uvm_hdl_read).
• To read larger signals, define read buffer with a size greater than 1024 bits. Use the
VCSDISTSIM_READ_ARRAY_SIZE macro to set the size. You can set this macro with the
+define option at compile time.

When you call these APIs, the source client gets the status of the target signal (and
its value, if you use the read API) at the next synchronization point. For example, if
synchronization happens every 5 time units and Client0 calls the API at time 7, the

Compile time: You need to ensure that the correct debug capabilities are enabled for the
signals involved in distributed calls. You must pass the -distsim option in your vlogan
command to activate distributed simulation support. During compilation, include both
-distsim and -distsim=config_file:<path> options. The configuration file specifies
which signals require debug capabilities such as force or read.
For specific HDL operations,
• HDL force: Signals used in force operations must have the force capability enabled.
• HDL read or path check: Signals used in read or path check operations require read
capability.
To enable these capabilities, use one of the following ways:
• Pass an appropriate tab file during compilation, which selectively assigns the required
debug capabilities to the relevant signals or modules.
• Use the -debug_access+f option when force macros are used, or -debug_access+r
when only read or path check calls are needed.
To enable the HDL access across simvs, use the selective capability using PLI tab or use
the -debug_access+f compile-time option. It does not require configuration file support.
Runtime: For this feature, no extra option is required.
Configuration file: The following is the syntax for the configuration file:
hdl_label:<label>:clientID
Where, <label> is specified in the macro call to map it to the destination client ID.
The following example displays a Verilog source demonstrating the usage of HDL access:
#1;
a22 = 100;
b22[31:0] = 32'h33;
b22[63:32] = 32'h77;
c22 = 1;
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("mysim0", "cpu_1.a11", a22, 1);
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_FORCE("mysim0", "cpu_1.b11", b22, 0);

#5;
`VCSDISTSIM_HDL_RELEASE("mysim0", "cpu_1.a11");
end

The HDL Access Across Simvs feature has the following limitation:
• This feature does not support the following data types: memory, real, time, memword,
and dynamic types.
HDL Access Across Simvs Using PLI Source
You can use HDL access to provide force, deposit, or release on the signals using a
PLI call. To enable this feature, Distsim supports the available APIs. The following PLI
functions are available:
Force and Deposit
To force a signal from any other client simv, use the following macro in the PLI source:
vcsdistsim_hdl_force_pli_call (char* label, char* targetsignal, char*
data, int is_force)
• <label> is a unique string label for the destination client.
• <targetsignal> is the hierarchical path for the destination signal.
• <data> is string with vpiBinStrVal (a binary string).
• <is_force> is 1 for force freeze and 0 for deposit.
Release
To release a signal from any other client simv, use the following macro in the PLI source:
vcsdistsim_hdl_release_pli_call(char* label, char* targetsignal)
• <label> is the unique string label for the destination client.
• <targetsignal> is the hierarchical path for the destination signal.
Compile time: Additional Distsim options are not required. For HDL connection, to enable
force capability, use selective capability using PLI tab, or use the -debug_access+f
compile-time option. Follow the same compile-time options used for HDL Access Across
Simvs Using Verilog Source.
Runtime: Additional Distsim options are not required. You must follow the same compile-
time options used for HDL Access Across Simvs Using Verilog Source.

Configuration file: You must add the HDL label in the HDL Verilog macros. . Refer to the
HDL Access Across Simvs Using Verilog Source section for details on configuration file.
Consider the following PLI example with two client simvs, cpu_1 and cpu_2. cpu_2 is with
PLI source and wants to access DUT signals from cpu_1:
pli_example.c

#include "sv_vpi_user.h"
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

void dsim_force_cpu1()
{
vcsdistsim_hdl_force_pli_call("0", "cpu_1.a2", "10", 1);
}

void dsim_force_cpu1()
{
vcsdistsim_hdl_force_pli_call("0", "cpu_1.a1", "101", 0);
}

void dsim_release_cpu1()
{
vcsdistsim_hdl_release_pli_call("0", "cpu_1.a3");
}

mypli.tab:
$dsim_force_cpu1 call=dsim_force_cpu1
$dsim_deposit_cpu1 call=dsim_deposit_cpu1
$dsim_release_cpu1 call=dsim_release_cpu1
• dsim_force_cpu1() calls vcsdistsim_hdl_force_pli_call to force the signal
cpu_1.a2 to the value 10 on the distributed simulation client labeled "0". The client
label, "0", corresponds to cpu_1.
• dsim_force_cpu1() calls vcsdistsim_hdl_force_pli_call to deposit the signal
cpu_1.a1 to the value 101 on the distributed simulation client labeled "0". The client
label, "0", corresponds to cpu_1.
• dsim_release_cpu1() calls vcsdistsim_hdl_release_pli_call to release (remove
the force from) the signal cpu_1.a3 on the distributed simulation client labeled "0",
that is cpu_1.

• The PLI table file, mypli.tab, maps user-defined system tasks in Verilog (for example,
$dsim_force_cpu1) to the corresponding C functions.
• When you invoke $dsim_force_cpu1 in the Verilog code, VCS calls the
dsim_force_cpu1() C function. Similarly, $dsim_release_cpu1 in Verilog calls
dsim_release_cpu1() in C.
The following is the configuration file:
s0:cpu_1.clk_1
s1:cpu_2.clk_1

s1:cpu_2.I_1_1 = s0:cpu_1.O_1_1

hdl_label:0:0
hdl_label:1:1
Where, s0 and s1 define simulation clients (partitions), each with their own clock and
associated with a Verilog module (cpu_1 and cpu_2). The mapping connects an output
of cpu_1 to an input of cpu_2 across the distributed simulation. The hdl_label assigns
labels to the simulation clients, which are referenced in the C code as "0" and "1".
Run the following compile-time commands:
mkdir S0
mkdir S1

vcs ../cpu_1.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim -debug_access+f

vcs ../cpu_2.v -sverilog -full64 -distsim ../pli_example.c
-P ../mypli.tab

-distsim=client_id:0,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf
o:../server.txt -distsim=launch_server &

-distsim=client_id:1,num_sockets:2,config_file:../mapping.txt,server_inf
o:../server.txt &

Testbench synchronization in VCS Distributed Simulation ensures coordinated operation
of multiple simulation executables (simvs) in distributed environments, critical for verifying
complex SoC designs. The distributed simulation includes features, such as phase
synchronization and data transfer of class objects. These features help to keep the
testbench in synchronization for tasks, such as functional reset and checking data
consistency across different dies during verification.
• Testbench Phase Synchronization
• Testbench Data Transfer of Class Objects
Testbench Phase Synchronization
The testbench phase synchronization is a way to synchronize phases (predefined or user-
defined phases) in the OVM, UVM, or SystemVerilog Testbench environments. The phase
change information is communicated across simvs at the nearest sync point only. Even
when you use testbench phase synchronization, simulation continues to run as usual.
• Generic Testbench Phase Synchronization
• Phase Synchronization for All UVM Runtime Phases
• Configuring Selective Clients
• Flush Phase
Generic Testbench Phase Synchronization
Use generic testbench phase synchronization when you want to synchronize a few UVM
phases or selected testbenches at a particular stage. To synchronize or block a phase
until all client simvs attain the specified simulation phase, you must add a VCS API
macro in the Verilog source. This API macro must be added at each place where phase
synchronization is required in your Verilog files. These places are called Switch Points.
Verilog Source Code
Add the `VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC macro in the Verilog source code at each point where
phase synchronization is required. The macro is added in the testbench at each switch
point to ensure synchronization across all clients.
`VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC(PHASE_NAME)

Where, PHASE_NAME is the string used for synchronizing phase across the clients.
During simulation, the VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC macro ensures that all worker simvs wait
until the specified synchronization point is reached.
By default, the API macro is considered for phase synchronization at each phase. You
can also specify it in the configuration file if certain phases are to be synchronized among
some specific clients.
Compile time and runtime: No additional options are required during compilation and
The following example shows how to use the VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC macro in a Verilog
testbench:
task run_phase();
…
//Phase Sync Point: SYNC1
`VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC("SYNC1");
…
//Phase Sync Point: SYNC2
`VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC("SYNC2");
In this example,
• SYNC1 and SYNC2 are strings used for synchronizing phase across the clients.
• The macro VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC("SYNC1") ensures that all worker simvs wait
until they reach the synchronization point labeled SYNC1.
• After all clients reach SYNC1, they proceed to the next phase.
• Similarly, the macro VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC("SYNC2") ensures synchronization at
the next phase.
• Clients resume when all worker simvs have switched phases.
Macro VCSDISTSIM_PHASE_SYNC waits until all worker simvs reach same phase or stage
(that is, first all worker simvs wait until sync point reaches SYNC1, then they block for
SYNC2). Clients resume when all worker simvs have switched phases.
To synchronize the default UVM Phases, the distsim macro is added
in the phase_ready_to_end() methodology function of the UVM. If the
phase_ready_to_end methodology function is called multiple times, only the
first call is honored.

Generic testbench phase synchronization has the following limitations:
• Multiple UVM components syncing to different phases is not supported for TB Phase
Synchronization.
• Jump backward or forward of UVM Phases is not supported for TB Phase
Synchronization; and cross UVM phase synchronization (synchronizing a phase
of one client with another phase of different clients) is not supported for TB Phase
Synchronization.
Phase Synchronization for All UVM Runtime Phases
To synchronize all UVM runtime phases, use the UVM Testbench Phase Synchronization
feature, which allows you to start the default UVM runtime phases together in all simvs.
Verilog Source Code
To apply implicit UVM phase synchronization, you must add a predefined UVM component
dist_tbsync_comp in the user environment.
The dist_tbsync_comp component adds automatic UVM switch point for all
predefined UVM runtime phases across simvs. That is, the reset_phase of all clients is
synchronized. Similarly, the main_phase is also synchronized across all clients. The next
runtime phase starts only after the current phase is completed across all clients.
The following example displays how to create the dist_tbsync_comp component in the
user environment:
class test_env extends uvm_env;
dist_tbsync_comp comp0;
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); super.build_phase(phase);
comp0 = dist_tbsync_comp::type_id::create("comp0",this);
Configuring Selective Clients
For the testbench phase synchronization, all clients must have distsim phase
synchronization macro at the required places. However, if you want only a few clients to
synchronize, you must use this feature.
Configuration file: To use this feature, configure the testbench phase synchronization
using the following configuration file syntax:
sync_phase=<Phase_Name>::s<Client_ID_i>:s<Client_ID_j>

Where, Client_ID_i, Client_ID_j are the clients where Phase_Name is to be
synchronized. Phase_Name is the name of the user-defined/OVM/UVM Phase which must
be defined in the specified client.
If a phase is not specified, it means that all phases are synchronization.
Each phase that you want to synchronize must have a unique Phase_Name.
Compile time and Runtime: No additional options are required during compilation and
Consider three Clients, s0, s1 and s2, and phases P1, P2, and P3.
The following configuration file specifies phases to synchronize:
master_sync_signal: test.mid.clock_sig

s1:<sig_path2> = s0:<sig_path1>
s2:<sig_path2> = s1:<sig_path1>
s0:<sig_path4> = s1:<sig_path3>

sync_phase=P1::s0:s1
sync_phase=P2::s1:s2
In this example, P1 is synchronized between s0 and s1, and P2 is synchronized between
s1 and s2. Therefore, no phase synchronization macro is used in s2. Because P3 is not
specified, it synchronizes with all the clients, s0, s1, and s2).
Flush Phase
To specify a specific user-defined phase after which the testbench phase synchronization
is stopped, use the following option:
-distsim=end_phase:<FLUSH_PHASE>
FLUSH_PHASE is common among all the clients testbenches. The order of phases remains
identical in clients testbenches.
Testbench Data Transfer of Class Objects
Testbench Data Transfer of Class Objects refers to the capability in to send and receive
SystemVerilog class-based objects, such as UVM transactions, sequences, or other user-
defined class objects, between different clients simvs during a distributed simulation run.

• Testbench Send and Receive Calls
• Release Receive Call for TB Data Transfer
• Support for Multiple TB Data Receive Requests
• TB Data Open Channels
• Testbench Data Transfer With C-Based Client
Testbench Send and Receive Calls
The testbench data transfer uses a one-on-one transfer method, that is, for every send
call there is one receive call. These calls are mapped using a unique channel name string
whose mapping is provided in the configuration file. The testbench data is transmitted or
received with respect to the nearest sync point.
VCS supports only bit arrays for TB data transactions.
For testbench data transfer, perform the following:
1. Specify the configuration file for the testbench data transfer connections across the
clients.
2. Use VCS APIs for testbench data send and data receive with channel name as bit
array. If you are using UVM or OVM, you can create bit array using the pack()
method on the send side and the unpack() method on the receive side of the
testbench.
Verilog Source Code
To send transaction, use the VCSDISTSIM_TB_SEND("Channel_name", bit_array)
macro.
Channel_name: This is a unique constant channel string name corresponding to data
transfer.
bit_array: This is a user-defined dynamic array of bits containing data to be sent.
To receive transaction, use the VCSDISTSIM_TB_RECV("Channel name", bit_array)
macro.
Channel_name: A unique constant channel string name corresponding to data transfer.

bit_array: This is a user-defined dynamic array of bits in which data is received.
You must include the vcsdistsim_pkg.sv file and import this package file at the global
level so that it is parsed before the macros in the test environment.
`include "vcsdistsim_pkg.sv"
Import vcsdistsim_pkg::*
Configuration file: The following is the configuration file syntax for testbench data
transfer:
tbtrans=<source_channel_name>:s<source_client_id>::<destination_channel_n
ame>:s<destination_client_id>
Where, source_channel_name and destination_channel_name are the strings used in
the Verilog system task distsim and source_client_id and destination_client_id
are the respective client IDs.
Compile time: For the Testbench Data Transfer feature, the -distsim and
-distsim=config_file:<file_name> options are required.
Runtime: No additional runtime option is required.
The following configuration file example shows testbench transfer between clients:
master_sync_signal: test.mid.clock_sig

s1:<sig_path2> = s0:<sig_path1>
s2:<sig_path2> = s1:<sig_path1>
s0:<sig_path4> = s1:<sig_path3>

tbtrans=CH1:s1::CH0:s2
tbtrans=CH3:s0::CH6:s2
tbtrans=CH4:s1::CH5:s3
Signal tbtrans=CH1:s1::CH0:s2 implies channel CH1 in the send call of Client 1 is to be
received by channel CH0 in the receive call of Client 2.
Signal tbtrans=CH3:s0::CH6:s2 implies channel CH3 in the send call of Client 0 is to be
received by channel CH6 in the receive call of Client 2.

Testbench Send and Receive Calls has the following limitations:
• Class member objects must have static size. Nested classes are supported.
• If dynamic members are present, you must unpack them accordingly. You can get
packing or unpacking into or from a dynamic array using the user-defined UVM
do_pack()/do_unpack() methods.
• A sender cannot have multiple receivers.
• Make sure your testbench data objects are compatible for transfer.
Release Receive Call for TB Data Transfer
When you use `VCSDISTSIM_TB_RECV_RELEASE(Channel_Name) to release any existing
TB data receive call, 'VCSDISTSIM_TB_RECV("Channel_Name", bit_array) in the
design, the following things happen:
• Release the wait in the receive call for the specified channel.
• When there is no active receive call for the specified channel, then no action is
performed.
• When it is called in the same sync cycle, it takes precedence over Receive call.
Support for Multiple TB Data Receive Requests
The Support for Multiple TB Data Receive Requests feature allows you to attend Multiple
Receive Requests at a time on the same TB Channel. This feature is used when you are
expecting to receive the TB Data in the parallel Verilog threads simultaneously. By default,
the Support for Multiple TB Data Receive Requests feature is disabled.
To enable this feature, use the following option:
-distsim=multiple_same_channel_req
TB Data Open Channels
The channel used in TB Data Send and Receive calls are configured during runtime using
runtime flags or the Distsim connectivity file. However, if any channel is left open, it is
honored.
Open Channel For Sender
The open channel for sender implies that there is no receiver channel specified for it. The
call made by sender, VCSDISTSIM_TB_SEND, issues a warning, ignores the data to be sent,
and continues the simulation.

Open Channel For Receiver
The open channel for receiver implies that there is no sender channel specified for it. The
call made by receiver, VCSDISTSIM_TB_RECV, keeps waiting in the Receive call, issues a
warning, and blocks the corresponding TB Receive thread.
You can use VCSDISTSIM_TB_RECV_RELEASE to unblock the thread
corresponding to that channel.

Before using the C APIs, you must initialize them. The following example shows how to
initialize APIs:
static int initialize_functions()
{
void* handle = dlopen("libvcsdistsimuser.so", RTLD_NOW);
if (!handle) {
fprintf(stderr, "Error: %s\n", dlerror());
std::cout<<"Handle Not Present"<<std::endl;
return EXIT_FAILURE;
}
*(void**)(&vcsdistsim_init) = dlsym(handle, "vcsdistsim_init");
assert(vcsdistsim_init);
*(void**)(&vcsdistsim_sync) = dlsym(handle, "vcsdistsim_sync");
assert(vcsdistsim_sync);
*(void**)(&vcsdistsim_send) = dlsym(handle, "vcsdistsim_send");
assert(vcsdistsim_send);
*(void**)(&vcsdistsim_recv) = dlsym(handle, "vcsdistsim_recv");
assert(vcsdistsim_recv);
*(void**)(&vcsdistsim_finish) = dlsym(handle, "vcsdistsim_finish");
assert(vcsdistsim_finish);
}
• dlopen loads the shared library at runtime.
• dlsym retrieves the address of each API function.
• assert ensures that each function pointer is valid.
This setup allows your C client to call the Distsim APIs as regular functions.
int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
if (initialize_functions() != 0) {
}

//Initiliaze API to connect with other DistSim Clients
vcsdistsim_init(argv[1], true);

//Push the data needed to sent to respective channels
vcsdistsim_send("CH10", bit_array, size);

//Synchronize with other Distsim clients to send and recv the data on
channels
vcsdistsim_sync();

//Put data on array from data received on channels in previous
synchronization
vcsdistsim_recv("CH11", &bit_array_recvd, &size_recvd);

//Finish call to terminate DistSim connections
vcsdistsim_finish();
}
You must define mapping between Verilog and C-clients in the configuration file as shown
in the following example where s0 and s1 are Verilog clients and s2 is a C-based client:
master_sync_signal:s0:cpu_1.clk_1
master_sync_signal:s1:cpu_2.clk_2

s1:cpu_2.I_1_1 = s0:cpu_1.O_1_1

tbtrans=CH0:s1::CH1:s0
tbtrans=CH10:s2::CH11:s0
tbtrans=CH10:s0::CH11:s2
In the example, s2 is not associated with the master_sync_signal, but with the testbench
transfer calls. The synchronization occurs with every call to the vcsdistsim_sync()
Debugging distributed simulation in VCS involves several features and options designed
to help you identify, analyze, and resolve issues that may arise when simulating multiple
SoCs or modules across different simulation executables (simvs).
For selective debug capabilities, you can use the compile-time configuration file support
by passing -distsim=config_file:<mapping.txt> at compile time. This enables debug
capabilities only on the relevant signals specified in the configuration file, avoiding global
debug overhead.
The following are the key debugging options and features:
• VCD Dump per Client
• Distributed Simulation Profile
• Configuration File Checker Utility
• Cygnus PDF Profile Summary

• Save Replay Support
• Save Restore Support
• User Task to Print Class Objects
VCD Dump per Client
Using the VCD Dump per Client feature, you can dump the load and driver DUT
connection signals of the Distributed Simulation configuration file in the VCD format. You
can load DUT connection signals into Verdi to view the waveform and can debug these
files using the nCompare and vcdiff features.
Runtime: To enable this feature, use the -distsim=diag:dumpvars runtime option.
By default, it dumps the VCD file per Client in the current simulation directory. You can
also specify the path for dumping the VCD file using the following runtime option:
-distsim=log_dir:<Directory_path>
Distributed Simulation Profile
The Distributed Simulation Profile feature dumps a time profile at the end of simulation
irrespective of the exit status. For each Client, the profile is dumped at the end of
the simulation log. For the Server process, the profile is dumped into a separate file,
cygnus.profile.txt. This file is created in the working directory of the master client.
This feature compares the synchronization time taken by different clients with the elapsed
time for simulation. By default, it dumps profiles for all the processes.
The time profile contains the following information:
• Total elapsed time: It is total real elapsed time by the client.
• Initial time: It is the time spent from beginning till first sync.
• Active simulation time: It is the time elapsed in running simulation besides distsim
processing.
• Imbalance time: It is the total time spent while waiting for other clients to reach the
distributed simulation sync points.
• Process time: It is the time spent in fetching and sending the data.
• Wait time: It is the time spent in waiting for messages as well as in network calls.

The following example displays the performance summary of a client with 1 as <Client
id>:
----------------------------------------------
Performance Summary for Client: 1
Safe Finish with PID: 25325
Total Sync Points: 2001

In the example, the Safe Finish with PID field displays the process ID and the Total
Sync Points field displays the total number of synchronizations based on the master-
