The following sections describe the position, order, and naming of the features created:
Position of the New Feature(s)
* Create Features: The newly created features are the last child of the parent (selected
item).
* Create Sibling Features: The newly created sibling features are the closest sibling of
the selected item. This is also applicable for multiple selection support.
Order of the New Feature(s)
The order of new features is the same as the order in which you select the instances using
the Ctrl key. When you select multiple instances using the Shift key, the resultant features
are ordered top-to-bottom.
Naming of New Features
By default, the name of a new feature is the name of the instance from the design
hierarchy. However, if the name is a keyword in the HVP language such as test
or feature, it is renamed by adding a suffix _renamed. For example, if a feature is
created from an instance named feature, the feature that is created from it is named
feature_renamed. You are notified of this change with warning message similar to the
following one, in the message window.

'feature' is a keyword and cannot be used as a feature name. It is
renamed to 'feature_renamed'.

Specification Linking in Planner
Verdi Planner enables you to track a verification project and ensures that all its verification
goals are achieved. It allows you to create a hierarchical verification plan to measure what
is important for each project.
A linked and executable verification plan ties every part of the original written specification
and test plan documents to their corresponding verification goals.
The following figure shows how the verification specifications, plans, and data come
together to track progress and status of the verification project:

Links to the specifications ensure that every feature in the specification has a
corresponding feature in the plan.
Links to verification data ensure that anything below target (low coverage, tests failing, and
so on) is presented and linked to the corresponding features to highlight needed actions.

Specification Linking Count
Verdi Coverage provides a set of link count attributes with the spec_link_count prefix.
These attributes identify all linked specifications with a plan. These attributes show the
number of links to a feature or sub-feature from a given specification document. These
attributes are automatically created when you associate specifications with the plan. You
can link the plan with more than one specification.
The number of associated specifications determines the number of spec_link_count
attributes in the plan. Each specification generates only one spec_link_count attribute.

The initial value of this attribute is zero. It gets updated when a plan feature links to or
unlinks from the specification. You cannot edit this attribute. It is automatically populated
when the specification is linked with its associated text.
When you associate a specification file with a plan, Verdi Coverage generates the
spec_link_count_<filename> attribute. This attribute counts the number of links in the
specification from the plan. The type of this attribute is integer. Its propagation is set to no.
The value does not propagate to the child node. The attribute is available in the Hvp pane
and in the Attributes section of the HvpDetail pane as shown in the following figure:

You can use the spec_link_count attribute for quick filtering and for creating modifiers,
like any other integer-valued attribute. To use the spec_link_count attribute, filter only
the features that link to a specific specification. For example, consider the following filter
statement:
remove feature where spec_link_count_my_doc == 0;

In the example, the statement creates a filtered plan with only features that link to the
my_doc specification.
For details on filters and modifiers, see the Using Modifiers section.

Excluding Ignore Sections From the Specification Coverage
Computation
Computing specification coverage for all features in the specification requires them to be
verified against the corresponding features in the verification plans. Normally for SoClevel testing, it is not required to verify IP-level features; therefore, these features of the
specification are not relevant for calculating specification coverage. Using specification
linking, you can search for these irrelevant sections in the entire specification and mark
them as ignored.
Previously, specification total lines were used as a denominator for calculating
specification coverage as follows:
Denominator = Total Lines
Uncovered Lines = Total Lines - Linked Lines - Todo Lines - Ignored Lines

Now, specification linking can exclude ignored sections from the specification total lines
and use its result as a denominator for calculating coverage as follows:
Denominator = Total Lines - Ignored Lines
Uncovered Lines = Total Lines - Linked Lines - Todo Lines - Ignored Lines

Color Settings of a Verification Plan
Verdi enables you to update the color settings of verification plans, their sub-plans,
specification linking colors, and coverage colors. To update the color settings, perform the
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences form.
2. In the Plan View Category, select Spec Colors or Plan Colors as per your
requirement:

Select Plan Colors to update the color settings of sub-plans, inactive cells, warning
and error messages, and an invalid score of an item in the Hvp pane.

Specification Linking With Coverage-Based Color Coding
The coverage-based color coding feature in Verdi Coverage enhances the visualization
of linked sections in specification documents. This feature assigns distinct colors to linked
sections based on the coverage score of the associated feature, making it easier to
identify uncovered, partially covered, and fully covered sections.
Follow these steps to enable and configure coverage-based color coding in specification
linking:
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the Plan View category, select Spec Colors. Select the Enable color coding for
linked sections check box. By default, it is deselected.

Figure 100

Color Coding for Linked Sections

3. Set the Threshold score(%) to define the boundary between partial coverage levels.
For example:
Uncovered: 0.00% coverage.
Partial Covered #1: Coverage between 0.00% and T.
Partial Covered #2: Coverage between T and 100.00%.
Fully Covered: 100.00% coverage.
4. Assign colors to each coverage level. Use the color picker in the Application
Preferences dialog box to select your preferred colors.
5. Click OK to save your preferences.
This feature is useful for quickly identifying the coverage status of individual features and
their linked sections in the plan view. The annotated overall score for each HVP feature
is divided into four levels 0.00%, (0.00%, T), (T, 100.00%), and 100.00%. If the plan does
not have an overall annotated score, the feature is ignored, and all linked sections use the
default color scheme. Sections linked to multiple features or overlapping linked sections
display an accumulated color. For example, overlapping light green sections appear as
dark green.

Figure 101

Overlapping Colors

Running a Specification Review
When you have an updated specification, you can update and review the linked
specification in the Spec Review Window.
There might be some mismatched and missing sections of the linking features between
the new and linked specifications. In these cases, unresolved sections have to be
reviewed.

The following sections describe how you can use this feature to perform the specification
review.

Using the Specification Review Flow
To start reviewing a specification, select a plan in the HVP tab and perform the following
steps:
1. Select the linked specification you want to inspect and review it in the Spec Files tab of
the HvpDetail pane. Refer to Figure Select a New Specification.
2. Click the
icon and select the specification file you want to compare in the invoked
Choose a spec file dialog box.
3. Click the Open button.
Figure 102

Select a New Specification

4. The Spec Review Window form opens with the comparison between the current and
the new specifications. An example is shown in Figure Spec Review Window.

Figure 103

Spec Review Window

The status field of the selected current specification is changed to Updating.
Figure 104

Status Field

The Current spec and New spec fields show the paths of the current and new
specifications.
The Review Summary field (as shown in Figure Review Summary) in the Spec Review
Window shows how many unresolved sections need to be reviewed, including mismatched
and missing ones.
Figure 105

Review Summary

The matched, unmatched, new, or missing sections or lines are identified. The current

Reviewing Specifications
In the Spec Review Window, you can click the Previous or Next button to find out and
check the previous or next unresolved section.
After checking it, you can use the Accept or Reject buttons to accept or reject the
mappings of the mismatched section links from the current specification to the new one.
For missing sections, you can only use the Reject button to reject it.
You can also use the Accept All and Reject All buttons to accept and reject all
unresolved sections.
After you accept or reject a mapped section, the Review Summary field is also updated
accordingly to show one less unresolved section.
After all the unresolved sections are reviewed and either accepted or rejected, the
Matched number in the Review Summary field displays 0 and disappears to signify that
there are no more updated sections to review.
You can click the Close button to stop review in the invoked Spec Review form.
When your review has no remaining conflicts, the following dialog box opens.

If you want to accept the updates during the review, click the Accept button. The linked
specification in the HVP planner is updated to the new one.
If you want to cancel updating the specification, you can click the Revert button to cancel
all decisions (accepted or rejected) made in this reviewing.
The linked specification remains the original one. The status is changed to `Linked' after
clicking either Accept or Revert the buttons.
Figure 109

Linked Status

Click Cancel to return to the review window.
When a review still has some unresolved sections, the following dialog box opens.

icon to continue the review

Click the Revert button to stop the review and revert the linked specification to the
previous version. You can also click the Cancel button to return to the current review. You

can click the review undo icon in the Hvp pane to undo the following actions during the
review:
* Start a specification review with a new specification
* Review all unresolved sections.
* Complete the review and the old specification is replaced by the new one.
Limitations of the Specification Review Flow
Only text in a document can be selected manually. This excludes text that cannot be
selected in tables. Images can also not be selected manually.

Measure Concealment in Reports
Currently, HVP provides the flexibility to create multiple measures and metric sources
within features. Though this flexibility is useful for many HVP use models, it might produce
complex reports for simple models. HVP is now enhanced to simplify usage and reporting
for portions of the plan that follow a simplified pattern of a single source for each feature.
This is referred to as a 1:1:1 feature because one feature contains one measure and one
source.

You can conceal a measure in a report if a feature qualifies the 1:1:1 compression. Verdi
can infer from the structure of the feature whether it is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression.
To qualify for the compression, the feature should meet the following criteria:
1. The feature is a leaf feature, that is, it does not contain any subfeature.
2. The feature contains exactly one measure.
3. The measure contains exactly one source.
4. The source name should not contain wildcard and regular expressions.
For example, the following feature is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression:
feature cd;
Metrics = "Line, Cond";
measure test Measure_1;
source = "cd";

The HVP planner cannot store items that it does not recognize. The following are the
various ways to generate XML files which can be loaded to Verdi:
* Use the command Save As to save an XML file without the skipped contents. See
Saving the Plan.
* Use the command hvp genxls -plan <plan_file> to generate an XML file without

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The csv2hvp_DPTX.py utility converts a CSV verification plan into an XML Spreadsheet
2003 file for use with Verdi Coverage and Verdi Verification Management System (VMS).
When VCS_HOME is set, the utility also runs hvp annotate to produce an HVP plan file that
can be loaded in Verdi Coverage.
This methodology converts a verification plan into the HVP format supported by Verdi
VMS. The utility generates the Excel XML plan and hvp annotate converts that XML
to HVP. Loading the plan into Verdi Coverage or uploading it to VMS is a separate step.
For details on annotation and loading Excel XML plans, see User Data As a Spreadsheet
Worksheet and Generating the HVP Excel XML Plan With Report.
The output is a standard Excel XML plan, not the extended loadable report format
produced by hvp genxls -report or Verdi Coverage save-report with Loadable set to
Yes. For details on the loadable report format, see Generating the HVP Excel XML Plan
With Report.
* Prerequisites
* Running the Utility
* Plan Data CSV Format
* Attribute Definition CSV (Optional)
* Attribute Name Sanitization Rules
* Output Files
* Limitations
* Loading the Generated Plan in Verdi Coverage

Prerequisites
Before running the utility, ensure that the following prerequisites are met:
* Python 3.x
* VCS_HOME environment variable set. This is required only for automatic .hvp file
generation. When VCS_HOME is not set, only the .xml output is produced.
For VCS and Verdi Coverage version compatibility when loading generated plans, see
User Data As a Spreadsheet Worksheet.

Running the Utility
Run the utility from the command line as follows:
python3 csv2hvp_DPTX.py \
-input_file_path <plan_csv_file> \
-output_dir <output_directory> \
[-attr_def_file_path <attribute_definition_csv_file>]

The following table describes the command arguments:
Table 11

Argument

Path to the input CSV file
containing the verification plan
data.

.xml (and .hvp if VCS is
available) files are written.
The directory is created
automatically if it does not

Path to a CSV file containing
attribute type definitions. If
omitted, all attributes are

python3 csv2hvp_DPTX.py \
-input_file_path /home/user/plans/dptx_plan.csv \
-output_dir /home/user/plans/output \

Example (Windows)

title: Verification ContinuumTM

Plan Data CSV Format
Save all CSV files in CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited) format.

The plan data CSV must meet the following requirements:
* Must contain a column named Title (case-insensitive). This is the primary feature
name column.
* Additional columns named Subtitle are treated as sub-feature hierarchy levels.
Multiple Subtitle columns from left to right represent feature hierarchy from top to
bottom.
* Columns prefixed with measure or value are passed through as-is (VMS metric
columns).
* All other columns are treated as attributes and are sanitized (spaces become
underscores; special characters are removed).
* Rows where all feature columns are empty are skipped.
The Title and Subtitle column names are CSV input conventions. The generated Excel
XML plan uses HVP feature columns for the feature hierarchy.

Attribute Definition CSV (Optional)
An optional attribute definition CSV defines the type and default value for each custom
attribute. The following column headings are expected:
Table 12

Attribute Definition CSV Columns

Column Heading

Required

Attribute Name

Yes

Must match a column heading in the plan
CSV.

Attribute Type

Yes

One of: string, integer, real, date,
enum{val1,val2,}, set{val1,val2,}

Default Value

No

Default value for the attribute. Required for
enum, integer, and real types.

No

Free-text description of the attribute. For
details, see Descriptions for Attribute and
Metric Definitions.

Propagation

No

Whether to propagate the attribute (yes / no).
Defaults to no.

The following table describes the supported attribute types:
Table 13

Supported Attribute Types

Type

Notes

string

Plain text

integer

Whole number. The default is 0 if the value is missing or invalid.

real

Floating-point number. The default is 0 if the value is missing or
invalid.

date

Date value. The invalid formats are handled with a warning.

enum{}

Enumeration. The default must be one of the listed values.
UNKNOWN is added if the default is empty.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Multi-value set. The default is {} if empty. For details, see Set
Type Attribute.

Attribute Name Sanitization Rules
Custom attribute names from the CSV header are sanitized as follows before use in the
output:
* Spaces are replaced with underscores (_).
* Only alphanumeric characters and _ are kept.
* Names that clash with VMS built-in metric keywords are suffixed with _.
* VMS built-in default attributes (owner, description, weight, at_least,
test.expected) are handled automatically and are not redefined. For details on
test.expected, see Using Derived Test Metrics.
Sanitization applies to attribute columns only, not to Title or Subtitle feature names.

Output Files
The utility writes the following files to the output directory:
* <output_dir>/out_Test_Plan.xml : XML Spreadsheet 2003 file containing two
sheets:
Test_Plan : the processed plan data
Attribute definition : the attribute type definitions
* <output_dir>/out_Test_Plan.xml.hvp : HVP plan file, generated automatically
when VCS_HOME is set.
When VCS_HOME is not set in the environment, the .hvp generation step is skipped and
only the .xml output is produced.

Limitations
The utility has the following limitations:
* Does not generate metric definition sheets.
* Does not support subplans, include sheets, or feature-type definition sheets.
* Does not produce the extended loadable report format. See Generating the HVP Excel
XML Plan With Report.
* Does not support user-data (hvp userdata) worksheets.
* Does not support goal columns or skip columns or rows.

Loading the Generated Plan in Verdi Coverage
After the utility generates the Excel XML and HVP files, load the plan in Verdi Coverage
using one of the following methods:
* To open the HVP file, use Plan > Open Plan. See Loading a Predefined HVP File.
* To load the Excel XML plan, use Plan > Load Excel XML. See User Data As a
Spreadsheet Worksheet.
In VMS mode, the loaded plan is also uploaded to the VMS server. Annotated scores are
not loaded from the XML plan. For details, see Loading a Report.

1. Choose Plan > Save Plan As.

2. Select Excel XLSX Plan from the Filter list in the Save As dialog box.

Viewing Plan Metadata
A saved plan records the following save-time metadata:
* hvp_version: The HVP or plan version.
* tool_version: The version or build of the tool that actually wrote the file.
* tool_name: Which product or command path last wrote the output; for example, Verdi,
URG, hvpexport, HVP utilities (Doc Plan Generator or HVP gendoc, HVP genxls, HVP
annotate), HVP dump, and reports.
* options: Comma-separated relevant save or export options.
The metadata is saved in the following file formats:
* Native HVP
* Plan XML
* DOC XML
* Excel XML
Example 1

Metadata in a Native HVP Plan

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Metadata in an Excel XML Plan

//@hvp_meta hvp_version "Y-2026.03-SP1-1"
//@hvp_meta tool_version "Y-2026.03-SP1"
//@hvp_meta tool_name "verdi"
//@hvp_meta options "save"
plan top_plan;

endplan

<Workbook >
<x:HvpMetadata
hvp_version="Y-2026.03-SP1-1"
tool_version="Y-2026.03-SP1"
tool_name="hvp genxls"
options="save-as"/>

</Workbook>

Previous metadata is always overwritten with the latest tool and HVP versions.

Saving the Plan as Older Version
To export your current HVP plan to use in older Verdi releases, you can use the Plan >
Save Plan As Older Version command.

While saving the current HVP as a backward-compatible HVP, the following syntaxes
are guarded or hidden for backward compatibility. The GUI displays which information is
hidden.
* SDC metrics
* Mandatory property
* Attribute value of measure and source

The macro gates SDC measure items in a backward-compatible mode.
ifdef HVP_BACKWARD_COMPATIBLE_NEW_SYNTAX_ENABLE
measure Sdc, Sdc.partial_active_count, Toggle, Line
Measure_sdc_first;
else
measure Toggle, Line Measure_sdc_first;
endif

In the abobe example, if the macro HVP_BACKWARD_COMPATIBLE_NEW_SYNTAX_ENABLE
is defined, Verdi includes measures Sdc, Sdc.partial_active_count, Toggle, Line,
and Measure_sdc_first. However, if the macro is not defined, only Toggle, Line, and
Measure_sdc_first are included.

Retaining Original Measures in HVP Excel XML Export/Import
Verdi Coverage can export and import Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) files in the
Excel XML format. By default, when multiple measures within the same feature share
identical metric definitions, the export process merges these measures into a single entry
in the Excel XML file.
Use the hvp genxls -merge_measures option to control this behavior during Excel XML
export and when the file is imported back into Verdi Coverage:
* -merge_measures 1 (default): Merge measures in the same feature that share
identical metric definitions into a single Excel XML entry. After you load that file back
into Verdi Coverage, those measures appear as one measure and their sources are
merged.

* -merge_measures 0: Keep each measure as a separate entry with its own score
columns, even when multiple measures in the same feature use identical metric
definitions. Use this when you need separate coverage scores for each measure in the
generated Excel plan and when you want export and import to preserve the original
HVP measure list.
You can retain the original measures during the export and import process in the following
two ways:
* Using Command-Line
* Using Verdi Coverage GUI
Using Command-Line
Run the following command to export your HVP file to Excel XML format while retaining all
original measures, even if they share identical metric definitions within the same feature:
hvp genxls -plan HVP_Example.hvp.xml -merge_measures 0

For a description of -merge_measures 1 and -merge_measures 0, see the list above.
You can also run hvp genxls --help for command-line option details.
Using Verdi Coverage GUI
Perform the following steps to retain original measures using the Verdi Coverage GUI:
1. Open your plan in Verdi Coverage.
2. Select Plan > Save Plan As.
3. Set the Filter to Excel XML Plan (*.xml).
4. In the Additional options text field, enter -merge_measures 0 and click Save.

This field supports only two options: -merge_measures 1/0 and

-download_spec.

You can use the XML-to-HVP conversion feature to integrate readable Excel reports into
your Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) and Verdi coverage flow. This feature allows
you to convert between XML or XLSX report files and HVP files, enabling round-trip data
exchange in both file mode and Verification Management System (VMS) mode.
The standard Excel report generated by hvp genxls has limited readability and does not
support the VMS mode. The Verdi coverage Save report produces a more readable report
that supports the VMS mode, but it cannot be imported back into Verdi coverage or HVP.
This feature bridges that gap by providing a loadable report format that works seamlessly
across both flows.
The extended loadable report format described here is produced by hvp
genxls -report or Verdi Coverage save-report with Loadable set to Yes. To
create an HVP plan from a CSV verification plan, use the CSV-to-HVP utility.
See Converting a CSV Verification Plan to HVP.

* Expanded Report Format
* Saving and Loading Reports in Verdi Coverage
* Using the HVP Utility to Generate and Convert Reports

Expanded Report Format
The loadable report format extends the original XML report with additional content
to support round-trip conversion. The expanded report contains the top plan and all
subplans. Each top-plan and sub-plan includes the following sheets:

Plan Contents Sheet
Each plan contents sheet uses the naming convention [index]_[plan_name] and
contains the following information:
* Hierarchy index
* Plan, feature, measure, or source name
* Score of metrics with annotated data
* All selected columns, including goal of metrics and attributes
* Measure metrics that record the reference metrics of each measure
In VMS mode, feature names use the format [feature_name] or
[feature_type]:[feature_name] when the feature type is not "common".

User-Defined Metrics Definitions Sheet
The metrics definitions sheet uses the naming convention [index]_metrics and captures
the same information as the hvp genxls metrics output. It contains the following columns:
Table 14

User-Defined Metrics Definitions

Column

Name

The name of the user-defined metric.

Type

The type of the metric (for example, percent, ratio, real, or enum).

Aggregator

The aggregation method used for the metric.

Apply

The scope or context to which the metric applies.

Table 14

User-Defined Metrics Definitions (Continued)

Column

Goal

The target goal value for the metric.

User-Defined Attributes Definitions Sheet
The attributes definitions sheet uses the naming convention [index]_attributes
and captures the same information as the hvp genxls attributes output. It contains the
following columns:
Table 15

User-Defined Attributes Definitions

Column

Type

The data type of the attribute.

Propagated Status

Indicates whether the attribute is propagated.

Name

The name of the user-defined attribute.

Default Value

The default value assigned to the attribute.

Feature-Type Definition Sheet
The feature-type definition sheet uses the naming convention [index]_featuretype and
contains the following columns:
Table 16

Feature-Type Definitions

Column

Name

The name of the feature type.

Attribute Limit

The maximum number of attributes allowed for this feature type.

Child Limit

The maximum number of child elements allowed for this feature
type.

Saving and Loading Reports in Verdi Coverage
Verdi Coverage provides GUI options for saving and loading loadable report files. These
options allow you to export plans in a format that can be re-imported, enabling round-trip
workflows in both file mode and VMS mode.

Saving a Loadable Report
To save a plan as a loadable report in Verdi Coverage, perform the following steps:
1. Select Plan > Report from the menu.
The Report dialog box opens.
Figure 118

Saving a Loadable Report

2. In the Excel XML Format section, set the Loadable option to Yes.
The default setting for Loadable is No. When you select Yes, the following options are
automatically configured and disabled to ensure a valid loadable format:
Columns is set to Selected Columns
Separate Column is set to Description
Excel XML Export Level is set to Source
More Options includes Export Subplan
3. Select the desired File Format:
XML (default): Saves the file in XML format (.xml)
XLSX: Saves the file in XLSX format (.xlsx)
4. Click Export to save the report.

Loading a Report
To load a previously saved report into Verdi Coverage, perform the following steps:
1. Select Plan > Open Plan from the menu.
The Load dialog box opens.
Figure 119

Loading a Report

2. From the Filter drop-down list, choose one of the following:
Excel XML Plan (*.xml) to load a report XML file.
Excel XLSX Plan (*.xlsx) to load a report XLSX file.
3. Select the report file and click Open.
When loading a report, only HVP information is imported. Annotated scores are
not loaded. In VMS mode, the loaded plan is also uploaded to the VMS server.

Using the HVP Utility to Generate and Convert Reports
The HVP utility provides command-line options for converting between HVP files and
report XML/XLSX files. You can generate a report from an existing HVP plan, or convert a
report back into HVP files.

Converting HVP to Report XML
Use the hvp genxls command with the -report option to generate an extended report
XML file from an HVP plan.
File mode:
hvp genxls -plan <input_hvp> -report

VMS server mode:
hvp genxls -hvp_server <web_server_url:port> -hvp_proj <project_name>
-plan <plan_hier_name> -report

The following table describes the command arguments:
Table 17

hvp genxls -report Arguments

Argument

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Specifies the input HVP plan file (file mode) or the plan hierarchy
name (VMS server mode).

-report

Outputs the report in the extended XML format.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text: Specifies the VMS server URL and port for VMS server mode.

Maintaining Original Measure Names during XML Conversion
From HVP
You can maintain original measure names during HVP to XML conversion. It is helpful
when multiple measures have the same name.

The default process adds a suffix (_rename[id]) for uniqueness, but using this feature
prevents unnecessary renaming, ensuring better traceability and consistency.
You can use the -hvp_measure_keep_original_name option with the hvp annotate
-plan _.xmlcommand to convert an Excel XML file to an HVP file without renaming the
measure names.
This option prevents the addition of a _rename suffix to measure names during HVP
generation.
You can add this option in the command line or using the Load dialog box in vdCov.
Using Command Line
Run the hvp annotate command with the -hvp_measure_keep_original_name option:
hvp annotate -plan HVP_Example.hvp.xml -hvp_measure_keep_original_name

This command ensures that the original measure names are retained during the
conversion process.
User Interface
1. Select Plan > Open Plan.
2. In the file type filter, select Excel XML Plan (*.xml).

3. In the hvp annotate options text field, enter -hvp_measure_keep_original_name.

Showing Missing Scores
Verdi enables unmatched coverage sources to affect plan scores using the Show Missing
Scores option in the Verdi GUI. These unmatched coverage sources are scored as
zero, by default. You might deselect this option to produce no scores for the unmatched
coverage scores. The option produces no score in the following scenarios:
* The sources do not match any object in the .vdb database.
* The measure statements have no sources.
* The sources match an object in the .vdb database but when no metric is measured.
Consider the top plan that has a feature f1 with has four sub-features, have_matchs,
no_match, no_source, and no_measure. The coverage score of no_match, no_source,
and no_measure is zero as shown in the following figure:

Calculating Custom Aggregate Metrics Vertically in Verdi Planner

In the figure above, even unmatched coverage features -- such as no_match, no_source,
and no_measure -- are considered for coverage computation as the Show Missing
Sc ores option is selected. If you deselect this option, then these unmatched coverage
features are not included for coverage computation as shown in the following figure:

The -hvp_no_score_missing option disables unmatched coverage sources to affect plan
scores. There is no score for unmatched coverage source.
The Show Missing Scores option and -hvp_no_score_missing CLI option apply to
both the Score and Level Score columns when the Level Score column preference is
enabled.

Calculating Custom Aggregate Metrics Vertically in Verdi Planner
The default horizontal calculation method can give less accurate results for verification
progress in certain plan hierarchies. If a metric appears only in a few deep-level features,
such as FSM coverage, it can have too much influence on the overall score. Vertical
calculation provides a clearer and more balanced way to combine progress from all levels
in the plan.
Verdi Planner enables you to define custom aggregate metrics for tracking the progress
of your verification plans. This feature introduces an optional vertical calculation method
for custom aggregate metrics, offering a more precise and dependable approach to
measuring verification progress.

Calculating Custom Aggregate Metrics Vertically in Verdi Planner

To minimize the significant impact of individual metrics originating from features in subhierarchies and to ensure that the custom aggregate calculation behaves similarly to
other metrics calculated vertically, the vertical custom aggregate calculation considers the
following:
* The leaf-level custom aggregate is calculated as it is now, horizontally from the defined
metrics.
* For every feature at the N level (other than a leaf feature), the value is an average of all
N1 level feature custom aggregate metrics, and an average of the measures used in
nodelevel features if they exist.
* Weighting is considered in the calculations. For example, if the N-1 level features
have weights, these weights are factored into the calculation of the N-level custom
aggregate value.
The following example illustrates how the custom metric values depicted in Figure 124 are
calculated using the vertical custom aggregate method.
Figure 124

With vertical calculation, the FSMBranchTest custom metric is calculated vertically through
the feature hierarchy from level N. The calculation considers the underlying measures
throughout the hierarchy below that contribute to the aggregate.

aggregate metrics, the default behavior for measure and source levels within the HVP

A new option, Compute Vertical Aggregation Score, has been added in the Hvp pane

Applies only to Feature, Subplan, and Top Plan levels for user-defined aggregate metrics.
Measure and Source levels remain unchanged. Weights are considered in calculations.
Two vertical calculation approaches:

For feature 1 A, this means the FSMBranchTest result comes from averaging:

Using these values, feature 1 A gets an FSMBranchTest result of 38.8 percent.
Since feature 1 A contains measures, it is treated as a nodelevel feature when
calculating the FSMBranchTest at the PLAN level.
This means that at the PLAN level, feature 1 A contributes only the average of its own
measures.
Because of the two different calculation methods, a difference appears between the PLAN
level results.
The default horizontal method gives 56.41 percent, while the vertical method gives 37.43
percent. The reason for the difference is that the horizontal method does not consider how
many measures exist at different feature levels.
In the horizontal method, metrics are collected at the PLAN level and then averaged. In
the vertical method, each feature level is calculated independently, and then these results
are averaged across the entire hierarchy.

Displaying the Level Score Column in Plan View
By default, the Score column in the Hvp pane shows the average percentage scores of all
built-in code and functional metrics mapped to a feature at the same hierarchy level. This
horizontal aggregation method treats every mapped metric at a node equally, regardless of
how the plan hierarchy is organized below that node.
Verdi Coverage provides an optional Level Score column that rolls up scores vertically
through the plan hierarchy. At plan and feature levels, the Level Score is the average of
child Level Scores. At measure, source, and region levels, the Level Score is the same as
the regular Score value.

Including test.percent.pass in Score and Level Score
By default, the Score and Level Score columns in the Hvp pane are calculated from builtin code and functional coverage metrics, such as Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, and
Assert. The built-in derived metric test.percent.pass is not included in these overall score
calculations unless you enable a Plan View preference.
When enabled, test.percent.pass is averaged together with the other built-in metrics that
contribute to the Score and Level Score at each hierarchy level. For the definition and
per-metric behavior of test.percent.pass, see Using Derived Test Metrics.

plan that exports data in the FreeMind format and allows you to see relationships between

The most common usage is to chart the relationship between features and their test pass/

Using Derived Test Metrics
Verdi Planner supports the following additional built-in derived test metrics to track
verification progress:
* Percent Metric for Test Metric
* test.completion Metric
Using these derived metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status
and test completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
In previous releases, the built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for submetrics test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;

Using Derived Test Metrics

In previous releases, the test metric reports the basic number of tests with status pass,
fail, warn, unknown, and assert in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the
percentage of these scores.
Verification Planner for Verdi reports percentage score for each enum value of the test
metric.
This enables you to get the percentage of tests with status pass, fail, warning, unknown,
or assert.
The following is the list of the derived percent sub-metrics:
* test.percent.pass
* test.percent.fail
* test.percent.warn
* test.percent.unknown
* test.percent.assert
The score of a percent metric is the percentage of each enum's value of the test metric
against the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if a is the integer count of the built-in test metric enum value and b is the
integer count of the total number of tests, then the percentage metric is computed as
follows:
(a / b)*100

test.completion Metric
The test.completion metric allows you to measure the progress of tests being written
against the number of tests expected to be written.
The score of the test.completion metric is the ratio of total integer count of all sub-metrics
of the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and the
expected number of tests in a plan/feature.
The expected number of tests should be set using the test.expected attribute.
Where, test.completion=total_test_count/test.expected and
total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.as sert+test.unknown

Test.expected Attribute
You can use the test.expected built-in attribute assignment, as shown below, to set the
expected number of tests in feature/plan scope.
test.expected = <number>;

value of test.expected is 0.

HVP Source Name Format for Covergroup Instances
The Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) source name format for covergroup instances in
Verdi Planner helps you identify and link coverage data to verification plan features.
The source name format for covergroup instances uses the following structure:
<covergroup_variant_scope_name>.<covergroup_instance_simple_name>

* <covergroup_variant_scope_name>: The hierarchical scope name where the
covergroup variant is instantiated.
* <covergroup_instance_simple_name>: The simple name of the covergroup instance.
If your covergroup variant scope name is top.cpu and the covergroup instance simple
name is cov_inst0, the HVP source name appears as:
top.cpu.cov_inst0

This format helps you match coverage data to the correct instance in your design
hierarchy.

HVP Source Name Format for Covergroup Instances in a Package
When a covergroup is defined in a package, the HVP source name format differs from the
general case described above.
In the general case, Verdi constructs the HVP source name by combining two separate
components:
<covergroup_variant_scope_name>.<covergroup_instance_simple_name>

However, for covergroup instances in a package, the UCAPI-provided instance simple
name already contains the full hierarchy path at VCS runtime. Because of this, Verdi uses
only the instance simple name as the HVP source name, without prepending the package
scope name:
<covergroup_instance_simple_name>

This means that the package name (for example, my_pkg) does not appear as a prefix in
the HVP source name. Instead, the source name reflects the instantiation hierarchy in the
testbench where the covergroup instance is used.
Consider a covergroup defined in a package my_coverage_pkg and instantiated through
the testbench hierarchy. In the general (non-package) format, you might expect the HVP
source name to be:
my_coverage_pkg.uvm_test_top.ubus_example_tb0.ubus0.bus_monitor.cov_trans

Instead, because the instance simple name already encodes the full hierarchy path, the
actual HVP source name omits the package prefix and appears as:
uvm_test_top.ubus_example_tb0.ubus0.bus_monitor.cov_trans

Set Type Attribute
Verification Planner provides an attribute type named set. A set is a group of discrete
objects or numbers, considered as an entity. Each object or number in a set is known as a
member or an element of the set.
When the elements of a set is listed, these elements are enclosed in curly brackets. For
example, a set (say, A) of natural numbers from 1 to 5 is denoted as follows:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

The order in which the elements of a set appear does not matter. For example, consider
another set (say, B) that consists of natural numbers from 1 to 5 as follows:
B = {4, 3, 2, 1, 5)
Set A and B are considered as equal as they have the same elements in different order.
If two sets have same elements but the elements appear multiple times in one set, even
then these sets are considered as same. For example, consider the following set C:
C = {4, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 5, 5}
Set A, B, and C are considered as same irrespective of multiple elements in different
order.
If every member of set X is also a member of set Y, then X is a subset of Y. For example, X
{1, 3} is a subset of Y {1, 2, 3}. However, Z{1, 4} is not a subset of Y as element 4 does not
exist in Y {1, 2, 3}.
The set type enables you to specify multiple values for an attribute.
To declare an attribute of the set type in the HVP, use the following syntax:
attribute set{<element_list>} identifier = <default_set_value>;
identifier = <set_value>;

where <set_value> is an identifier. Identifiers in <set_value> must start with an
alphabetic character, but otherwise can use alphanumeric or the underscore character in
their names.
For example, the following code shows the definition of the my_set attribute of type set
with values as S0, S1, S2, and S_other:
attribute set{S0, S1, S2, S_other} my_set = {};
my_set = {S0, S2};

Attributes of type set in a plan can be propagated to sub-plans by setting their
propagation value to Yes.
The attributes propagated from a parent plan cannot be modified in a sub-plan. The
attributes defined in a sub-plan can be used within the sub-plan but are not visible in the
parent plan.
The set attribute type allows you to perform filtering. The set type can be filtered using
the == and != operators. Operators such as >, <, >=, <=, +, -, * and / are not supported.
For example, consider the following filter that shows the usage of == and != operators:
filter eg_filter;
//# == and != is an exact match,
//# {S0} == {S1,S2} returns false
//# {S0,S1,S2} != {S0,S1} returns true

remove feature where my_set == {S0,S1};
keep feature where my_set != {};
endfilter

In the example above, the my_set == {S0,S1} filter removes the features where my_set is
exactly {S0,S1}.
However, the my_set != {} filter restores any feature that has a null my_set.
Verification Planner also provides the contains function for filtering with the set type
attribute:
contains(<set_attribute_identifier>, <set_val>)

HVP
Consider the following HVP file, spec.hvp, which shows the definition of the set type
attribute, my_set and six features (F_1, F_2, F_3, F_4, F_5, F_sub1, and F_sub2) that
contains different values of the attribute:
plan New_Plan;
attribute set{S0,S1,S2,S_other} my_set = {S0,S2};
feature F_1;
my_set = {S0,S1};
feature F_2;
my_set = {S0,S2};
feature F_3;
my_set = {S1,S2};
feature F_4;
my_set = {};
feature F_5;
my_set = {S0,S1,S2,S_other};
feature F_sub1;
my_set = {S0,S2};
feature F_sub2;
my_set = {S0,S2};
endplan

Verdi GUI
The following section describes how to create and edit an attribute of set type in the
Attribute pane of the HvpDetail pane of Verdi GUI:
Adding a Set Type Attribute by Using the Verdi GUI
To create a set type attribute in Verdi, perform the following steps:
1. Click the Create an attribute

icon to display the New Attribute dialog box.

2. In the New Attribute dialog box, specify Identifier as the name of the attribute (say,
my_set).
To make an attribute of type set, select Type as set and specify its values as follows:

3. To add the values of this attribute in the sub-plans along with the main plan, mark
Propagation to Yes.
4. To specify the default value of this attribute, use the Default value field.
If you do not specify the default value of this attribute, the default value of this attribute
is considered as an empty set, that is {}.
5. Click OK to add the my_set attribute in the Attributes tab of the HvpDetail window.

Filters on a Plan
You can apply filters on the features of the plan using the following methods:
* Load Modifiers
* Quick Filter
Load Modifiers
To apply filters on the plan using the .hvpmod file, click the Load modifiers
Hvp window. The icon enables you to load the modifiers in the Verdi GUI.

icon in the

To load a specific modifier, select its file name from the Hvp window.
Loading the modifier implements the criteria specified in the .hvpmod file.
For example, consider the my_filter.hvpmod file that contains the following criteria:
filter my_filter;
remove feature where contains (my_set, {S1, S2});
endfilter

When the my_filter.hvpmod file is loaded, it implements the above criteria on the
New_Plan plan and removes the F_3 feature and the F_5 feature as they match the criteria
(see the figure below):

To see whether modifiers are active on the plan tab and in the Status column, see Viewing
Modifier Application Indicator.

Adjusting Weight in a User-Defined Aggregate Metric
Verdi enables you to define weight for each base metric of a user-defined aggregate
metric.
Weight for each base metric is set as 1, by default. You can specify the weight using the
following interfaces:
You can apply filters on the features of the plan using the following methods:
* Using Verdi Planner
* Using HVP
Using Verdi Planner
Verdi Planner enables you to specify weight in a user-defined aggregate metric while
creating a new metric or while editing an existing user-defined metric.
To specify the weight while creating a new user-defined aggregate metric, perform the
1. Click the
dialog box.

icon in the Metrics pane of the HvpDetail pane to open the New Metric

2. Specify the name of the metric in the Identifier text box, say MyAggr_Line_Cond, and
select Type as aggregate.

Then, click Define to open the Metrics dialog box to edit Weight of the selected
metric:
Figure 144

Metrics Dialog Box

It is recommended that the value of Weight should be more than
0. Otherwise, Verdi Planner displays a warning message.
3. Click OK.
You can calculate the aggregate score using the Recalculate

icon in the Hvp pane.

To specify the weight while editing a user-defined aggregate metric, perform the following
steps:
1. Select the user-defined metric, say MyAggr_Line_Cond, and click the Edit Metric
icon in the Metrics pane of the HvpDetail pane to display the Edit Metric dialog box:
Figure 145

Edit a Metric

2. Click Define to open the Metrics dialog box to edit Weight of the selected metric.
3. Click OK.
You can calculate score using the Recalculate

icon in the Hvp pane.

Using HVP
To specify weight in a user-defined aggregate metric, use the following HVP syntax:
metric metric-type identifier;
goal = goal-specification;
aggregator = aggregator-specification;
endmetric

metric-type: Specify metric type as aggregate and its syntax is as follows:
metric aggregate {metric_reference(weight=<value>)}

Consider the following example in which MyAgg_Line_Cond is a user-defined aggregate
metric that calculates average of Line and Condition metrics:
metric aggregate {Line(weight=1.0), Cond(weight=2.0)} MyAgg_Line_Cond;
apply = explicit;
goal = (MyAgg_Line_Cond > 0.1);
endmetric

You can calculate the aggregate score of the metric using the following:
Score of the user-defined metric = (metric1 * metric1_weight + metric2 *
metric2_weight)/(metric1_weight + metric2_weight)

Therefore, you can calculate the score of MyAgg_Line_Cond using the following:
(Line*1 + Cond*2)/(1 + 2)

Descriptions for Attribute and Metric Definitions
Verification Planner provides two types of attributes and metrics: Built-in and Userdefined. Built-in attributes and metrics are implicitly computed during annotation for every
verification plan and you cannot customize them. On the other hand, you can create
your own user-defined attributes and metrics based on your requirements. For details on
creating user-defined attributes and metrics in Verdi, see Creating Attributes and Creating
Metrics.
Verification Planner provides a new feature, which allows you to add a description to your
user-defined attributes and metrics. The feature works as follows:
* You can add descriptions to all attribute types, that is, integer, real, string, enum,
and set. Also, this option is applicable to all metric types, that is, integer, enum, real,
and percent.
* You might specify more than one line as a description.
* You might use special and escape characters in the description.
This section consists of explaining how the description feature works with the following
interfaces:
* HVP
* Verdi GUI

This section also consists of the following subsection:
* Limitation

HVP
To add a description to an attribute definition in a plan, use the following syntax:
<att_name>.description = <enquoted_description_string>

Verdi GUI
To add a description to an attribute definition in a plan, perform the following steps:
1. Click the Create an attribute

icon to display the New Attribute dialog box.

2. In the New Attribute dialog box, specify Identifier as the name of the attribute (say,
Attr_Integer). To make an attribute of type integer, select Type as integer.
3. To add the values of this attribute in the sub-plans along with the main plan, mark
Propagation to Yes.
4. To specify the default value of this attribute, use the Default value field.
5. To add a description to the attribute, use the Description field as follows:

6. Click OK to add the attribute in the Attributes tab of the HvpDetail pane. To see the
description of this attribute, hover the pointer over the attribute in the Attributes tab. For
example, see the figure below for the description of Attr_Integer:

To add a description to a metric definition in your plan, perform the following steps:
1. Click the Create a metric

icon to display the New Metric dialog box.

2. In the New Metric dialog box, specify Identifier as the name of the metric (say, color).
To make a metric of type enum, select Type as enum and specify its values as {red,
yellow, green, purple, black}.
3. You can specify the coverage goal of the metric in the Goal field. For example, specify
(color.green >=4); in the Goal field.
4. Select Aggregator as sum or uniquesum based on your requirement.
5. To add a description to the metric, use the Description field (see the figure below):

Limitation
The feature has the following limitation:
* If you add a description for an attribute in the main plan, the planner does not add
the description to its sub-plans. Similarly, if you add the description in a sub-plan, the
planner does not add the description to the attribute/metric in the main plan.

You can load modifiers to modify a plan hierarchy outside of Hvp planner definition files
using plan modifiers: override and filter.

You can use one of the following methods to load modifiers:
* Click the

icon and select the modifier file(s) in the invoked Load Modifier form.

* Add the -mod <modifier_file> option on the command line when you invoke Verdi
Coverage. For example,
%> verdi -cov -plan <plan>.hvp -mod <modifier_file>.hvpmod

After the modifier is loaded into Hvp planner, the planner is modified accordingly and the
Modifier pane is shown with the modifier.
To change a loaded local modifier file, use the Edit Modifier and Reload Modifier actions
described in .

Load Modifier

For detailed syntax and usage of modifiers in HVP, refer to the Plan Modifiers
section in the VCS Verification Planner User Guide.

Activating or Deactivating Modifiers
You can activate or deactivate the modifiers to apply or remove their effects on your plan.
To activate or deactivate a modifier, do the following:
1. Locate the modifier item in your plan.
2. Toggle the check box in front of the modifier item.
Select the check box to activate the modifier. The modifier applies to the plan.
Clear the check box to deactivate the modifier. The modifier is removed from the
plan.
Figure 147

Activating Modifiers

The modifier file item acts as a master control check box for its child items. Selecting or
clearing this check box activates or deactivates all child items at once. This applies in both
file-based and database modes.
When you activate a modifier instruction group, the group applies to the plan, even if the
master check box is not selected. Only deactivated local modifier groups and their child
items appear disabled. The local modifier file and its child items appear disabled if all child
groups are deactivated.
Database modifiers do not change their visual appearance when deactivated.

Identifying Invalid Modifier Operands
Verdi highlights invalid operands in modifier expressions. When you enter an invalid
operand, the system marks it visually. This immediate feedback helps you correct errors
before applying the modifier. You do not need to run the plan to discover mistakes.

The Modifier pane in the HVP pane includes an Error column. For each instruction, the
column displays:
* Empty when the instruction is valid and applied successfully.
* Error text when the instruction is invalid, for example:
Unknown attribute 'X' was found

* Other validation errors from the Hierarchical Verification Plan Application Programming
Interface (HVP API).
The same error message appears as a tooltip when you hover over the error cell.
Figure 148

Error Column in the Modifiers Pane

Viewing Modifier Match Counts
When you apply modifiers to a plan, the match counts and affected-item lists give you permodifier metrics so you can verify modifier behavior without inferring results from the plan
view alone.
The Modifier pane in the HVP pane includes a Matched column. The column appears in
front of the modifier expression and shows how many plan items each modifier matches.
Match counts include features, measures, and sources matched by each instruction.
* For each instruction, view the match count from the Hierarchical Verification Plan
Application Programming Interface (HVP API).
* For each group, view the aggregated sum of match counts from active (checked) child
instructions.
* For each file, view the aggregated sum of match counts from checked child groups.

Viewing Selected or Removed Items in the Message Pane
When modifiers select or remove plan items, the Message pane logs the affected features
and other matched plan items. Use this log to review which items each modifier instruction
affected during apply.
Viewing Modified Item Names
To see which plan items a modifier affects, right-click any active (checked) modifier
instruction and select Items Affected by Modifiers. The Items Affected by Modifiers
dialog box lists the plan items affected by the selected modifier instruction.

Figure 150

Items Affected by Modifiers Dialog

When you hover over the Status column on a feature, measure, sub-plan, or source row
in the plan hierarchy, a tooltip displays the modifier instructions affecting that row. The
tooltip also shows any warnings or errors if present.

Editing and Reloading Loaded Modifiers
Verdi Coverage lets you update a loaded local modifier file (.hvpmod) in an external text
editor and reload it in the current session. You do not need to remove the modifier from the
GUI and load the same file again.
Configuring the External Editor
The Edit Modifier action is available only when an external editor program is configured.
To configure the external editor:
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the Plan View category, specify the external editor program.
3. Click OK to save your preferences.
If no external editor is configured, a warning message appears in the Edit Modifier button
tooltip.

Figure 151

Edit Modifier Tooltip When External Editor Is Not Configured

Editing a Modifier File
To edit a modifier file in an external editor:
1. In the Modifier pane, select the local modifier file that you want to change.
2. Click the Edit Modifier icon.
The selected modifier file opens in the configured external text editor.
Figure 152

Edit Modifier Icon

3. Edit the modifier instructions, and then save the file in the external editor.

Reloading the Loaded Modifier
After you save your changes in the external editor:
1. Return to the Verdi Coverage GUI.
2. With the same local modifier file selected, click the Reload Modifier icon to load the
updated file.
When the reload operation completes, a confirmation message appears in the Message
pane. The modified file name is shown in italic font in the Modifier pane list, indicating that
the file was updated on disk.
Figure 153

Modified Modifier File Name in Italic Font

Server-Based Mode
In server-based (DB) mode, the same toolbar control is used for both refresh and reload
operations. The icon displayed depends on the type of modifier you select:
* When a server modifier is selected, the blue Refresh Modifier icon is displayed. This
action refreshes modifier data from the server.
* When a local modifier file is selected, the Reload Modifier icon is displayed. This
action reloads the local file from disk.
Use the icon shown for the current selection to tell whether the action refreshes data from
the server or reloads a locally edited modifier file.

Viewing Modifier Application Indicator
If the Modifier pane is closed but modifiers remain applied to the plan, visual indicators on
the plan tab and in the plan hierarchy let you confirm applied modifiers without reopening
the Modifier pane.
Tracking Active Modifiers
The modifier list tracks the count of checked (active) modifiers at the file, group, and
instruction level. When this count changes, the plan tab label and icon and the plan
hierarchy Status column update. Updates occur when you:
* Check or uncheck a modifier file, group, or instruction.
* Load modifiers during plan populate.
* Close the Modifier pane while modifiers remain applied.
Modifier Icon on the Plan Tab
When modifiers are checked (active), a modifier icon ( ) appears on the plan tab. Both
filter modifiers and override modifiers trigger the tab icon.
The tab label and icon update immediately when you check or uncheck modifiers. The
icon stays visible if modifiers are applied, even after you close the Modifier pane. When
no modifiers are active, either because all modifiers are unchecked or all modifier files are
removed, the plan tab shows no modifier icon.
Figure 154

Modifier Icon on the Plan Tab

Refreshing Plan Hierarchy Status
The Status column refreshes for all hierarchy items when the modifier state changes.
Feature, measure, sub-plan, and source rows show an override icon in the Status column
when they have overridden attributes, metrics, or sources.
In an expanded view, only rows with overrides show the override icon. In a collapsed view,
parent rows show the override icon if any descendant has overrides. The Status column
can show error, warning, and modifier override icons together.
The override icon in the Status column appears only for override modifiers. For
filter modifiers, this icon does not appear. The override icon does not appear on
the plan (root) row.
Use these indicators to confirm active modifiers without reopening the Modifier pane. To
see how many plan items each modifier matches, see Viewing Modifier Match Counts.

Viewing Applied Modifier Status in Generated Reports
Verification Planner adds modifier status rows to the generated report when you apply a
modifier with the -mod option on the hvp annotate or hvp genxls -report command.
The rows appear at the end of the first sheet in the XML or XLSX output. Use these rows
to confirm that the modifier file was applied and to debug unexpected results.
For example, the first sheet ends with a rows similar to the following:
HVP modifier file modifier_set.hvpmod was successfully loaded.
HVP modifier file top_mod.hvpmod was successfully loaded.
For more information about applying modifiers from the command line, see the "Applying
Modifiers" section in the VCS Verification Planner User Guide.

Verdi enables you to toggle between complete and incomplete features of a plan. A
feature is an incomplete feature if it satisfies the following rules:
* A feature is a leaf feature if it does not have any sub-feature or sub-plan.
* A feature has no measures or a feature has measures but these measures have no
source.

Feature icon in the Hvp pane. The icon hides all complete features of a plan to focus

follows:
measure Group, Group.bin_count, Group.covered_count,
Group.uncovered_count, Group.excluded_count measure_1;
source = "group/group instance/group bin/
group instance bin: <group object name>";

Post-Recalculate Hook Framework
The Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) post-recalculate hook framework lets you register
Tcl procs that fire automatically after every HVP plan recalculate. Use this framework
to build custom automation that responds to recalculate completion without manually
invoking Tcl commands each time.
A common use case is updating the RM_status attribute based on GOAL state: when a
feature meets its GOAL, set RM_status to Complete; otherwise, set RM_status to Open.

Registering a Post-Recalculate Hook
To register a Tcl proc as a hook, use the gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook
command. The proc runs automatically at the end of every HVP plan recalculate, whether
triggered from the GUI toolbar, menu, or the gui_hvp_recalculate command.

Post-Recalculate Hook Framework

To register a hook, perform the following steps:
1. Source the Tcl script that defines your hook proc:
source my_hook_proc.tcl

2. Register the proc:
gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook -proc my_hook_proc

3. Verify the registration:
gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook -list

After registration, the hook fires synchronously each time a recalculate occurs. The
gui_hvp_recalculate command does not return until all registered hooks complete.

Unregistering Hooks
Remove hooks when they are no longer needed or before timing-sensitive operations:
* To remove a specific hook:
gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook -unregister my_hook_proc

* To remove all hooks:
gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook -unregister_all

Writing Hook Procs
A hook proc takes no arguments. Inside the proc, query the current context with existing
Tcl commands. Follow these guidelines when authoring hook procs:
* Resolve the active HVP window or detail at runtime with gui_get_current_window.
Do not assume fixed window IDs such as HVP.1.
* Use gui_hvpeditor_is_feature_meet_goal to check whether a feature, plan, or
subplan meets its GOAL.
* Wrap the proc body in catch for diagnostic visibility, because hook errors are caught
silently by the framework:
proc my_hook {} {
if {[catch {
# hook logic here
} err]} {
puts stderr "my_hook error: $err\n$::errorInfo"

Post-Recalculate Hook Framework

}

}

* A hook proc can call gui_hvp_recalculate to trigger a second recalculate pass.
The re-entrancy guard ensures hooks do not re-fire on the nested recalculate, which
prevents infinite recursion.

Reference Proc: Automatic RM_status Update
The following reference proc demonstrates the intended use of the hook framework. It
iterates all plan and feature nodes after recalculate and sets RM_status = Complete
when the GOAL is met, or RM_status = Open otherwise.
proc check_goal_set_rm_status {} {
set items [gui_dump_list -hvp_tcl_names]
foreach item $items {
set meets_goal [gui_hvpeditor_is_feature_meet_goal $item]
if {$meets_goal eq "1"} {
gui_hvpdetail_override_attr -name RM_status -value Complete
} else {
gui_hvpdetail_override_attr -name RM_status -value Open
}
}
# Trigger a second pass to display updated RM_status values.
# The re-entrancy guard prevents hooks from firing again.
gui_hvp_recalculate
}

This reference proc uses a two-pass design:
1. Pass 1: A normal recalculate runs against the previous RM_status values. On
completion, the framework fires the hook, which updates RM_status based on GOAL
state.
2. Pass 2: The hook calls gui_hvp_recalculate at its end. The nested recalculate runs
with the updated RM_status values, but hooks do not re-fire. The chain terminates after
exactly two passes.
Only plan and feature nodes carry an RM_status attribute. Calling
gui_hvpdetail_override_attr -name RM_status on a metric or source
node has no effect; the override is silently dropped.

Backward Compatibility
With an empty registry (the default state), there is no behavioral change. After you register
hooks, gui_hvp_recalculate blocks until every hook finishes. Existing automation that
measures recalculate wall-clock duration or uses a timeout near the historical recalculate
runtime might observe delays proportional to the Tcl runtime of the hooks.
To work around this behavior, call gui_hvp_register_post_recalculate_hook
-unregister_all before a timing-sensitive section.

Using the Exclusion Manager
Verdi Coverage provides the Exclusion Manager feature to increase coverage by taking
out the exclusions that are not needed for the design.
When a design has a lot of code or combinations that never occur or there are parts of the
design that designer does not care about, then the exclusion features are used to exclude
the above coverage targets from the coverage score.
Thus, you can focus on the coverage results from the design that can happen.
When you identify a coverage target that can be ignored, or is impossible by design, you
can mark it for exclusion directly in the GUI and add an annotation explaining why it is
excluded.
You can then save those exclusions and annotations to an exclude file that can be reused
in the next and future sessions.
Excluded objects are removed from the coverage score calculation and appear disabled in
reports.
You might exclude an object either at a module level or an instance level. An exclusion on
a module excludes the corresponding object in all of its instances.
For example, consider the coin_fsm module that has five instances as shown in the

If coin_fsm is excluded, all the instances under it are automatically excluded as shown in
the following figure:

If a new instance is created for the excluded module, the new instance is automatically
excluded. On the other hand, if you exclude an object at the instance level, then its other
instances are not excluded automatically.
For example, if you exclude test_jukebox.st0.coin1 at the instance level, then its
other instances in test_jukebox.st1, test_jukebox.st2, test_jukebox.st3, and
test_jukebox.st4 are not excluded as shown in the figure below:

Instance exclusions do not affect the coverage score of a module, even if all of its
instances are excluded.
For example, if you exclude test_jukebox.st0.coin1, Line 73, Line 78, Line 90, and so
on are excluded as shown in the following figure:

Note that these lines are not excluded at the module level (see the figure below).

If you intend to exclude an object for all instances of a module, ensure that you are in the
module exclusion mode and not the instance exclusion mode. These two modes look
similar.
The main difference is that for module exclusions, a module scope is selected in the
Modules tab of the Summary pane. For instance-based exclusions, you select an instance
scope in the Hierarchy tab of the Summary pane.
As it is not possible to convert instance exclusions to module exclusions, if you intend
to create module exclusions confirm that you are in the module exclusion mode before
excluding objects.

Following are the three ways to save exclusions:
* Save all exclusions: Saves all exclusions in the Exclusion Manager pane into a
specified file.
To save all exclusions in an *.el exclusion file, click File->

Save all exclusions.

* Save exclusions not saved: Saves exclusions that are not yet saved into a specified
file including the exclusions that are already existing in the file.

To save new exclusions for entire design, click the
icon from the toolbar.
Alternatively, click File>

Save Exclusions Not Saved

Save Exclusions Not Saved.

* Save selected exclusions: Saves exclusions for selected instances, trees, modules,
and groups into a specified file including the exclusions that are already existing in the
file.
To save exclusions for the selected instances, trees, modules, and groups, click
Exclusion->Save Exclusions for Selected Objects/Trees.
To save the exclusion file with the selected metrics, enable the Save propagated
exclusions from module of covergroup variant Metrics option.

Loading Exclusion Files
You can click the

icon to load an *el exclusion file to the Exclusion Manager pane.

You can load exclusion files (.el files) using the File menu commands Load Exclusions
from File or Load Exclusions from File List as shown in the following figure:
Figure 170

Loading Exclusion Files From the File Menu

You can specify the .el file that needs to be loaded using the Load Exclusions from File
option.
You can also load a file which contains a list of .el files using the Load Exclusions from
File List option.

These options are also available in the Exclusion menu as shown in the following figure:
Figure 171

Loading Exclusion Files From the Exclusion Menu

The command corresponding to the Load Exclusions from File option is vdCov -elfile

<ElFile>.

The command corresponding to the Load Exclusions from File List option is vdCov
-elfilelist <ElFileList>.
Here, the elfile file path specified in the <ElFileList> file can be the absolute path or
relative path.
By default, the relative path in the <ElFileList> is relative to the <ElFileList> itself.
Therefore, there is no effect on the path even if you change the current working directory.
However, if you want <ElFileList> to consider the relative path to the working directory,
you can use the -relative_to_workingdir option while specifying the elfile.
You can also specify the file path using a user-defined environment variable added in the
<ElFileList> file.
For example, run the command setenv ANY_ENV_VAR_NAME /remote/exclude_dir in
the console, then add $ANY_ENV_VAR_NAME/exclusion1.el in the <ElFileList>.
When there is an existing excluded item in the .el file loaded using
-elfilelist, there might be a conflict while trying manually performing
exclusion operations on the existing excluded item/scope.

Module Exclusion Annotations at the Instance Level
When an object is excluded at the module level, it is also excluded in all of the module's
instances.
Also, when you add exclusion annotations to the object at the module level, these
annotations are added to the object at the instance level.
These annotations are visible at the instance level in the tooltips of the object. The tooltips
display the exclusion annotations from the module level. The scope of these annotations is
applicable to Hierarchy and Modules tabs in the Summary pane.

Attributes on Coverage Exclusions

Attributes on Coverage Exclusions
Define custom attributes on coverage exclusion objects in Verdi and apply filter
expressions to selectively control which exclusions are active in your design.
Use exclusion project files to define user-defined attributes of type integer, real, string,
date, enum, or set alongside the built-in Annotation attribute. Attach attribute values to
exclusion objects through the Annotation Manager, then apply filter expressions using
AND/OR logic (for example, status=approved AND phase>1) to determine which
exclusions affect coverage scores. Save named filters for reuse across sessions. Integrate
with URG using the -elfilter option to apply attribute-based filtering in batch report
generation. Load exclusion projects at invocation with -excl_project.
Verdi Coverage enables you to define attributes in an exclusion project file, attach them to
exclusion objects, and use filtering expressions to select which exclusions are applied.
* Defining and Creating Attributes
* Editing Attribute Values
* Exclusion Filter
To load an exclusion project and exclusion file while invoking Verdi, use the following
command:
verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb -excl_project excl.proj -elfile 1.el

where, excl.proj is the name of an exclusion project and 1.el is the name of an
exclusion file.

Defining and Creating Attributes
Verdi Coverage supports a built-in attribute, Annotation, but also allows you to define
your own integer, real, string, date, enum, or set-type attributes.
A couple of examples are shown below:
attribute integer phase = 0;
attribute string assignee = "";
attribute enum {new,in_progress,approved,rejected} status = new;

Editing Attribute Values
Verdi Coverage allows you to edit the value of the built-in attribute, Annotation as well as
supported attributes, such as integer, string, and real, enum and date directly in the
Exclusion Manager window.

Exclusion Filter
Verdi Coverage provides a filter that determines which exclusions are applied to the
design.
It allows conditions based on user-defined attributes instead of only on built-in Annotation
and Elfile fields. Annotation is the one built-in attribute type that is used for filtering.
Also, if the Elfile attribute is enabled, it appears in the Annotation Manager table and
can be used for filtering.

Filter Support for Annotations and Elfile

Here are few examples of filter expressions using user-defined attributes:
owner="Bob"
phase>1 OR status=inprogress
status=approved AND datecreated<06/01/2021

The following figure shows the group of exclusions with a filter (owner = bob AND
ETA>11/01/21). Only one exclusion matched the criteria and it is the only one that is
applied to the design:

When an attribute of type enum or set is used, the GUI shows a drop-down that allows you
to pick the value or values to be used in the filter as shown below:

Filter expressions can be named and saved for later use. For example, a complex filter
such as, can be named saved:
priority = 1 AND owner = "Lucy" AND status = approved

Displaying Multiple Annotated Exclusions

Displaying Multiple Annotated Exclusions
Coverable objects in Verdi are marked as excluded when they have one or more
exclusions applied to them. Exclusions can be loaded from one or more exclusion files or
can be applied interactively in Verdi.
By default, if an object is excluded due to exclusions loaded from multiple exclusion
files, and two or more of those exclusions have annotations, the exclusion file that is
loaded last overwrites the annotation from any previous exclusion file. If Verdi Coverage is
invoked with the -excl_append_annotation switch, Verdi appends annotations from all
exclusions to the excluded coverable object. For example, there are exclusions of cd1 in
both 1.el and 2.el, and each of those files contains an annotation on its exclusion, then
the switch concatenates both in the Exclusion Manager pane for cd1, as follows:

The -excl_append_annotation switch is now removed. If more than one annotation
exists for an excluded object, then all annotations are displayed as separate rows (see the
figure below):

Exclusions With Checksum Mismatch
When the design changes, you may load exclusions created with a previous version.
Verdi may require you to review some exclusions before it applies them. Review removes
corresponding coverable objects from coverage scoring. An exclusion is flagged when the
checksum saved for it in the elfile does not match the checksum saved in the coverage
database. Flagged exclusions can be accepted, rejected. or left unreviewed.
If a reviewed exclusion is accepted, it is saved to its associated elfile with a new
checksum. If a reviewed exclusion is rejected, it gets removed from Verdi. If an exclusion
is unreviewed, it is saved to its associated elfile with its original checksum.

Adding Annotations to an Excluded Object

Adding Annotations to an Excluded Object
You may add an annotation to an excluded coverable object. The annotation propagates
to its exclusion objects. The following figure shows a coverable object, cd1 and its
exclusions:

To add an annotation to an exclusion, perform the following steps:
1. Double-click the object to enter the edit mode.
2. Specify an annotation in its Annotation column. The specified annotation is
propagated to the Annotation column of all of its contained excluded objects.
For more details on how to add annotations to an exclusion, see the Adding
Annotations for Exclusions section.

Handling Duplicate Annotations of an Excluded Object
If the annotation of an excluded object is changed and is similar to another annotation of
the same excluded object, then only one entry of that exclusion is retained in Exclusion
