Marking Exclusions
You can mark exclusions on a topology folder using the Exclude

The icon applies exclusions on all coverable objects in the topology folder. The icon is
available in the main menu, the Exclusion toolbar, and in the right-click menu.
For example, consider a topology folder, instruction that contains coverable objects as
trackgroup, ticksgroup, tickcoincross, opgroup, and coingroup.
To mark this folder as excluded, perform the following steps:
1. Click the Display Covergroup Instance tree

icon in the Summary pane.

2. In the Groups tab, select the topology folder, instruction. When you select the
topology folder, the Exclude icon becomes enabled.
3. To exclude the instruction folder and all the coverable objects under it, click the
icon in the main menu or in the Exclusion menu. Alternatively, right-click the folder to
select Exclude as shown in the following figure:

4. After the exclusions are applied on the folder, exclusion markers are applied on the
coverable objects. For exclusion markers, see the highlighted icons in the following
figure:

No exclusion marker is displayed next to the topology folder (see
instruction in the above figure).

Tree Exclusions
You can apply exclusions to either a topology folder or its sub-folders, or a tree (that
is, both a topology folder and its sub-folders). When you select a topology folder, Verdi
enables the Advanced Exclusion Options
icon in the main toolbar.
When you click this icon, Verdi displays the following exclusion toolbar:

You can decide the scope of applying exclusions using any of the following options from
the exclusion toolbar:
* Self Only:
If you select this option, Verdi applies exclusions to the coverable objects that exist in a
topology folder.
The exclusions are not applied on the coverable objects that are present inside the
sub-folders of the topology folder.
For example, consider the following figure that shows a topology folder, cd1, its direct
coverable object, disc, and its sub-folder, honker.
The honker sub-folder contains one coverable object, song.

If you select Self Only, Verdi applies exclusions only to its direct coverable object,
which is disc.
* Children Only
If you select this option, Verdi applies exclusions to the coverable objects that exist in
the sub-folders of a topology folder. The exclusions are not applied on the coverable
objects that are present directly in the topology folder.
In the example, if you select Children Only, Verdi applies exclusions only to the
coverable objects inside the honker folder, which is song.
* Self&Children
If you select this option, Verdi applies exclusions to all coverable objects inside the
selected topology folder.
In the example, if you select Self&Children, Verdi applies exclusions to both song and
disc.

Saving Exclusions
Verdi allows you to save exclusions for coverable objects that you want to exclude. Note
that exclusions are not saved for a topology folder but for its coverable objects. For
example, consider a folder, cd1, which contains coverable objects cg1, cg2, and cg3.
If you save exclusions for cd1, exclusions are saved for cg1, cg2, and cg3, and not for
cd1.
Therefore, if a new coverable object, cg4, is added to the cd1 folder and it needs to be
excluded, you need to explicitly exclude cg4.

To save exclusions, Verdi provides the following two options:
* Save Exclusions for Selected Objects: This option saves all exclusions applied to
only direct coverable objects in the topology folder.
This option does not save exclusions applied to the coverable objects in its sub-folders.
* Save Exclusions for Selected Trees: This option saves all exclusions applied to
coverable objects in the topology folder and its sub-folders.
To save exclusions, perform the following steps:
1. Right-click the folder on which the exclusions are already applied and select Save
Exclusions for Selected Objects or Save Exclusions for Selected Trees.
2. Specify the exclusion file name, excl_instruction.el, in the Save Exclusions for
Selected Objects or Save Exclusions for Selected Trees dialog box and click Save.

Exclusion Propagation From Line Coverage
Verdi allows you to automatically propagate line exclusions to condition and branch
coverage metrics. This propagation reduces manual effort in creating the same exclusions
again for condition and branch metrics.
* Use Model
* Example
* Limitations

Use Model
To propagate line coverage exclusions to condition and branch metric, use the following
command while invoking Verdi:
verdi -cov -excl_propagation

You can also enable exclusion propagation from inside Verdi. For this, perform the
1. Select Tools -> Preferences to display the Application Preferences dialog box (Figure
Application Preferences Dialog Box).
2. In the Application Preferences dialog box, select the Exclusion category.
3. In the Exclusion category, select the following option:
Propagate Exclusion from Line metric to Condition and Branch metric. This only takes
effect after reloading the database.
4. Reload the database.
5. Right-click a signal in the Hierarchy pane and select Exclude to propagate line
coverage exclusions to condition and branch metric.

Loading and Saving Sessions
Verdi Coverage provides save and load session features to save the current process or
restore a previously saved session to continue the unfinished process.
The analyzed coverage, Exclusion Manager and HVP planner status can be recorded
using the File -> Save Session command. Specify a name and path for the session file in
the Save Session form and click the Save button. The following information is saved in the
session file:
* General status
* Preferences settings
* Docked panes layout
* Coverage status in the Summary pane
* Each Coverage Source Code and corresponding Coverage details status
* Exclusion Manager status
* HVP Planner and corresponding status in the HvpDetail pane
You can use the File -> Restore Session command to restore the saved session, and the
Verdi Coverage session is restored.
To save the session including additional changes in the HVP Planner and
Exclusion Manager panes, the changes must first be saved in these separate
panes.

Interactive Debug capabilities between Verdi Coverage and the Verdi platform:

Using Verdi VMS
Verdi VMS is a versatile, modular system for managing compilation, regression, and
tracking of the design verification process. The execution engine automatically merges
VCS coverage data from each test run.
Verdi VMS's main functionality is to run a set of regression simulations, collect results,
and generate interactive reports for exploring those results. Verdi VMS stores regression
results in a relational database. A web-based user interface lets you browse regression
results and files generated by verification tools. In addition, results can be viewed from
within Verdi Coverage.
To aid in quick analysis of simulation failures, Verdi VMS can rerun the fastest running
examples of each unique failure category. It automatically prepares detailed debug results
for analysis.
As regressions involve running many tests on a large set of hardware, Verdi VMS includes
features to overcome common system failures. Disk access interruptions and failed hosts
are tolerated, for example.
Verdi VMS is preconfigured to work with VCS and UVM methodologies but can be
configured to run any verification tool. It works with grid managers, such as LSF of Sun
Grid. It can also run simulation jobs directly on local hosts.
The licensing scheme for Verdi VMS might differ from that of Verdi Coverage. For detailed
and up-to-date information regarding license requirements and setup, contact Synopsys
Customer Support.
You can run Verdi VMS and view run results from Verdi Coverage. To invoke Verdi VMS
from the Verdi Coverage GUI, use either of the following methods:
* Tools > Open Tests Browser
* Tools > Run Tests
For more details on Verdi VMS, see the Verdi VMS User Guide on SolvNetPlus.

Overview
The Verdi(R) Debug Decision Tree (DDT) GUI-based tool is used for capturing and
converting debug knowledge into executable code in Python. With DDT, you can easily
drag and drop the intended debug operations from the DDT libraries and focus on how to
record the process of the bug without the need to write any source code.

Debug Decision Tree
Debug Decision Tree (DDT) has the following modules to perform debug operations in the
DDT libraries:
* Debug Decision Tree Usage
* Run a DDT Session
* Debug Decision Tree Library
* Import a Customized Library
* Hierarchical DDT
* External Link DDT Session
* Batch Mode
* Demo Examples

If running on RHEL7 OS, make sure singularity can be used.

Launch DDT
Run the command ddt gui to launch DDT GUI as following:
%> ddt gui &

DDT has following five widgets:
1. Tree (decision tree drawing canvas)
2. Libraries
3. Global variables
4. Config (DDT node input arguments)
5. Selection Pane (list view of DDT nodes)
Use the mouse to drag any widget, and dock the widget to any place. You can also
hide some of the widgets for your working mode.

You can click View menu to unhide the panes.

Add a Node by Selecting a Library
Use one of the predefined DDT libraries to create a DDT node through the following steps:
1. Expand the tree of the library category
2. Select a library, and double-click, a new DDT node is added to the tree as shown in the
following figure:

When you select the node, the corresponding Node widget is also shown and the title
of Node widget changes to <Node ID>: <Node Name>.
3. Under Config tab, enter the input arguments for the node.
Additional information can be entered in Description, if the node name is
not enough to describe the debug operation of the node.
Each library has its match function to determine the decision according to the input
arguments. Details of the libraries is described later.

Pan Mode and Selection Mode
By default, DDT's Canvas is in "Pan Mode". To switch pan mode to the selection mode,
follow the given steps:
1. Move the canvas by pressing and holding the left mouse button.
2. Drag the button to the required position.
3. Click the
The

icon on the toolbar to switch it to the selection mode.

icon changes to

to show that the selection mode is active.

Selection mode enables you to select several items through a rubber band.
4. Click the

icon on the toolbar to switch it to the pan mode.

Set up the Global Variables
You can set up global variables for the entire DDT in the Global Variables tab. Usually,
the global variables can be the log name, the FSDB name, the frequently used regular
expressions, the signal names in an FSDB, and known data that are expected to be used
globally.

Use Add to add one more global variable and Remove to delete the selected global
variable.
Under DDT, it is necessary to use the quote (`) or double quote (") to embrace
string characters. DDT follows the Python syntax to set up the variables.

With the setting of global variables, when filling in the arguments of a node, clicking the
combo box shows the available variables.

Global Variables
You can define general purpose global variables in Global Variables tab. The left side
name should be a valid Python identifier. The right side value should be a valid Python
expression.
String variables should use single-quote ' or double-quote ".
Environment Variables
DDT lets you to set up the variable to represent the environment variables. The usage is
the same as Global Variables except that you can use environment variable in Value field.
For example, define a variable CPU_FSDB that uses environment variable $VERDI_HOME to
locate the cpu.fsdb file.

Regular Expressions
DDT has a tab for regular expression variables. To help users define and check regular
expressions, there is a regular expression wizard.
To use the wizard, perform the following steps:
1. Go to Regular Expressions tab in the Global Variables widget.
2. Click

to add a new field to define a global variable.

3. Click

edit button to open the regular expression wizard.

The wizard has three parts as follows:
"sample message"
"regular expression"
"value entry"
4. Enter a regular expression and a sample message.
5. Use the add

or remove

buttons to change the rows in the table.

Each row has three columns as follows:
Attribute: Is the group name in the regular expression.
Expected Value: Is what you want to find.
Captured Value: Is what the regular expression matches.
For example, a regular expression can define groups like "time," "Pattribute,"
"pADDR," "pWRITE," and "pREADY."
The wizard matches these values in the sample message automatically.
The order of rows in the value entry is important. The wizard uses this order to find
captured values. To change the row order, use the move up
or move down
buttons.
The Attribute column is optional. You do not have to use named groups, but it is
recommended.

Named groups make it easier to set up node configurations. If you use the Attribute
column, all cells need to have a value or all needs to be empty.

Signal Mappings
DDT provides a separate tab to define signal mappings, which helps users enter the field,
signal_names, with ease.
The left side name should be a valid Python identifier, which is the name of the signal
mapping. The right side value should be a SignalMapping. Every SignalMapping is
a one-to-one mapping from a str to another str where keys are aliases and values
are signal full name. An alias is usually a short name of a signal full name, enhancing
readability.
After defining signal mappings, they can be selected by their name in the node config in
signal-choosing fields in Fill in Arguments of a Node. Instead of signal full names, signal
aliases shows in the node result, which makes it easier to read. Furthermore, you can also
access the values by the keys of SignalMapping as a dict.
For example, given a SignalMapping, my_sig_map = {"r": "top.r", "e":
"top.e"}, the value, "top.r", by my_sig_map["r"].
DDT provides SignalMappingWizard to help users to create valid signal mappings. To
button to launch SignalMappingWizard.

such as moving, adding, deleting, sorting data. For validity checking, the wizard checks

empty and duplicate entries by default. Users can also turn on the waveform sanity check
function to check if signals exist in the provided waveform file.
SignalMappingWizard only accepts mapping that passes the validity check, in

Data Flow and Packet
The following picture shows the data transferred from parent to children node:

In DDT, use a dictionary `packet' to transmit the data. After evaluating the result of a parent
node, the extracted data (for example, the `time' and the `attribute', depends on which
library used) is put to the tree branch and its children's nodes can get the information.
This is useful because in many situations the child node might evaluate some conditions
followed by the data extracted from its parent.
When filling the arguments of a DDT node, for example, if a parent's packet contains the
"time" field, the input of its child node can use below two ways to access the value of the
"time" field:
* packet["time"]
* B.time
(The `B' stands for `branch' and can be changed in preference)

Fill in Arguments of a Node
Fill in the input arguments by editing texts or selecting the variables from the combo box.
The available variables in the combo box comes from two sources as following:
1. The global variables (refer to Set up the Global Variables) which data type (string, int,
and float and so on) matches the argument.
2. The parent's node output variables which data type matches the argument.
To edit the text, click edit icon. This icon pop-up a multiple-line editor. The editor is useful
when you need to type a long text like regular expressions.

Mode Decide
In addition to filling argument values during execution, you can also change the default
behavior whether DDT should run a node or not. By default, DDT runs a node if its parent
node's execution result is PASS. For example, the "result" field from parent packet is
True.
To change the default behavior of this decision, you can first click the "Decide" option
in "Mode", and then change the arguments accordingly. For example, changing a node's
execution criteria to be checking a field "num_vc" from parent packet which value is less
than 10, you can fill in "B.num_vc", "LESS", and "10" in arguments "decide_field",
"decide_compare", and "decide_value" accordingly.

Different library might have different "Decide" arguments. For example, the "Switch"
library in Miscellaneous category, its "Decide" argument has only one "control", and it
runs a node depending on the given "control" value.

Fill in Node's Properties
For better readability and maintainability, add a description on each node. Thus, you do
not need to worry about forgetting what the intension and behavior of the node. Similar to
filling in the node arguments, you can add simple description to the line edit or long texts
via the multiple line edit.

For some important nodes that you want to quickly locate from Canvas, change the node
color from property tab. By clicking the color button, a color palette appears, and you can
choose the color of your choice easily.

Fit Window, Zoom in, Zoom out, Select Nodes, Move Nodes
To view the DDT display functions, Use the menu `View', click Right Mouse Button
(RMB). Use the toolbar icon to Zoom In / Zoom Out / Fit to Selection / Auto Layout.

The keyboard shortcuts are also shown in the menu of RMB. For example, you can use
the keyboard shortcut f to fit the DDT drawing window, or use Ctrl+d to duplicate a node.
The keyboard shortcut character is case insensitive.

Duplicate a Nodes
Select one or many nodes, and use the RMB or the keyboard shortcut Ctrl-D to duplicate
the node.

Connect Two Nodes
Each DDN contains following two ports:
1. Input port
2. Output port
Since the DDT logic is `decision', the connection of two nodes must start from the Output
port of one node to the Input port of the other node.
One Output port can connect to `many' Input ports of other node (that is, one parent node
connects to many children nodes). This means if the evaluation of a parent node is True,

port of one node to the Input port of the other node.
One Output port can connect to `many' Input ports of other node (that is, one parent node
connects to many children nodes). This means if the evaluation of a parent node is True,
then the next step is to check all possible children nodes to see if they match the logic with
specified input arguments.

You can also connect two nodes via the node's context menu by clicking the right mouse
button on the node. Choosing Connect Input to or Connect Output to pops
out a dialog box that allows the user to choose which node the user tends to create a
connection from the drop-down menu.
This pop-out dialog box is useful when the user finds it hard to find nodes within Canvas.

When connecting two nodes, in the Config Tab, the child node can see the output data
passed by its parent. Those data is displayed with the prefix B. in the combo box (B
stands for tree branch). The following figure shows the B.time passed from a parent node
to its children.

You can change the prefix from B. to any word in the menu Preference, and go to the
Construct tab.

Use Selection Pane to Select Nodes
Use the Selection Pane to select one or many nodes. You can use the filter box to type
the string that matches the name or ID of the nodes. The filter criteria in the Selection
Pane use regular expression.

GUI Preference
Go to the menu Preference to set up the GUI preference, including the default node
name, the node size, and the background color and so on. You can save the preference
to a file and load it back next time.
By default, DDT creates a preference file ddt.conf in your working directory. If you work in
the same directory to open DDT GUI next time, the local preference file ddt.conf is loaded
automatically.

Use the command option --preference <preference_file> to specify the preference when
launching DDT GUI. For example:
%> ddt gui --preference /tmp/my_ddt.conf &

Save or Restore a DDT Session
To save and restore a DDT session, follow the given steps:
1. Click File > Save/Save As to save the DDT session (in JSON format).

2. Click File > Restore to restore the DDT.

Use the batch mode command ddt gui <session> to load the session. For example,
%> ddt gui dvfs_ddt.json &

Multi-DDT
You can open multiple DDT sessions in the DDT GUI, and these sessions are displayed in
different tabs. For example, two DDT sessions golden_session.json and ip.json are
opened in DDT GUI.

Every time you tend to open a DDT session through File menu, a new session appears in
a new tab. To change the behavior of opening a session in a new tab, update the settings
under Preferences as highlighted in the following figure:

When multiple tabs are open and some of the tabs contains unsaved DDT sessions and
you intend to close DDT, a message pop-up listing all the unsaved sessions appears.
Click Yes to save all unsaved sessions before closing.

User-Defined Node Properties
Users can assign a custom property to every node in a DDT. To set up user-defined node
properties, follow the given steps:
1. From the menu bar, select Edit > Add Customized Property.
A file dialog box appears through DDT.
2. Select a JSON file that describes your user-defined attributes.
The Custom Property tab appears wherein you can define attributes.

The format of user-defined attributes is as follows:
{

}

attribute-name: {
"type": ,
"default input": ,
"visible": ,
}

The user-defined attribute file uses a JSON format. Each key is an attribute name.
The value for each key is another dictionary. This dictionary includes the following
attributes:
type: The data type of the attribute value.
default input: The default for the attribute.
visible: Shows if the attribute is visible in the DDT.
For example, the following content defines two attributes:
description: Uses a string type. The default for description is signature.
However, the description attribute is not visible or editable in DDT because its
visible property is set to false.
signature: Uses an integer value type. The default for signature is 0.
{
"description": {
"type": "str",
"default input": "\"attribute\"",
"visible": false
},
"signature": {
"type": "int",
"default input": "0"
}
}

The value of a user-defined attribute is a Python expression or a block of Python
statements. For example, the description and priority fields use Python
expressions (FCC and 7).

The signature field uses a block of Python statements, as shown in the following
figure:

When using Python statements, assign a value to the variable with the same name as
the field. In this example, the variable signature is assigned a value at line 14 for the
signature field.
DDT also provides the self.syscall() function. Use this function to run UNIX commands.
In this example, the UNIX command grep is called at line 6.
Users can use user-defined attributes from a parent node to set user-defined attributes
in the current node. To access a user-defined attribute from the parent node, use
B.custom_property.
You can change the name B through DDT's preferences. For example, in the figure
below, the weight attribute in the current node is set to the parent node's weight
attribute plus 3.
If a node's decision logic returns False, its user-defined attributes are not
evaluated. In this case, the node does not have any value for its userdefined attributes, not even a default.

Adding a user-defined attribute file is similar to adding a user-defined library. After
a user-defined attribute file is added to a DDT, the attributes can be edited in open
sessions in the DDT. This can be done by using the Custom Property tab.
You can add more than one user-defined attribute file. If multiple files define the same
attribute, the file added later overwrites the earlier one.

Multi Parent Topological Mode
In some cases, you need to reuse an entire subtree. For example, you have to reuse
a subtree designed to check a module's behavior when the module is used in several
places. DDT offers features such as Hierarchical DDT and External Link DDT Session for
the same.
However, creating many DDT sessions for small trees can make session management
more complex. Duplicating DDT nodes in many places also makes updates harder,
because you have to find and update each node individually.

Multi parent mode is another way to reduce tree construction complexity. In multi parent
mode, a node has more than one parent. This means different nodes can share the same
subtree.
It is possible to build trees more easily in the GUI by sharing nodes. DDT expands the
shared topology into a tree during runtime.
To enable multi parent mode, set up the following environment variable:
setenv DDT_GUI_MULTI_PARENT 1

When you turn on multi parent mode, a node has more than one parent. The first parent
is called the master parent and is shown with a solid line. Any other parents are called
reference parents and are shown with a dashed line.

After completing the creation of a DDT, you can run the created session for automatic
diagnostic via DDT. Here DDT provides following two modes for running a session:
* Batch run
* Regression run

Batch run uses the settings in your session file to run a DDT session. After the run, it
creates a report that shows the results. You can use this report to find any diagnostic
failures.
The report also helps you check if your DDT settings are correct. If you have many errors
to diagnose, you need to run and configure DDT for each error. To make this easier, DDT
offers another mode called regression run.
Regression run mode allows users configuring multiple run settings at once, and then run
all the settings sequentially or concurrently.

Debug Decision Tree (DDT) offers several handy libraries for you to create the decision
tree to capture the debug process. The libraries can be found in the library pane of DDT
GUI. For more details, refer to Debug Decision Tree Usage.
A tree node is created by a pre-defined or Customize Library. You can config input
arguments of a node, such as source file name, searching window, matching condition,
and so on.
Dependent nodes are connected to form a tree. A packet is transmitted from parent to
children, such that a child node could use information from its parent.
A node would first Decide to run or not, according to certain condition of parent and
arguments. If true, then Execute to produce its output packet, such as finding certain
pattern in log or matching signal value in the waveform.

There are Text-Log Libraries, Waveform Libraries, Signature Libraries, Miscellaneous
Libraries, and Customize Library that belong to the tree library.
The following are the introduction to some of the arguments for these libraries:

In this section, go through the decision logic of each library.

Specify Attributes and Signals
Decision logic of Specify Attributes and Signals library contains the following sections:

Textlog Attributes
For textlog related libraries, attributes are specified with the regex in two types: str or dict.
In a simulation text log, a log-line is the texts of a line in a log. For each log-line, it could
contain several attribute values. Users can use regular expression (regex) to extract
attributes values from log-lines, also give a name for each attribute.

The regular expression can be written using named-group syntax where the attributes
are implicitly specified in the pattern. For example, the following regex defines the named
group time, Pattribute, pADDR, pWRITE, and pRDATA. The value of the group time in the
regex is used for the time in a message.
r"\[(?P<time>\S*) .*: Pattribute=(?P<Pattribute>\S*)
pADDR=(?P<pADDR>\S*) pWRITE=(?P<pWRITE>\S*) pRDATA=(?P<pRDATA>\S*)"

Named-group is extremely useful when multiple expressions or-ed together where different
fields could be mapped to the same attribute. Use the syntax | to concatenate multiple
regex string. Below is an example to specify multiple regex with named-group.
regex = '|'.join([
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+)\..+ns.*PSTATE
(?P<throttle_type>\S+)_THROTTLE_START message expected.*",
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+)\..+ns.*PSTATE (?P<throttle_type>)NO_THROTTLE
message expected.*"
])

Without named-group syntax, the default attribute names are numbered from 1 to k, where
k is the number of groups associated with the regular expression pattern.
Attribute names can be explicitly specified by a dict where the key is the pattern, and the
value is a list of attribute names. In this case, the length of the list must be the same as the
number of groups.

Waveform Signals
For waveform related libraries, signals can be specified in three types: str, list, or
SignalMapping.
In a simulation waveform, a signal contains several value-changes.
A signal is specified in its full name with scope separated by `.', such as "top.cpu.clk".
A list of signal full names is also accepted, such as ["top.cpu.clk", "top.cpu.rst"].
Signal Mappings is a format produced by Signal Mapping Wizard, which is a tab named
"Signal Mappings" and located in Global Variables. In a Signal Mapping, the keys are
simple names or aliases, and the values are signals' full names, for example, {"clk":
"top.cpu.clk", "rst": "top.cpu.rst"}.

It is recommended to use Signal Mapping for better readability and maintainability.
The value in the returned Packet shows values corresponding to the signals that are
chosen in signal_names. Notice the Signal Mapping keys are simple names or aliases for
ease of access.

Search Range
Search Range contains the following sections:

Line Range
For textlog related libraries, the start of line range line_start is default to 0, where the
line range starts from the beginning or the end of the log, according to search_forward. It
ends at line_start +- line_delta where the end line is not included.

Time Range
For textlog related libraries, the time range applied if `time' is in the attributes, but it is
always applied in waveform related libraries. Time is assumed to be monotonic increasing
in the log or waveform. The start of time range time_start is default to None, where
the time range starts from the beginning or the end of the log or waveform, according to
search_forward.
The ends at time_start +- time_delta where the end time is not included. The
exclude_time_start argument means if the search start from the same time of
time_start. If it is False, the search starts from time_start +- 1, according to
search_forward.
For waveform related libraries, time can be specified in two formats: int or str. When
an integer is given, the time-unit of the waveform is used. When a time-with-unit string is
given, it is converted to the time-unit of the waveform. For example, `1us' is converted to
1000 when the time-unit of the waveform is `ns'.

Value Compare
The values to compare can be specified in three types: str, list or dict.
For a single value as str, it is broadcasted and compared with all items. For a list of
values, its length should be matched with the number of items in regex or signal_names.
They are zipped to be compared one-by-one. A dict of signal-value mappings can
compare a subset of items.
When there are more than one attribute to be compared, all_match determines the
overall behavior. If it is set to True, all attributes must match the given values. Otherwise,
any attribute matches the given value is treated as successful.

Textlog Value Compare
For textlog related libraries, the value format is text string, as extract by regular
expressions by default. If the given right side value is in another type, then the attribute is
implicitly converted this type.
Assume the given regular expression contains two attributes pstate and pcode, in addition
to time.
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+).*PERF_P(?P<pstate>\S+).*trigger (?P<pcode>.*)_PSTATE"

Take a single value "43" as an example, all attributes are compared with the string "43".
For a list of values ["31", "CSTATE"], the attribute pstate is compared with "31" and
pcode is compared with "CSTATE".
A dict of signal-value mappings {'pcode': "CSTATE"} means the attribute pcode is
compared with "CSTATE".

Waveform Value Compare
For waveform related libraries, the value format is binary string with x/z, example, "100x"
by default. Users can explicitly specify the radix as binary, octal, decimal, or hexadecimal
with prefix "0b", "0o", "0d", or "0h", respectively. For example, "0hc" and "0d10"
both equivalent to the binary string "1010". The value can be an integer as well, which is
converted to a binary string format implicitly.
Assume two 8-bit signals are given: addr and data.
Take a single value "10101111" as an example, all signals are compared with the binary
value "10101111".
For a list of values ["0haf", 127], addr is compared with "10101111" and data is
compared with "11111111".
A dict of signal-value mappings {'data': "0d127"} means data is compared with
"11111111".
The key should be simple-name or alias when signal_names is specified as a

dict.

UVM_ERROR = 2

DDT text-Log libraries allow users to get, find, and match attribute values of a log.
To set up text-log libraries, you might need to know Textlog Attributes. In Find and Match

Signature Libraries
DDT signature libraries allow users to extract the signatures by several ways. A signature
is a special string that is known for a specific feature.
For example, if a test case runs with SVA, a signature can be the scope where the SVA
errors happened.
To set up textlog and waveform related libraries, you might need to know Specify
Attributes and Signals.
In Find and Match libraries, the search range is determined by Line Range and Time
Range. In Match libraries, user have to set up Value Compare.
For UVM-log related libraries, there is an argument UVM Severity.

Weight
There is an int type argument weight default to 1 using for bucketing for each node.
It refers to assigning different levels of importance to signatures during the bucketing
process and allows user to prioritize certain signatures over others based on their
significance.
By assigning weights, you can control the influence of specific signatures on the bucketing
results, resulting in more meaningful and tailored buckets. For some nodes whose
signatures are not used in the bucketing, the weight can be set to 0.

Encode Option Usage
The encode_option default to categorical is used for data preprocessing. In some
situation, the datatype could not be inferred implicitly.
For example, in the case of Get Signature by Shell Command, the output of the command
execution is always a string, However, some signatures want to be set to a numerical type.
For those signatures you cannot get the types, you need to define the encode option for
them. Typically, integers and floating-point numbers are numerical signatures, and others
are categorical signatures.

Customize Python Library
In some cases, the built-in DDT libraries cannot meet your needs. For these cases, you
can use the Customize Python Library. This library lets you change how a node decides
and runs actions using Python code.
The Customize Python Library is listed under Miscellaneous Libraries. To change a
node's decision or execution behavior with this library, follow the given steps:
1. Go to the Config tab.
2. Select either the Execute or Decide button. The Arguments field updates to
execute_code or decide_code.
3. Enter your Python code by clicking the

button.

When you customize decision or execution behavior, you have to use a return statement.
DDT uses the return value to make decisions.
For decision behavior, return a Boolean value. If you return True, DDT checks the userdefined attributes and then run the node's execution. For execution behavior, return a
dictionary with a result field.
Child nodes uses result in their own decision logic. By default, the decision behavior is
return True and the execution behavior is return {'result': packet['result']},
where packet is the input argument.

NewHierarchy and NewLibrary
DDT library view uses the class inheritance hierarchy to display. Thus NewHierarchy
class in the template library becomes a new level under CustomizeLibrary in library
view because it inherits CustomizeLibrary class. Following the same rule, NewLibrary
becomes the leaf item under NewHierarchy.
You can change NewHierarchy and NewLibrary to whatever name you like or create
more hierarchies or libraries via following the same rule.
register_name()
register_name() defines the name showing on library view. Unlike the class names
NewHierarchy or NewLibrary that follows python naming style, name returned by
register_name() can be any valid python string. However, DDT does not accept

duplicated names to avoid potential confusion. Hierarchy and library names returned by
register_name() SHALL be unique.

decide()
Method decide() defines when a node should run according to the return value of its
parent node (argument packet). The default behavior of decide() is based on the result
field in packet that DDT activates the execution of a node only if result field evaluates to
True.
execute()
This method defines the main behavior of a node when it is activated. Once complete,
execute() should return a Packet describing the return value of this library. Every
argument in execute() becomes a configuration on config view.
To give hints to user configuring a node on GUI, library developer can give type hint and
short description for every argument. Type hint of an argument allows DDT to list data with
the same type in the combo box, and description detailed in docstring of execute() can
be divided into 3 parts for different purposes:
1. Method description: Comments for library developers to know the behavior of this
library.
2. Args: Every argument is described in format name: description in one line, and DDT
then scans all these descriptions and presented on GUI.
All the arguments and their order should be the same in the argument list
and Args.
3. Mode: When a powerful library contains many arguments, and not all arguments is
used at the same time, developer can divide arguments to several groups, and each
group is formatted as name: comma separated argument list. Thereafter, GUI has
the same number of radio buttons as the name developer specified in groups. Only
arguments specified in the argument list of a group is shown on GUI. This allows user
focusing on necessary arguments.
Packet
Execution result of a node contains two parts: execution result and generated data.
Execution results are always provided via member result, which is a reserved member in
DDT and SHALL not be removed.
Each generated data should provide a name and associated data type. Since the
generated data is passed to its descendant nodes, and allow descendant node choosing
generated data from combo box, provided data type allow DDT filtering out data with
incompatible data type, and shows only parts of possible data in combo box.

How to Configure Regression Runs in Run Manager
To configure regression runs, perform the following steps:
1. Open Run Manager dialog box.
2. Click Regression Run tab.
Here, you can define different runtime configurations. DDT can run these
configurations in order or at the same time.
The Regression Run tab displays a table for runtime configurations.
The columns in this table are based on the global variables you define.
When you add, remove, or change global variables, the table columns
update. Undo and redo actions also change the columns.
Use the add or delete buttons to manage rows in the table. Each row
is a separate runtime configuration. Click the index cell to select a row.
Selected rows are highlighted. Fill in each cell with the value you want for
each global variable.
For example, the table in the figure shows two configurations as follows:
1. The first row sets WAVEFORM to "data/waves.fsdb".
2. The second row sets TIME_START to 1000 and LOG to "data/riscv.log".
You can leave the cells empty if their values are not required to be changed. After finishing
the settings of runtime configurations, click Run ( ) button to start the process of
regression run.

In this example, DDT runs the two configurations defined in the table.
For the convenience of modifying or creating configurations from daily regression, you can
save or restore regression run configurations to/from files via the buttons and . The
saved regression run configurations can then be used via command line usage.

Organize Run Report
You can generate organized reports based on the file summary.log. The usage can be
found by ddt summary --help command.
For example,
%> ddt summary --help
usage: Process execution from command line. summary [-h] [--output
OUTPUT] [--format FORMAT] [--listall]
summary_file
positional arguments:
summary_file specify summary file
optional arguments:
-h, --help show this help message and exit
--output OUTPUT specify output file
--format FORMAT specify convert format (table, report,
log, json)
--listall list all nodes even if it is not executed

The format `table' means the CSV format. The format `json' means the JSON
format.
%> ddt summary summary.log --format csv --output dvfs_ddt_csv.log
%> cat dvfs_ddt_csv.log

The report format appears similar to a tree.
For example,
%> ddt summary summary.log --format report --output dvfs_ddt_report.log
%> cat dvfs_ddt_report.log

The format log shows the inputs/outputs of each node during the DDT evaluation as
following:
%> ddt summary summary.log --format log --output dvfs_ddt_report.log
%> cat dvfs_ddt_report.log

The summary.log can be loaded back to the DDT GUI through the following steps:
1. Click Run > Show Results on Tree
2. Select summary.log, the DDT execution result is shown as shown in the following
illustration:

The green node is the node which is PASS, the red node is the node which is FAIL, and
the gray node is the node which is NOT RUN.
Use the menu Run > Reset Status, to reset the DDT to the state of not-yetexecution.

Debug Decision Tree (DDT) offers several handy libraries for you to create the decision
tree to capture the debug process. The libraries can be found in the library pane of DDT
GUI. For more details, refer to Debug Decision Tree Usage.
A tree node is created by a pre-defined or Customize Library. You can config input
arguments of a node, such as source file name, searching window, matching condition,
and so on.
Dependent nodes are connected to form a tree. A packet is transmitted from parent to
children, such that a child node could use information from its parent.
A node would first Decide to run or not, according to certain condition of parent and
arguments. If true, then Execute to produce its output packet, such as finding certain
pattern in log or matching signal value in the waveform.

There are Text-Log Libraries, Waveform Libraries, Signature Libraries, Miscellaneous
Libraries, and Customize Library that belong to the tree library.
The following are the introduction to some of the arguments for these libraries:

In this section, go through the decision logic of each library.

Specify Attributes and Signals
Decision logic of Specify Attributes and Signals library contains the following sections:

Textlog Attributes
For textlog related libraries, attributes are specified with the regex in two types: str or dict.
In a simulation text log, a log-line is the texts of a line in a log. For each log-line, it could
contain several attribute values. Users can use regular expression (regex) to extract
attributes values from log-lines, also give a name for each attribute.

The regular expression can be written using named-group syntax where the attributes
are implicitly specified in the pattern. For example, the following regex defines the named
group time, Pattribute, pADDR, pWRITE, and pRDATA. The value of the group time in the
regex is used for the time in a message.
r"\[(?P<time>\S*) .*: Pattribute=(?P<Pattribute>\S*)
pADDR=(?P<pADDR>\S*) pWRITE=(?P<pWRITE>\S*) pRDATA=(?P<pRDATA>\S*)"

Named-group is extremely useful when multiple expressions or-ed together where different
fields could be mapped to the same attribute. Use the syntax | to concatenate multiple
regex string. Below is an example to specify multiple regex with named-group.
regex = '|'.join([
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+)\..+ns.*PSTATE
(?P<throttle_type>\S+)_THROTTLE_START message expected.*",
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+)\..+ns.*PSTATE (?P<throttle_type>)NO_THROTTLE
message expected.*"
])

Without named-group syntax, the default attribute names are numbered from 1 to k, where
k is the number of groups associated with the regular expression pattern.
Attribute names can be explicitly specified by a dict where the key is the pattern, and the
value is a list of attribute names. In this case, the length of the list must be the same as the
number of groups.

Waveform Signals

Attribute names can be explicitly specified by a dict where the key is the pattern, and the

Waveform Signals
For waveform related libraries, signals can be specified in three types: str, list, or
SignalMapping.
In a simulation waveform, a signal contains several value-changes.
A signal is specified in its full name with scope separated by `.', such as "top.cpu.clk".
A list of signal full names is also accepted, such as ["top.cpu.clk", "top.cpu.rst"].
Signal Mappings is a format produced by Signal Mapping Wizard, which is a tab named
"Signal Mappings" and located in Global Variables. In a Signal Mapping, the keys are
simple names or aliases, and the values are signals' full names, for example, {"clk":
"top.cpu.clk", "rst": "top.cpu.rst"}.

It is recommended to use Signal Mapping for better readability and maintainability.
The value in the returned Packet shows values corresponding to the signals that are
chosen in signal_names. Notice the Signal Mapping keys are simple names or aliases for
ease of access.

Search Range
Search Range contains the following sections:

Line Range
For textlog related libraries, the start of line range line_start is default to 0, where the
line range starts from the beginning or the end of the log, according to search_forward. It
ends at line_start +- line_delta where the end line is not included.

Time Range
For textlog related libraries, the time range applied if `time' is in the attributes, but it is
always applied in waveform related libraries. Time is assumed to be monotonic increasing
in the log or waveform. The start of time range time_start is default to None, where
the time range starts from the beginning or the end of the log or waveform, according to
search_forward.
The ends at time_start +- time_delta where the end time is not included. The
exclude_time_start argument means if the search start from the same time of
time_start. If it is False, the search starts from time_start +- 1, according to
search_forward.
For waveform related libraries, time can be specified in two formats: int or str. When
an integer is given, the time-unit of the waveform is used. When a time-with-unit string is
given, it is converted to the time-unit of the waveform. For example, `1us' is converted to
1000 when the time-unit of the waveform is `ns'.

Value Compare
The values to compare can be specified in three types: str, list or dict.
For a single value as str, it is broadcasted and compared with all items. For a list of
values, its length should be matched with the number of items in regex or signal_names.
They are zipped to be compared one-by-one. A dict of signal-value mappings can
compare a subset of items.
When there are more than one attribute to be compared, all_match determines the
overall behavior. If it is set to True, all attributes must match the given values. Otherwise,
any attribute matches the given value is treated as successful.

Textlog Value Compare
For textlog related libraries, the value format is text string, as extract by regular
expressions by default. If the given right side value is in another type, then the attribute is
implicitly converted this type.
Assume the given regular expression contains two attributes pstate and pcode, in addition
to time.
r"\s*(?P<time>\S+).*PERF_P(?P<pstate>\S+).*trigger (?P<pcode>.*)_PSTATE"

Take a single value "43" as an example, all attributes are compared with the string "43".
For a list of values ["31", "CSTATE"], the attribute pstate is compared with "31" and
pcode is compared with "CSTATE".
A dict of signal-value mappings {'pcode': "CSTATE"} means the attribute pcode is
compared with "CSTATE".

Waveform Value Compare
For waveform related libraries, the value format is binary string with x/z, example, "100x"
by default. Users can explicitly specify the radix as binary, octal, decimal, or hexadecimal
with prefix "0b", "0o", "0d", or "0h", respectively. For example, "0hc" and "0d10"
both equivalent to the binary string "1010". The value can be an integer as well, which is
converted to a binary string format implicitly.
Assume two 8-bit signals are given: addr and data.
Take a single value "10101111" as an example, all signals are compared with the binary
value "10101111".
For a list of values ["0haf", 127], addr is compared with "10101111" and data is
compared with "11111111".
A dict of signal-value mappings {'data': "0d127"} means data is compared with
"11111111".
The key should be simple-name or alias when signal_names is specified as a

dict.

Signature Libraries
DDT signature libraries allow users to extract the signatures by several ways. A signature
is a special string that is known for a specific feature.
For example, if a test case runs with SVA, a signature can be the scope where the SVA
errors happened.
To set up textlog and waveform related libraries, you might need to know Specify
Attributes and Signals.
In Find and Match libraries, the search range is determined by Line Range and Time
Range. In Match libraries, user have to set up Value Compare.
For UVM-log related libraries, there is an argument UVM Severity.

Weight
There is an int type argument weight default to 1 using for bucketing for each node.
It refers to assigning different levels of importance to signatures during the bucketing
process and allows user to prioritize certain signatures over others based on their
significance.
By assigning weights, you can control the influence of specific signatures on the bucketing
results, resulting in more meaningful and tailored buckets. For some nodes whose
signatures are not used in the bucketing, the weight can be set to 0.

Encode Option Usage
The encode_option default to categorical is used for data preprocessing. In some
situation, the datatype could not be inferred implicitly.
For example, in the case of Get Signature by Shell Command, the output of the command
execution is always a string, However, some signatures want to be set to a numerical type.
For those signatures you cannot get the types, you need to define the encode option for
them. Typically, integers and floating-point numbers are numerical signatures, and others
are categorical signatures.

Any script or program that can be run in the UNIX system can be used
in command-arguments. Therefore, you can use Python, Perl, C-shell, or

In some cases, the built-in DDT libraries cannot meet your needs. For these cases, you

When you customize decision or execution behavior, you have to use a return statement.
DDT uses the return value to make decisions.
For decision behavior, return a Boolean value. If you return True, DDT checks the userdefined attributes and then run the node's execution. For execution behavior, return a
dictionary with a result field.

return True and the execution behavior is return {'result': packet['result']},
where packet is the input argument.

During the implementation of a library, developer might want to know the information of

NewHierarchy and NewLibrary
DDT library view uses the class inheritance hierarchy to display. Thus NewHierarchy
class in the template library becomes a new level under CustomizeLibrary in library
view because it inherits CustomizeLibrary class. Following the same rule, NewLibrary
becomes the leaf item under NewHierarchy.
You can change NewHierarchy and NewLibrary to whatever name you like or create
more hierarchies or libraries via following the same rule.
register_name()
register_name() defines the name showing on library view. Unlike the class names
NewHierarchy or NewLibrary that follows python naming style, name returned by
register_name() can be any valid python string. However, DDT does not accept

duplicated names to avoid potential confusion. Hierarchy and library names returned by
register_name() SHALL be unique.

decide()
Method decide() defines when a node should run according to the return value of its
parent node (argument packet). The default behavior of decide() is based on the result
field in packet that DDT activates the execution of a node only if result field evaluates to
True.
execute()
This method defines the main behavior of a node when it is activated. Once complete,
execute() should return a Packet describing the return value of this library. Every
argument in execute() becomes a configuration on config view.
To give hints to user configuring a node on GUI, library developer can give type hint and
short description for every argument. Type hint of an argument allows DDT to list data with
the same type in the combo box, and description detailed in docstring of execute() can
be divided into 3 parts for different purposes:
1. Method description: Comments for library developers to know the behavior of this
library.
2. Args: Every argument is described in format name: description in one line, and DDT
then scans all these descriptions and presented on GUI.
All the arguments and their order should be the same in the argument list
and Args.
3. Mode: When a powerful library contains many arguments, and not all arguments is
used at the same time, developer can divide arguments to several groups, and each
group is formatted as name: comma separated argument list. Thereafter, GUI has
the same number of radio buttons as the name developer specified in groups. Only
arguments specified in the argument list of a group is shown on GUI. This allows user
focusing on necessary arguments.
Packet
Execution result of a node contains two parts: execution result and generated data.
Execution results are always provided via member result, which is a reserved member in
DDT and SHALL not be removed.
Each generated data should provide a name and associated data type. Since the
generated data is passed to its descendant nodes, and allow descendant node choosing
generated data from combo box, provided data type allow DDT filtering out data with
incompatible data type, and shows only parts of possible data in combo box.

Reusing an existing DDT can largely improve productivity when creating a new DDT since,
most of the designers reuse existing IP blocks to create a new design. Thus, reusing a
DDT created for existing IP blocks is a great concern when applying DDT to a new project.

This section describes how to leverage existing DDT sessions to form a larger DDT, which
is called hierarchical DDT herein, so that you can focus on creating DDT nodes for the
new part as follows:
1. A new tree library decision node under the Miscellaneous Libraries section,
Reference Session allows you to create a tree node to refer to an existing session, as
shown in the following figure:

2. To setup the path to the referenced session in the node config widget,
a. Click
icon of a reference session. A file pop-up appears from the node.
Meanwhile, you can change the content using the line-edit or combo-box directly.

DDT supports nested reference session, as shown in the following figure:

Trees connected after the reference node is the associated navigation
graph of the reference node. Thus, in this example there are two levels of
Reference Sessions.
3. A special tab named Navigation appears while opening a session with Reference
Session. It allows you to review the expanded hierarchical DDT session.

All the content in the navigation tab is read-only, and you cannot make
changes in navigation tab. Instead, make changes from the associated
session.

4. Perform the following steps to open the session of a node:
a. Right-click from a node to open the context menu. Go to File drop-down appears,
as shown in the following figure:

b. Click Go to File to open the associated DDT session.
c. Select the corresponding node.
5. Soon after you make changes on any of the Reference Sessions, DDT refreshes the
content.
For example, Canvas, Node Config, Global Variables of the navigation tab.
It is mandatory to save changes of the Reference Sessions before DDT can
refresh navigation tab. This is similar to commit step of the changes so that
DDT can capture the committed changes and then refresh the navigation
tab.
6. Tabs other than navigation tab provides the reverse direction of Go to File, called
Locate in Navigation.
This option helps you to locate the same node (request node) in the navigation tab.

Changes not committed via saving session still cannot be displayed in the
navigation tab. In this case, DDT raises an error.
For example, clicking Locate in Navigation from an added node in the
Reference Session results in warning pop-up, if the session is not saved
after adding the node.

Hierarchical Node
Nodes from different sessions have the same UID, it is thus hard to distinguish nodes with
the same UIDs. Selection Pane in the navigation tab has a new column for distinguishing
nodes, where the new column Session Node Name shows the hierarchical name of a
node as shown in the following figure:

The hierarchical name of a node is defined to

TOP::<ref_session_1>::<ref_session_2>::<>::<node_name>

External Link DDT Session

TOP means the topmost session. According to the hierarchical name, you can track the

node through the following:
* Topmost session.

* Find Reference Session with node name <ref_session_1>.
* Find the node with name <ref_session_2> in <ref_session_1>,
* Locate the node with <node_name>.
For example, the TOP::reference::Ref golden::Find UVM Event 12 node can be
located through finding the node named reference in the topmost session that tracks the
node Ref golden in the session associated with reference node, and finally, find the
node name Find UVM Event 12.

Navigation Graph
Running a DDT session with Reference Session inside is equivalent to running the
corresponding navigation graph. The running report summary.log is loaded to DDT, and
you can view the result on navigation graph as shown in the following figure:

External Link DDT Session
To reduce the work needed to build a DDT, users often ask their CAD team to create a
basic DDT session. This basic session helps catch common issues, such as environment
problems.
Project teams can then use this basic DDT as a starting point and build their own DDTs to
handle bugs found during development.
However, updating these DDTs can be difficult. If the CAD team needs to fix a node's
settings or add new nodes for unexpected bugs, they are required to inform all project
teams and update each DDT one-by-one. This process is slow and can lead to mistakes.

External Link DDT Session

To solve this, DDT offers a feature called External Link. With External Link, you can link
other DDT sessions to their current DDT, similar to a soft link in a file system.
For example, the CAD team creates a central DDT with nodes 1, 2, and 3. A project team
can link to this central DDT to create its own client DDT, then add more nodes (such as A,
B, and C) and connect them as needed.
If the central DDT is updated, such as adding node 4, the client DDT automatically reflects
this change through the link. Users do not need to update each client DDT manually.

To to add External Link Sessions in DDT, perform the following steps:
1. Select Edit > External Link.
A dialog box appears in DDT. You can use this dialog box to configure external links.

2. Specify the link-session path in the line edit.
Or

External Link DDT Session

Click the
icon to select a DDT session file in the Link Session - Debug Decision
Tree file dialog box and choose the required DDT session file.
3. Click the Add button to confirm and add the selected session as an external link
session.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 to add more external link sessions as needed.
5. Check the drop-down menu in the Session field to view all the external link sessions
you have added.
The above figure shows an example after adding an external link session.
To help you distinguish between them, nodes added by the external link session are called
link nodes, and nodes created by the user are called local nodes.
Link nodes have a different color with some transparency, and their labels use the format
UID (UID in link session).
For example, the label 6 (7) on the node Match Signal X 9 means the local UID is 6 in the
client DDT, and the link UID is 7 in the central DDT.
In this document, the UID in the client DDT is known as the local UID and the UID in the
central DDT the link UID.
Showing both UIDs helps you to trace the original node in the central DDT through the
UID. DDT also uses the local UID in summary reports after a run to prevent UID conflicts.

All link nodes are in read-only mode. Therefore, the client DDT cannot directly
update or delete link nodes.

External Link DDT Session

To manage external link sessions, follow the given steps:
1. Deleting an Added External Link Session:
a. Open External Link dialog box in client DDT.
b. In the Session field, click the drop-down button to display the list of added link
sessions.
c. Select the link session you want to delete.
d. Click the Delete button to remove the selected external link session from client
DDT.
2. Updating All External Link Sessions:
a. Open External Link dialog box in client DDT.
b. Click Update All.
DDT automatically updates all the added external link sessions in client DDT.
Since link nodes are read-only, you have to use the Delete or Update All
buttons in the External Link dialog box to manage external link sessions.
Direct modification or deletion of link nodes is not supported.
Node Connection Restrictions
You cannot change the connections between link nodes. This means you cannot add new
connections or delete existing connections between link nodes. You also cannot make a
connection that would break an existing connection between link nodes.
For example, you cannot connect node 2(3) Find UVM (Universal Verification
Methodology) Event 13 to node 8 <add node name>.
The DDT does not allow a node to have more than one parent. Making this connection
would break the link between node 2(3) Find UVM Event 13 and node 7(2) Find UVM
Event 12.
However, you can connect a local node to a link node. For example, you cannot delete the
connection between node 3(4) Find Waveform Clock 6 and node 6(7) Match Signal X 9.
You also cannot add a connection between node 3(4) Find Waveform Clock 6 and node
7(2) Find UVM Event 12. But you can add a connection between node 8 <add node
name> and node 7(2) Find UVM Event 12.

Command File
In Verdi, every operation is recorded to a Tcl command file and each operation in DDT
GUI mode is recorded to a DDT command file. The recorded command file name is
ddt_history.log under the current directory.

The recorded DDT command file is played by DDT, that helps to reproduce the steps in
GUI and batch mode:
%> ddt gui --cmdfile ddt_history.log &

or
%> ddt batch --cmdfile ddt_history.log &

This capability allows you to generate a DDT session through scripts. Furthermore, all the
valid Python syntax and libraries are available in the DDT command file.
For example,
import os
def add_lib():
root = os.path.join("userlib")
root = os.path.abspath(root)
for name in ["util", "use_util"]:
lib = os.path.join(root, name)
add_customized_lib(lib)
def create_node(idx, pos):
node = add_tree_node("verdilearn.ddt.treelib.textlog",
"FindAttributeEvent", pos=pos)
set_node_name(node, str(idx))
return node
def main():
add_lib()
n1 = create_node(1, [0, 0])
n2 = create_node(2, [1, 1])
n3 = create_node(3, [2, 2])
n4 = create_node(4, [3, 3])
n5 = create_node(5, [4, 4])
#---------------------------------------------# new line represents the end of this function
# use comment to separate instead
#---------------------------------------------connect_tree_node(n2, n1)
connect_tree_node(n3, n1)
connect_tree_node(n4, n2)
delete_ddt_nodes([n2])
undo()
# undo 13: delete nodes
connect_tree_node(n5, n2)
disconnect_tree_node(n4, n2)
connect_tree_node(n4, n3)
auto_layout()
# set node size on tree node
set_node_size(n2, 300, 150)
save_session("replay.json")
main()

Import a Customized Library
You can develop a customized library for DDT. An example of the customized DDT library
can be found in the following path:
$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/python/demo/ddt/Customized_Lib/
customized_log_parse.py

Import a Customized Library

In the Library widget, use the `+' button to add the customized library. A customized library
is shown in the Libraries Pane as following:

The path of the customized library file is recorded to the DDT session. To
launch DDT GUI or run the DDT, the session file as well as the customized
library is required to be existent.

DDT_WORK_ROOT
By default, DDT session uses the absolute path to record the location of the customized
library (.py). It is possible to replace the absolute path with a specific environment variable
"DDT_WORK_ROOT" for that path. For example, you can modify the DDT session of the
aforementioned example to the following:

By setting the environment variable "DDT_WORK_ROOT", you can organize the path of
the customized libraries to run DDT.

Reusing an existing DDT can largely improve productivity when creating a new DDT since,
most of the designers reuse existing IP blocks to create a new design. Thus, reusing a
DDT created for existing IP blocks is a great concern when applying DDT to a new project.

This section describes how to leverage existing DDT sessions to form a larger DDT, which
is called hierarchical DDT herein, so that you can focus on creating DDT nodes for the
new part as follows:
1. A new tree library decision node under the Miscellaneous Libraries section,
Reference Session allows you to create a tree node to refer to an existing session, as
shown in the following figure:

2. To setup the path to the referenced session in the node config widget,
a. Click
icon of a reference session. A file pop-up appears from the node.
Meanwhile, you can change the content using the line-edit or combo-box directly.

DDT supports nested reference session, as shown in the following figure:

Trees connected after the reference node is the associated navigation
graph of the reference node. Thus, in this example there are two levels of
Reference Sessions.
3. A special tab named Navigation appears while opening a session with Reference
Session. It allows you to review the expanded hierarchical DDT session.

All the content in the navigation tab is read-only, and you cannot make
changes in navigation tab. Instead, make changes from the associated
session.

4. Perform the following steps to open the session of a node:
a. Right-click from a node to open the context menu. Go to File drop-down appears,
as shown in the following figure:

b. Click Go to File to open the associated DDT session.
c. Select the corresponding node.
5. Soon after you make changes on any of the Reference Sessions, DDT refreshes the
content.
For example, Canvas, Node Config, Global Variables of the navigation tab.
It is mandatory to save changes of the Reference Sessions before DDT can
refresh navigation tab. This is similar to commit step of the changes so that
DDT can capture the committed changes and then refresh the navigation
tab.
6. Tabs other than navigation tab provides the reverse direction of Go to File, called
Locate in Navigation.
This option helps you to locate the same node (request node) in the navigation tab.

Changes not committed via saving session still cannot be displayed in the
navigation tab. In this case, DDT raises an error.
For example, clicking Locate in Navigation from an added node in the
Reference Session results in warning pop-up, if the session is not saved
after adding the node.

Hierarchical Node
Nodes from different sessions have the same UID, it is thus hard to distinguish nodes with
the same UIDs. Selection Pane in the navigation tab has a new column for distinguishing
nodes, where the new column Session Node Name shows the hierarchical name of a
node as shown in the following figure:

The hierarchical name of a node is defined to

TOP::<ref_session_1>::<ref_session_2>::<>::<node_name>

External Link DDT Session

TOP means the topmost session. According to the hierarchical name, you can track the

node through the following:
* Topmost session.

* Find Reference Session with node name <ref_session_1>.
* Find the node with name <ref_session_2> in <ref_session_1>,
* Locate the node with <node_name>.
For example, the TOP::reference::Ref golden::Find UVM Event 12 node can be
located through finding the node named reference in the topmost session that tracks the
node Ref golden in the session associated with reference node, and finally, find the
node name Find UVM Event 12.

Navigation Graph
Running a DDT session with Reference Session inside is equivalent to running the
corresponding navigation graph. The running report summary.log is loaded to DDT, and
you can view the result on navigation graph as shown in the following figure:

External Link DDT Session
To reduce the work needed to build a DDT, users often ask their CAD team to create a
basic DDT session. This basic session helps catch common issues, such as environment
problems.
Project teams can then use this basic DDT as a starting point and build their own DDTs to
handle bugs found during development.
However, updating these DDTs can be difficult. If the CAD team needs to fix a node's
settings or add new nodes for unexpected bugs, they are required to inform all project
teams and update each DDT one-by-one. This process is slow and can lead to mistakes.

External Link DDT Session

To solve this, DDT offers a feature called External Link. With External Link, you can link
other DDT sessions to their current DDT, similar to a soft link in a file system.
For example, the CAD team creates a central DDT with nodes 1, 2, and 3. A project team
can link to this central DDT to create its own client DDT, then add more nodes (such as A,
B, and C) and connect them as needed.
If the central DDT is updated, such as adding node 4, the client DDT automatically reflects

title: 1 node
text:
1, 2, and 3. A project team
can link to this central DDT to create its own client DDT, then add more nodes (such as A,
B, and C) and connect them as needed.
If the central DDT is updated, such as adding node 4, the client DDT automatically reflects
this change through the link. Users do not need to update each client DDT manually.

To to add External Link Sessions in DDT, perform the following steps:
1. Select Edit > External Link.
A dialog box appears in DDT. You can use this dialog box to configure external links.

2. Specify the link-session path in the line edit.
Or

External Link DDT Session

Click the
icon to select a DDT session file in the Link Session - Debug Decision
Tree file dialog box and choose the required DDT session file.
3. Click the Add button to confirm and add the selected session as an external link
session.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 to add more external link sessions as needed.
5. Check the drop-down menu in the Session field to view all the external link sessions
you have added.
The above figure shows an example after adding an external link session.
To help you distinguish between them, nodes added by the external link session are called
link nodes, and nodes created by the user are called local nodes.
Link nodes have a different color with some transparency, and their labels use the format
UID (UID in link session).
For example, the label 6 (7) on the node Match Signal X 9 means the local UID is 6 in the
client DDT, and the link UID is 7 in the central DDT.
In this document, the UID in the client DDT is known as the local UID and the UID in the
central DDT the link UID.
Showing both UIDs helps you to trace the original node in the central DDT through the
UID. DDT also uses the local UID in summary reports after a run to prevent UID conflicts.

All link nodes are in read-only mode. Therefore, the client DDT cannot directly
update or delete link nodes.

External Link DDT Session

To manage external link sessions, follow the given steps:
1. Deleting an Added External Link Session:
a. Open External Link dialog box in client DDT.
b. In the Session field, click the drop-down button to display the list of added link
sessions.
c. Select the link session you want to delete.
d. Click the Delete button to remove the selected external link session from client
DDT.
2. Updating All External Link Sessions:
a. Open External Link dialog box in client DDT.
b. Click Update All.
DDT automatically updates all the added external link sessions in client DDT.
Since link nodes are read-only, you have to use the Delete or Update All
buttons in the External Link dialog box to manage external link sessions.
Direct modification or deletion of link nodes is not supported.
Node Connection Restrictions
You cannot change the connections between link nodes. This means you cannot add new
connections or delete existing connections between link nodes. You also cannot make a
connection that would break an existing connection between link nodes.
For example, you cannot connect node 2(3) Find UVM (Universal Verification
Methodology) Event 13 to node 8 <add node name>.
The DDT does not allow a node to have more than one parent. Making this connection
would break the link between node 2(3) Find UVM Event 13 and node 7(2) Find UVM
Event 12.
However, you can connect a local node to a link node. For example, you cannot delete the
connection between node 3(4) Find Waveform Clock 6 and node 6(7) Match Signal X 9.
You also cannot add a connection between node 3(4) Find Waveform Clock 6 and node
7(2) Find UVM Event 12. But you can add a connection between node 8 <add node
name> and node 7(2) Find UVM Event 12.

DDT supports batch mode for operating DDT via commands.
%> ddt batch &

An interactive shell gets a prompt and waits for you to enter the commands as shown in
the following figure:

You can enter the DDT commands and a valid Python code in the interactive shell.
Available DDT commands can be queried via typing help() , or via the documentation
provided in the Hierarchical DDT.

Command File
In Verdi, every operation is recorded to a Tcl command file and each operation in DDT
GUI mode is recorded to a DDT command file. The recorded command file name is
ddt_history.log under the current directory.

The recorded DDT command file is played by DDT, that helps to reproduce the steps in
GUI and batch mode:
%> ddt gui --cmdfile ddt_history.log &

or
%> ddt batch --cmdfile ddt_history.log &

This capability allows you to generate a DDT session through scripts. Furthermore, all the
valid Python syntax and libraries are available in the DDT command file.
For example,
import os
def add_lib():
root = os.path.join("userlib")
root = os.path.abspath(root)
for name in ["util", "use_util"]:
lib = os.path.join(root, name)
add_customized_lib(lib)
def create_node(idx, pos):
node = add_tree_node("verdilearn.ddt.treelib.textlog",
"FindAttributeEvent", pos=pos)
set_node_name(node, str(idx))
return node
def main():
add_lib()
n1 = create_node(1, [0, 0])
n2 = create_node(2, [1, 1])
n3 = create_node(3, [2, 2])
n4 = create_node(4, [3, 3])
n5 = create_node(5, [4, 4])
#---------------------------------------------# new line represents the end of this function
# use comment to separate instead
#---------------------------------------------connect_tree_node(n2, n1)
connect_tree_node(n3, n1)
connect_tree_node(n4, n2)
delete_ddt_nodes([n2])
undo()
# undo 13: delete nodes
connect_tree_node(n5, n2)
disconnect_tree_node(n4, n2)
connect_tree_node(n4, n3)
auto_layout()
# set node size on tree node
set_node_size(n2, 300, 150)
save_session("replay.json")
main()

Preface
Verdi provides fault analysis and debug support through the nTrace and nWave windows.
This document provides detailed information about the fault analysis and debug features
supported by Verdi.

Customer Support

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to

access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Fault Analysis and Debug
Verdi provides fault analysis and debug support through the nTrace and nWave windows.
This chapter contains the following sections:
* Analysis of Fault Coverage
* Management of Exclusions in Fault Coverage
* Using the Fast Signal Database for Fault Analysis
* Viewing the nWave Display of a GM/FM Waveform
* Comparing FSDB files Containing GM+nFM Data in nCompare

Verdi provides an interface to explore fault coverage quality for a design.
Using this interface, you can perform the following tasks:
* Examine fault coverage, test coverage, undetected faults, and the total number of
faults.
* View faults based on their types, such as Stuck at Zero, Stuck at One, Toggle, and so
on.
* Infer faults based on their classes, such as Port, Wire, Array, and so on.
* Quickly scan a design for areas of low coverage using coverage bars.
* Adjust the weights of individual statuses in coverage calculations.
* Check coverage details in the Fault and Unselected panes.
For more details, see the following sections:
* Enabling The Fault Coverage View
* Loading a Fault Coverage Database in the GUI
* Viewing Fault Coverage Details

* Configuring Fault Coverage Windows
* Using the FaultSummary Window
* Using the FaultDetail Window
* Marking of Unrecognized Instances During Fault Analysis
Verdi calls the Fast Signal Database (FSDB) dumping script directly from
$VCS_HOME if
* the VERDI_FUSA_DUMP_FSDB_CMD environment variable is not set
* and, the fault simulation results are written to the fault database by VC
Z01X.
The script is located at:
$VCS_HOME/etc/fcm/dump_fm_fsdb_from_verdi.csh
