From the above register names and the Rel and Nr columns, you can create the following
configuration file with the syntax given below. A Perl script is available to translate the
GDB log into the XML syntax.
% hwsw_reg_to_xml.pl archname logcore_name.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<esw_debug_configuration>
<architecture name="MyCore">
<reg name="zero" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="r1" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[1]"/>
More GPRS info here
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>
<reg name="status" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="estatus" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[1]"/>

<mem name="mem" addrsize="28" path="memory_access"/>

The Verdi HW/SW Debug tool must know which register is the program counter. The Perl
script tries to detect this (any register called pc). Check that this is correct. Edit if needed,
so that you have one is_pc='1' tag, and it is attached to the PC of your core as follows:
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>

Testing and Debugging
This final step validates the configuration file which you created earlier in the process. This
step involves testing the register configuration file and log pattern file along with the GDB
integration.

Validating the Converter Pattern File
The converter can be executed on a sample CPU log file, FSDB file, or generated text
file. It is recommended to initially generate a text file output as this is easier to manually
validate the results of a short test.
% hwsw_debug_convert \
cpuType=MyProc \
patternFile=MyProc.pat \
configName=MyProc \
exeFile=test.elf \
gdbPath=custom_gdb \
clockPeriod=1ns \
-C pwd \
-i cpu.log \
-o output.txt

The Register definition file is specified by configName, and hwsw_debug_convert
searches for MyProc.xml in the current directory (or the directory specified by the -C
argument).
The clockPeriod is required if your CPU log has cycle counts. This parameter should be
removed if you have ns or ps (or other time units) in the log file.
The output format is Verdi FSDB if the .fsdb extension is specified. Any other extension

Testing and Debugging

If any lines do not match a pattern from the log pattern file, then an error is issued. You
can use these errors to debug the line that does not match any pattern.
If register names do not match, then review the MyProc.xml file to see if the register
names are correct.
It is useful to view the original CPU log file and the generated output.txt file together and
perform some basic manual checking for some program counter values, register values,
and memory read/write transactions. Just a few of these lines should be checked to
ensure that the data was parsed correctly. Note that a single pattern with ".*" matches all
lines but does not extract data from the CPU log.
Rerun the conversion, and specify -o hwsw.fsdb to generate an FSDB file for validation.

Invoking Verdi HW/SW Debug Tool
Start by invoking Verdi HW/SW debug from the eclipse side. It is easier to debug any
simple issue with this invoke method. If required, invoke from the Verdi tool later.
% hwsw_debug -C pwd -ssf hwsw.fsdb

If the Eclipse environment does not invoke or fails to invoke GDB, you can troubleshoot as
follows:
1. Register-Configuration File Not Found
Specify the path to the directory containing the register configuration file
% hwsw_debug -C config_directory
% hwsw_debug -config_path config_directory

Check if the name of the configName parameter during conversion is correct. Verdi
automatically adds ".xml" to the end of this name.
2. GDB not found
Invoke your custom_gdb from the PATH environment variable.
Check if the gdbPath=custom_gdb name is correct during the
hwsw_debug_convert step.
Ensure that the custom_gdb is on your path:
% which custom_gdb

3. Other Errors

Testing and Debugging

Check the Verdi console for any error message and correct the problem
Check for any GDB connection error message in the $cwd/hwswDebugLog/
HwSwDebug.log

Check if the .gdbinit files under $cwd or $HOME exist, and if they are correct.
If the Eclipse and GDB tools do not invoke, contact Synopsys for further assistance.

Demo Example 1
This demo uses the dhrystone example located in the $VERDI_HOME/demo/
hwsw_debug/dhrystone directory. This example demonstrates how to invoke Eclipse from
the Verdi platform to debug the design.
Perform the following steps to run the demo:
1. Copy the test case to your local directory:
%> cp -r $VERDI_HOME/demo/hwsw_debug/dhrystone.

2. Import the design with the recorder module library and load the generated FSDB file to
the Verdi platform:
%> gmake hwsw_debug

The following command displays the list of available targets and the description:
%> gmake help

3. Enter Hardware Debug Mode:
In the Welcome Page, click the Work Mode icon.
Select the Hardware Debug Mode option.
Click the Go to Work button to enter Hardware Debug Mode.
4. Invoke HW/SW Debug using the Tools -> Invoke HW SW Debug command. Click the
OK button to confirm the design path field of the FSDB file. Then, specify a workspace
to store the debug project the first time HW/SW Debug is invoked.

5. Click the Yes button in the Confirm Perspective Switch form to confirm the perspective
switch and click the Yes button in the Customize Preference form to use the
recommended value for preference.
6. Get the opcode and pc signals of the verdiHwswDebugTop.cpu0.instruction scope in
the nWave window using the Signal -> Get Signals command to see the executed
operation code and the program counter of the Cortex-A15 ARM core.

hwsw_debug/convert/multi_core directory and demonstrates how to use
hwsw_debug_convert functionality to convert a default log file format to a FSDB file which
is used in HW/SW Debug Solution.
The design consists of two clusters, each with two cores and each core runs different

Known Issues and Limitations
The following known issues exist in the HW/SW Debug feature:
* The hwsw_debug_convert tool does not support specifications of reference cycle
counter signal from an FSDB to calculate timestamps, when the timestamps are based
on cycle counts of an unfixed core clock.
* The hwsw_debug_convert tool does not support the interactive use model.
* It is not possible to alter the embedded core's state (registers, memory, and program
flow) in Eclipse.

Preface
IDX enables reusing waveforms to avoid continually re-creating and re-running stimulus.
A waveform (usually FSDB) records the values each signal or bus contains throughout the
simulation run.
It is a good source to replay those values as stimulus in a simulation.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of non-inclusive language in our

software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction
SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) describe legal or illegal behavior.
Simulation or formal verification can observe this behavior at the point of insertion. The
tool then flags the behavior as passed or failed. The benefits of assertions fall into the
following categories: reducing verification time, catching errors earlier, focusing the design
effort, and pinpointing sources of error.
Assertion IPs (AIP) have pre-built assertions that help to verify and signoff the IPs in
System on Chip (SoC) designs.
They can significantly reduce verification effort and improve design quality. They monitor
a target design without modifying the corresponding RTL. You can apply them in either
simulation or formal verification.
In the simulation environment, it is quite complex to compile the Testbenches and the RTL.
Therefore, once the existing simulation environment is ready, applying the SVA/AIP
afterwards become a challenge.
The following figure illustrates three issues that you need to overcome:
* The SVA/AIP must be bound to the DUT; an additional bind file must be provided.
* The recompilation is needed after applying the SVA/AIP and the bind file.
This may introduce unexpected errors due to the complex existing simulation
environment.

Chapter 1: Introduction

* The simulation runtime performance may be downgraded due to the additional SVA/
AIP checkers.

Setting Up the Environment

% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_installation_path>

Figure 3

IDX Assertion Verification Acceleration

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
As the flow illustrates, IDX assertion verification acceleration flow consists of the following
two steps:
Step 1: IDX assertion testbench compilation.
IDX contains two usage flows for this step. You can choose any one of the flows to fit your
requirement.
* idx -compile_sva flow
* idx -compile_aip flow
Step 2: IDX waveform replay simulation
The differences between the idx -compile_sva and the idx -compile_aip flows are:
* Whether DUT (compiled KDB) is required:
AIP, as the name suggests, does not contain the external reference (XMR) inside.
Therefore, IDX can generate the assertion testbench without considering the DUT.
The idx -compile_aip flow does not require the compiled KDB of the DUT.
SVA modules can contain the XMR. In the idx -compile_sva flow, to successfully
compile the SVA modules, IDX requires the compiled KDB to extract the types and
the signals in the DUT.
* Whether specifying the bind file is required:
The idx -compile_aip flow requires you to specify the bind file to let IDX
understand the connections between AIP and the DUT.
The idx -compile_sva flow does not require you to specify the bind file. IDX can
extract the bind information from the KDB.
The table below outlines the differences between the idx -compile_sva and the idx
-compile_aip flows to generate the assertion testbench:

3. (For the idx -compile_aip flow) The bind file that is used to bind the AIP to the
simulation environment; only one bind file is allowed
4. The configuration file for IDX assertion verification acceleration flow

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The Waveform (FSDB)
IDX allows to read the waveforms, that is, FSDB generated by any of the tools:
Note:
The assertions are not necessary to be included in the source waveform used
for assertion debug.

SVA/AIP Source File and the Corresponding VCS Compilation
Script
The SVA/AIP source files should be provided. An alternative is to specify these files with
the -f option. In addition, the corresponding VCS compilation script is necessary. Some
SVA related options like -assert enable_diag are strongly suggested to add to the
script.

The Bind File
The bind file means, a SystemVerilog file which contains the "bind" statements to bind
the SVA/AIP to the design. Here the design hierarchies and the design signals must
be existent in the waveform. Note that only one bind file is allowed in the IDX assertion
verification acceleration flow.
The syntax for bind statement is as follows:
bind <inst_name | module>
[SVA_ports]

SVA_module

#[SVA_parameters]

SVA_inst_name

The <inst_name> is the design full hierarchical name in the waveform. The <module>
is the module definition name. IDX supports only one <inst_name | module> in a bind
statement.
For example, given the design below:
module top ();
DUT u_dut_01 ( .*);
DUT u_dut_02 (.*);

TEST u_test ();

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
endmodule

IDX supports the bind file with below description:
// bind <module>
bind DUT SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0))
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

u_sva_checker

or
// bind <inst_name>
bind top.u_dut_01 SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0))
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

u_sva_checker

The following// is not supported:
bind top.u_dut_01, top.u_dut_02
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

SVA_MOD

#(.p(1'b0))

u_sva_checker

// not supported
bind DUT, TEST SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0)) u_sva_checker
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr); multiple bind instances or modules are not
supported:

Refer to Limitations and Known Issues for more limitations about the bind file description.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
IDX Assertion Verification Acceleration Configuration File
IDX requires a configuration file to describe the above inputs.
Compile SVA Flow (idx -compile_sva idx_sva_comp.cfg)
Below is the format of the idx_sva_comp.cfg configuration file in the idx -compile_sva
flow:
//waveform file abs. path.
WAVEFORM
= $PWD/novas.fsdb
//SVA source files and the compilation script
SVA_FILE
= -f $PWD/checker_file.f

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
//Specifying the -f file in the configuration file moves the running
directory. Therefore, it becomes necessary to provide either the
absolute path or the root directory along with the relative path.
COMPILE_OPT = +define+DUT_TOP=system.i_cpu.i_ALUB -sverilog
-timescale=1ns/1ns -assert enable_diag -kdb -debug_acc+all
//SVA top scope
SVA_BIND_SCOPE
SVA_TOP_MOD
SVA_TOP_INST

used in the DUT hierarchy
= system.i_cpu.i_ALUB
= alu_checker
= u_checker

//run time simulation options
SIMV_OPT
= -l replay_aip.log -assert report=sva.report
+fsdbfile+replay_aip.fsdb +fsdb+sva_success +fsdb+sva_vacuous
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate tasks
(Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note:
The SIMV_OPT and WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK attributes are the placeholder
for IDX runtime simulation. To enable the assertion verification in the VCS
simulation, the VCS runtime options like -assert success are suggested to be
used. Similarly, to enable the assertion debugging in Verdi, the FSDB dumping
command fsdbDumpSVA is also suggested.
Compile AIP Flow (idx -compile_aip idx_aip_comp.cfg)
Below is the format of the idx_aip_comp.cfg configuration file used in the idx
-compile_aip flow:
//waveform file abs. path.
WAVEFORM = $PWD/novas.fsdb
//bind file abs. path.
BIND_FILE = $PWD/bind.sv
//SVA/AIP source files and the compilation script
COMPILE_OPT = -sverilog -f $PWD/../src/run.f -assert enable_diag -kdb
-debug_acc+all
//run time simulation options
SIMV_OPT = -l replay_aip.log -assert success+report+summary+vacous
+fsdbfile+replay_aip.fsdb +fsdb+sva_success +fsdb+sva_vacuous
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate
tasks (Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note:
The attributes SIMV_OPT and WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK are the placeholder
for IDX runtime simulation. To enable the assertion verification in the VCS
simulation, the VCS runtime options like -assert success are suggested to be
used. Similarly, to enable the assertion debugging in Verdi, the FSDB dumping
command fsdbDumpSVA is also suggested.
Attribute

Description

+in

Maps the input ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +in

+out

Maps the output ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +out

+inout

Maps the inout ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +inout

+mda

Maps the multi-dimensional array signals
under the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +mda

+reg

Maps the registers under the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +reg

Refer to the IDX Waveform Replay Simulation documentation to learn more about IDX
runtime simulation usages.

Debugging the SVA/AIP Simulation Results
Once the replayed FSDB is generated, we can use Verdi to debug the SVA/AIP simulation
results. In Verdi, open Tools > Property Tools > Statistics to check the assertion
simulation results. The following is a snapshot in Verdi:
Figure 5

Debugging the SVA/AIP Simulation Results

In the IDX SAV debug flow, only SVA is dumped in the newly generated FSDB, and no
reference signals are dumped. However, you need to load the original signal FSDB to
debug the issue effectively. You can set up a virtual FSDB to do so.

The stitch virtual file allows hierarchy overlap, but it cannot ensure which file will be read
first. However, you can manually decide the priority of a file that you want to display as
follows:
@FSDB rc file Version 1.0
[VRTL_FILE_HEADER]
1. !! DON'T EDIT [VRTL_FILE_HEADER] SESSION !!
Version = 1
[VRTL_FILE_SOURCE]
FileType = stitch
File1 = idx_sva.fsdb 2
File2 = rtl.fsdb 1

The small number means the higher priority.

Improving the Performance of SVA Compilation Flow
Replaying the value of high frequency signals can take a significant portion of replay
simulation runtime. Clock signals are a common example. IDX proposes the VHF (Verilog
code to handle High Frequency signals) flow for replaying such signals in SVA. This flow
achieves performance similar to that of a native simulation.
The following figure illustrates the IDX VHF flow:
Figure 6

title: Verification ContinuumTM

As the flow illustrates, IDX VHF analyzes signal attributes from the waveform. These
attributes include shape, duty cycle, frequency, and so on. It then generates the Verilog
design for high frequency signals.
The IDX SVA compilation flow elaborates the Verilog design for high frequency signals with SVA checkers and DUT skeleton together - to generate the following:
* a new IDX assertion simulation binary
* the configuration file for IDX waveform replay simulation later

Steps to Enable the IDX VHF Flow
To enable the IDX VHF flow, set the % setenv REP_ENABLE_VHF_ANALYSIS 1
environment variable prior to running the SVA compilation flow.
Limitation of the IDX VHF Flow
Currently, the VHF flow can support periodic signals only. VHF does not support irregular
signals such as gated clock and frequency scaling signals.

Limitations and Known Issues
The limitations of IDX assertion verification acceleration flow are listed as follows:
* IDX AIP compilation flow does not support Mixed-language/VHDL design.
* Only one bind file is allowed in the IDX AIP compilation flow.
If you have multiple bind files, concatenate them into a single bind file.
* In the bind file, below port mapping style are not supported:
Positional port map
* The following example illustrates the unsupported port mapping style:
// not supported - positional port mapping
bind DUT SVA_MOD u_sva_checker ( clk_i, rst, addr );

* If the bind file uses a signal of unpacked type, see the following AIP example:
module SVA_CHECKER ( input i_clk, );
logic i_clk [1:0]; // unpacked typel

endmodule

* The bind file shown in the following example may cause VCS compilation failure:
// not supported - unpacked port mapping
bind DUT SVA_CHECKER u_sva_checker ( .i_clk (i_clk), );

To resolve the issue, split the unpacked bus into individual bit-wise signals. For
example:
// supported - concatenation port mapping
bind DUT SVA_CHECKER u_sva_checker ( .i_clk ( {i_clk[0], i_clk[1]} ),
);

Introduction
The pre-silicon verification involves running simulation at unit-level (or IP level), clusterlevel, and finally at SoC level. The tests at different levels are usually different. When
a simulation failure happens at SoC level, it requires a lot of iterations to create a test
scenario to replicate the bug at all lower levels of validation, especially the IP level as
shown in the following figure. This bug replication process is very challenging as an SoC
environment is always very complex. In many cases it is possible the bugs cannot be
reproduced at lower levels. As a result, the engineers must debug at SoC level directly.
What is even worse, any context changes (a patch that contains the suspected fix of the
bug) requires the recompilation and resimulation at SoC level, which is time consuming
and inefficient.
Figure 1

Reproduction of SoC Simulation Environment to IP level

To resolve above problem, IDX enables reusing waveforms from SoC simulation to the IP
environment as shown in the following figure. As the waveform (usually FSDB) records
the values each signal/bus contains throughout the simulation run, it is a good source to
'replay' the values as the stimulus in a simulation. The 'replayed' values can be applied to
every level of validation, thus substantially save debug time and improve productivity. The
flow that reuses an SoC waveform to replay the simulation scenario at IP level is referred
to as 'IDX IP Debug Acceleration'.
Figure 2

Replay SoC Simulation Waveform (FSDB) to IP Level by IDX

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
IDX IP Debug Acceleration Usage Model
The following sections describe how to enable IDX IP Debug Acceleration flow and gives a
demo case to show how it works.
* Setting Up the Environment
* The Flow
* Limitations and Known Issues

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Setting Up the Environment
You need to run the following command in the C (CSH) shell environment before running
IDX:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_installation_path>
% setenv PATH $VERDI_HOME/bin:$PATH

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following figure illustrates the flow of IDX IP Debug Acceleration:
Figure 3

IDX IP Debug Acceleration

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
As the flow illustrates, IDX IP Debug Acceleration flow consists of two steps:
Step 1: IDX IP map compilation
Step 2: IDX waveform replay simulation
The detailed usage of above steps is described in the following sections.
To enable IDX runtime simulation, the following data needs to be prepared as the inputs.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Preparing the Inputs
1. The waveform (FSDB) for reuse
2. The VCS compiled simv executable for simulation
3. The mapping file that specifies the signal names to be 'replayed' from the waveform to
the simv
4. The IDX configuration file

The Waveform (FSDB)
IDX allows to read the waveforms, that is, FSDB generated by any of the tools.

The VCS Compiled simv Executable for the IP Level Design
The following VCS compilation options must be added:
* -debug_acc+f+w+cbk+fwn (or -debug_acc+all)
* -kdb
The following VCS compilation options are optional but suggested to be added:
-deraceclockdata=lerupdate

The option -deraceclockdata=lerupdate can resolve most of the race conditions during
the IDX waveform replay simulation.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The Scope Mapping File
The scope mapping between the SoC hierarchy in the FSDB and the IP hierarchy in the
simv executable must be provided.
The following is an example of the scope mapping file used in IDX. The left hand side of
the symbol '=>' is the IP-level full hierarchical name in the simv executable, while the righthand side is the SoC-level full hierarchical name in the FSDB.
// <simv_scope_full_name> => <waveform_scope_full_name>
wrap.u_cpu_ip => testbench.soc.dut_wrap.dut.cpu_ip_01

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
IDX IP Debug Acceleration Configuration File
To put all above necessary inputs together, IDX requires a IP Debug Acceleration
configuration file. The following example shows the format of the configuration file:
###############################################################
# Common fields
# The field here will give impact on all waveform files
###############################################################
//simv.daidir abs. path. [MUST HAVE] (Optional in simv. first usage)
SIMV_DAIDIR = $PWD/simv.daidir
//necessary runtime options for running original simulation. (Optional)
SIMV_OPT = -l simv_eth.log
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate tasks
(Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA
#################################################################
# Record fields (Waveform dedicated fields)
# The field here will give impact to the waveform file for each record
only ################################################################
############## record 1 ##############
{
//waveform file abs. path. [MUST HAVE]
WAVEFORM = $PWD/novas.fsdb
//specify the IP scope mapping between waveform and the simv. [MUST HAVE]
SCOPE_MAP =
scope_map_file
AUTO_MAP = +in +inout
}
############## record 2 ##############
{
//can be empty as a placeholder
}

In general, the configuration file inherits all fields and settings of the configuration file used
in IDX 'waveform replay' simulation. The only difference is, in the record field, instead of
specifying the mapping file, the SCOPE_MAP and AUTO_MAP are used.
The SCOPE_MAP describes the scope mapping file, see The Scope Mapping File). The
AUTO_MAP can be one or many of the following:
Attribute

Description

+in

Maps the input ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +in

Attribute

Description

+out

Maps the output ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +out

+inout

Maps the inout ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +inout

+mda

Maps the multi-dimensional array signals
under the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +mda

+reg

Maps the registers under the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +reg

The AUTO_MAP setting can use multiple attributes, for example:

AUTO_MAP =

+in +inout

Running IDX IP Map Compilation
Perform the following command to run IDX IP map compilation:
% idx -compile_map <IP_map_compilation_config_file> [-o
<ip_map_directory_name>]

The command executes the step as shown in the following illustration:
Figure 4

IDX IP Debug Acceleration

If the option -o <ip_map_directory_name> is not specified, the default output directory
idx.map.dbdir/ is generated under the current path.
After finishing the step, the IDX gives the following messages:
[IDX_INFO]Generate new config file '<ip_map_directory>/idx.cfg' begin.
[IDX_INFO]Generate new config file end.
[IDX_INFO]Please use the command below to run replay process:
> idx -cfg <ip_map_directory>/idx.cfg -work WORK_DIR_NAME_YOU_WANT
[IDX_INFO]Compile MAP done.

The message instructs how to proceed the follow-up IDX waveform replay simulation.

Running IDX Waveform Replay Simulation
After finishing IDX IP map compilation described in the Running IDX IP Map Compilation
section, all the necessary files are available and described in the generated IDX runtime
configuration file. Therefore, just follow the message to perform the IDX waveform replay
simulation, such as:
% idx -cfg ./idx.map.dbdir/idx.cfg -work replay_work

Executing an Example
The Design
You need to use the MinSoC (Minimal OpenRISC System on Chip) design as an example
to run IDX IP Debug Acceleration. The design case can be found in the following path:
$VERDI_HOME/demo/IDX/IP_Debug/

The MinSoC architecture is shown in the following figure:
Figure 5

MinSoC Architecture

The entire design hierarchy including the Testbench is illustrated as follows.

Figure 6

MinSoC Simulation Hierarchy

The simv_ethmac executable does not contain any stimulus to drive the IP ethmac. The
Testbench module test_ethmac is just a wrapper to instantiate the IP.

Perform IP Map Compilation
To perform IP Map Compilation, go to the idx_ip_work/ directory and execute the
following command to perform IDX IP map compilation. You need to copy $VERDI_HOME/
demo/IDX/IP_Debug to a directory idx_ip_work in your workspace.
% cd idx_ip_work
% idx -compile_map compile_ip_map.cfg

The configuration file compile_ip_map.cfg is shown as follows. You should use '+in
+inout' attributes in the 'AUTO_MAP' setting.
#################################################################
# Common fields
# The field here will give impact on all waveform files
#################################################################
SIMV_DAIDIR = $ROOT/ethmac_ip/simv_ethmac.daidir
SIMV_OPT
= -l ethmac.log +fsdbfile+ethmac_replay.fsdb
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all;
#################################################################
# Record fields (Waveform dedicated fields)
# The field here will give impact to the waveform file for each record
only
#################################################################

Limitations and Known Issues

############## record 1 ##############
{
WAVEFORM = $ROOT/sim/soc.fsdb
SCOPE_MAP = ./ethmac_to_soc_scope_map.txt
AUTO_MAP = +in +inout
}

The scope mapping file, ethmac_to_soc_scope_map.txt, used in the SCOPE_MAP setting
is shown in the following example:
test_ethmac.u_ethmac => minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0.ethmac

Replaying SoC Waveform Stimulus to the IP Design
In the idx_ip_work/ directory, run the following command to perform IDX waveform replay
simulation:
% make run_replay

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Or
% idx -cfg idx.map.dbdir/idx.cfg -work replay_ETHMAC_work

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
After the IDX simulation, the replayed FSDB ethmac_replay.fsdb and the simulation log
file ethmac.log are generated. We can begin the IP level debug with these files.

Limitations and Known Issues
The limitation of the IDX IP debug acceleration flow is listed as follows:
* IDX IP map compilation does not support Mixed-language/VHDL design.

Introduction
Waveform (FSDB) records the signals activities in simulation or emulation. These activities
are usually a very good source to reuse to accelerate the debug and validation iterations.
IDX (Intelligent Debug Acceleration) is an intelligent waveform reuse tool. It reads signal
value changes in a waveform. It applies those values to the specified signals in a VCS
compiled simulation executable (simv). By reusing signal activities in simulation, IDX
avoids continually re-creating and re-running stimulus.
IDX enables many valuable use cases to speed up debug and validation. Examples
include SoC to IP debug, Encrypted IP debug, Assertion Modules Validation, and
Testbench Interactive Debug Acceleration. The kernel of these use cases is the IDX
`waveform replay' simulation engine. This chapter focuses on the usages of IDX waveform
replay simulation.

IDX Waveform Replay Simulation Usage Model
The following sections describe how to enable IDX Waveform Replay Simulation flow and
gives a demo case to show how it works:
* Setting Up the Environment
* Preparing the Inputs
* IDX Waveform Replay Simulation Configuration
* IDX With Multiple Waveforms
* Executing an Example
* Limitations and Known Issues

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Setting Up the Environment
You need to run the following command in the C (CSH) shell environment before running
IDX:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_installation_path>
% setenv PATH $VERDI_HOME/bin:$PATH

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following figure illustrates the flow in IDX waveform replay simulation:

To enable IDX waveform replay simulation, below four data are necessary to be prepared
as the inputs:
1. The waveform (FSDB) for reuse
2. The VCS compiled simv executable for simulation
3. The mapping file which specifies the signal names to be `replayed' from the waveform
to the simv
4. The IDX configuration file

The Waveform (FSDB)
IDX allows to read the waveforms, that is, FSDB generated by any of the tools.

The simv Executable
IDX intends to put values to the VCS compiled simv executable. Therefore, the following
VCS compilation switches must be used:
-debug_acc+f+w+cbk+fwn, (or -debug_acc+all)

The following options are not mandatory but strongly suggested to add to:
* -kdb
* -deraceclockdata=lerupdate
The -deraceclockdata=lerupdate option is used to resolve the potential race condition
issues during in waveform replay simulation.

The Mapping File
IDX reads the mapping file with the following format per line:
* <simv_signal_full_hierarchical_name> =>

<waveform_signal_full_hierarchical_name>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
Verification ContinuumTM
text:
With the mapping, IDX is going to read the values of RHS from the waveform and put the
values to LHS of simv during the simulation.

The Configuration File
IDX requires a configuration file to describe the inputs and the options used during the
waveform replay simulation. Following is the basic format of the configuration file:
//simv.daidir abs. path. [MUST HAVE] (Optional in simv. first usage)
SIMV_DAIDIR = $PWD/simv.daidir
//necessary runtime options for running original simulation. (Optional)
SIMV_OPT = +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_HIGH +UVM_TESTNAME=eth_test -l simv_eth.log
//specify the path where the simv executable is going to run. (Optional)
//default is the current directory if not specified
SIMV_RUN_PATH =

//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate
tasks (Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA
################################################################
only #################################################################
{
//waveform file abs. path. [MUST HAVE]
WAVEFORM = $PWD/novas.fsdb
//signal mapping list. [MUST HAVE]
MAP= $PWD/wave_rep.map
}
############## record 2 ##############
{
//can be empty as a placeholder
}

In general, there are two fields used in the configuration file.
* Common field:
This field describes the information about the VCS compiled simv executable. The
SIMV_DAIDIR setting is a must-have.
* Record field:
This field describes the information about the waveform and the mapping file.
As IDX allows `replaying' multiple waveforms, it is possible to have multiple
records. Each record must describe the information about the waveform and the
corresponding mapping file.
The record field can be empty as a placeholder; but the entire configuration file
must contain at least one record field.
IDX Waveform Replay Simulation Configuration gives detailed description to the
configuration setting. IDX With Multiple Waveforms describes how to use multiple record
fields to run IDX waveform replay simulation.

Running IDX Waveform Replay Simulation
idx Command Usage
IDX uses the "idx" executable for waveform replay simulation. The syntax of "idx" usage is
as follows:
% idx -cfg <IDX_configuration_file> -work <IDX_working_directory>

Where:
* <IDX_configuration_file>: the configuration file described in the Checking IDX
Results.
* <IDX_working_directory>: the directory where the IDX results are present.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
simv Command Usage
IDX allows to use the simv executable to launch IDX waveform replay simulation. The
simv runtime options are as follows:
% simv -ucli +idx_cfg <IDX_configuration_file> \
+idx_work <IDX_working_dir> <other_simv_options>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Where -ucli is a necessary option to enable IDX on simv.
In the simv first usage, IDX can identify the simv executable and the simv options
automatically. Therefore, it is unnecessary to set the following attributes in the common
fields in the configuration file:
* SIMV_DAIDIR =
* SIMV_OPT =
If the configuration file still contains the SIMV_DAIDIR attribute, IDX will choose the simv
executable described in the configuration file. That is, the priority of IDX invoking simv is:
* SIMV_DAIDIR attribute in the configuration file > simv executable used in the command
line.
If you specify the simv runtime options both in the command line and in the SIMV_OPT
attribute in the configuration file, IDX will join all the runtime options together.

Using IDX in Verdi/VCS Interactive Debugging
Use the option +idx_interactive_gui to enable IDX waveform replay simulation in
Verdi/VCS interactive debugging:
% simv -ucli +idx_cfg <IDX_configuration_file>
+idx_work <IDX_working_dir> \
+idx_interactive_gui
<other_simv_options>

\

In the Verdi/VCS interactive debugging, IDX does not exit and stop simulation until
user exits Verdi or exits simulation by giving the UCLI command `exit' through the Verdi
console.

Checking IDX Results
Checking Files After IDX Simulation
After IDX waveform replay simulation, the resultant simulation logs are recorded at
the working directory and the replayed waveform is recorded at the path where the
simv executable locates. For example, consider the following SIMV_OPT attribute in the
configuration file:
SIMV_DAIDIR = /tmp/user1/simv.daidir
SIMV_OPT = -l idx_sim.log +fsdbfile+replay.fsdb

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
After running the following IDX command:
% idx -cfg test.cfg -work IDX_WORK

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The simulation log idx_sim.log is recorded to the directory IDX_WORK and the replayed
FSDB replay.fsdb is generated at the path /tmp/user1/, which is the path that the simv
executable locates.

Sanity Checks Between the Used Waveform and the IDX Results
Based on the signals mapping described in the mapping file, IDX intends to capture the
values from the waveform and put the values to the corresponding signal in the simv
during the simulation. To make sure IDX really applies the `replay' process, the following
command can be used for sanity checking by waveform comparison:
% idx -sanitychk <mapping_file> <replayed_waveform>
<idx_used_waveform> [+time min max] [+x] [+z] [+maxerror num]
[+sigmaxerror num]

Where,
* <mapping_file>: the mapping file described in The Mapping File
* <replayed_waveform>: the resultant waveform after IDX runtime replay simulation
* <idx_used_waveform>: the waveform described in the configuration file The Mapping
File
* [+time <min> <max>]: the time window to do the waveform comparison
If not specified, default time window is the entire time window of
<replayed_waveform>

Time unit is necessary for min and max time

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
* [+x]: if specified, the `x' value will be compared
* [+z]: if specified, the `z' value will be compared
* [+maxerror <num>]: if specified, when the total mismatched number exceed the
number <num>, the comparison process will be terminated
* [+sigmaxerror <num>]: if specified, when the mismatched number of a signal reach
the number <num>, the comparison process will be terminated
Following is an example of sanity check command:
% idx -sanitychk
+maxerror 500

replay.map

replay.fsdb

source.fsdb

+x

+z

Overview
The following are the valid attributes in the IDX waveform replay configuration file:
//simv.daidir abs. path. [MUST HAVE] (Optional in simv. first usage)
SIMV_DAIDIR =
//runtime options for running original simulation. (Optional)
SIMV_OPT =
//specify the path where the simv executable is going to run. (Optional)
//default is the current directory if not specified
SIMV_RUN_PATH =
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate
tasks (Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK =
//control the simv simulation time (Optional)
SIMV_TIME_CONTROL =

only #################################################################
{
//waveform file abs. path. [MUST HAVE]
WAVEFORM =
//signal mapping list. [MUST HAVE]
MAP=
//the priority of the signal list when IDX put values to the simv.
(Optional)
KEY_MAP=
//control the time window IDX put values to the simv. (Optional)
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION=
//global time shift to control the time IDX put values to the
simv. (Optional)
DELAY=
//control the strength IDX puts values to the simv. (Optional).
//possible options [+force|+deposit|+force +release]. default: +force
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE=
}

Common Fields
The following table lists the common field attributes:
Attribute

Description

SIMV_DAIDIR =

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
[MUST HAVE] (Optional in simv. first usage)
simv.daidir abs. path

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
SIMV_DAIDIR = /tmp/guest/user1/simv.daidir
SIMV_OPT =

(Optional) runtime options for running original simulation.
SIMV_OPT = -l simv_eth.log
+UVM_TESTNAME=eth_test +fsdbfile+idx_sim.fsdb

SIMV_RUN_PATH =

(Optional) specify the path where the simv executable is
going to run. Default is the current directory if not
specified.
SIMV_RUN_PATH = /tmp/user/work/

WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK =

(Optional) waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use
semicolon to separate tasks.
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars 0 +all;
fsdbDumpSVA

SIMV_TIME_CONTROL =

(Optional) control the simv simulation time.
Syntax:
SIMV_TIME_CONTROL = [+simv] [+stop=$num[unit]]
[+record=[$num|last] [,$extend_num[unit]]]
+simv: the simulation time is controlled by the simv
executable. If simv was terminated at time T, IDX will stop
at time T. If simv never stops when user gives `run' in the

UCLI prompt, then IDX never stops
+stop=$num[unit]: stop the simulation at a specific
simulation time. If the [unit] is not specified, the simv
resolution time unit will be used
SIMV_TIME_CONTROL = +simv
SIMV_TIME_CONTROL = +stop=1550
SIMV_TIME_CONTROL = +stop=2550ps

Record Fields
The following table lists the record field attributes:
Attribute

Description

WAVEFORM =

[MUST HAVE] waveform file abs. path.
WAVEFORM = /tmp/guest/user1/novas.fsdb

MAP =

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
[MUST HAVE] signal mapping list file. One signal
mapping per line.
Mapping File Format:
<simv_full_hier_name> =>
<waveform_full_hier_name>
<simv_full_hier_name> => <const_value>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
MAP = /tmp/guest/user1/sig_map.txt

KEY_MAP =

(Optional) specify the signal list that has the priority to
notify IDX when putting values to the simv.
The KEY_MAP file is used to specify the clock/reset signals
such that IDX can have clock/reset signals put values
to the simv with higher order, and then put the values to
the other signals. With this way the race condition in the
simulation can be avoided.
The signals described in the KEY_MAP file must be found
in the <RHS> of the mapping file. That is, the signal in the
KEY_MAP file is the signal in the waveform.
Key_Map File Format:
<waveform_sig_full_hier_name> [P = <num>]P =
<num>: specify the priority of the signal to put value. The
higher <num>, the higher priority.
If not specified "P = <num>", IDX treats the signal as "P =

1"
Example:

KEY_MAP = clk_rst.list
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION =

(Optional) specify the time window IDX put values to the
simv. If not specified, IDX will use the time window of the
waveform.
Syntax:
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = [([<num>[unit]]
- [<num>[unit]])][, ([<num>[unit]] [<num>[unit]])
The [unit] can be one of the following words (s, ms,

us, ns, ps, fs) and can be ignored; if not specified, the
waveform time unit will be applied.
The simple format is:
(<BEGIN_TIME> - <END_TIME>)
<BEGIN_TIME> can be ignored; then the minimal time in

the waveform will be used.
<END_TIME> can be ignored; then the maximum time in
the waveform is used.
Example:
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = (1100 - 5500)
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = (100ns - 300ns)
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = (0ns-200ns),
(300ns-500ns), (700ns-900ns)
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = ( - 6500ns)
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION = (10ns - )

DELAY =

(Optional) global time shift to control the time IDX put
values to the simv. The concept is as below picture
illustrates.

With the setting of DELAY value, IDX will apply the
stimulus to the simv since the time "A + W" to the time "B
+ W".
Note:
The DELAY value `W' can be positive or negative. If `A
+ W' is smaller than 0, then time 0 is used in simv

MAP_REPLAY_TYPE =

simv.//possible options. default: +force
Syntax:
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE = [ +force | +deposit |
+release | +force +release ]
If not specified MAP_REPLAY_TYPE, +force will be applied.
When MAP_REPLAY_TYPE = +force +release, IDX

will force the values since the begin time described in
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION, and release those signals at the
end time
Example:
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE = +force +release
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE = +deposit

The IP module we are going to demo the IDX is the Ethernet (ETH). The full hierarchical

The following table shows the environment variables that can be used when running IDX
waveform replay simulation:
Environment Variable

Description

REP_PROF

When this environment variable is set to 1, the
memory and runtime summary for all processes
(idx, simv, rep_wavereader) invoked by IDX is
dumped.

REP_WAVEREADER_HBNF_NOREPLAY
_DISABLE

By default, if the <LHS> signal exists in the simv
executable but the <RHS> signal does not exist in
the waveform file, IDX gives ERROR messages
and stops the runtime replay simulation.
When this environment variable is set to 1,
IDX prints the WARNING messages instead
of stopping the process. By this way, you can
identify which signals described in the mapping
file do not exist in the waveform file.

REP_DISABLE_PERL_VERSION_CHECK

IDX requires the Perl version >= 5.006 to ensure
that the functionality of the key map file is correct.
By default, IDX checks the version if you specify
the key map in the IDX configuration file. When
this environment variable is set, IDX ignores the
checking instead of stopping the process.

REP_VCS_INCR_COMPILE_EXECUTION_P
ATH

IDX requires VCS re-elaboration on a pure VHDL
design to generate the new simv executable for
waveform replaying.
By default, IDX uses the same execution path
of simv.daidir that you provide to do VCS
re-elaboration.
The execution path can be controlled by this
environment variable.

REP_VCS_INCR_COMPILE_OUTPUT_PATH

IDX requires VCS re-elaboration on a pure VHDL
design to generate the new simv executable for
waveform replaying.
By default, IDX puts a new simv executable and
intermediate files under the hidden directory:
.snps_idx_vcs_incr_compile_dir. The path of
this hidden directory is under the path where IDX
was invoked.
The output path of hidden directory can be
controlled by this environment variable.

REP_VCS_ENV_SYNOPSYS_SIM_SETUP

IDX requires VCS re-elaboration on a pure VHDL
design to generate the new simv executable for
waveform replaying.
By default, IDX refers to the synopsys_sim.setup
specified in simv.daidir for re-elaboration.
The path of synopsys_sim.setup for IDX
reference can be controlled by this environment
variable.

REP_VL_RECOG_CLK_DISABLE

By default, IDX utilizes the technique provided by
VerdiLearn to recognize the clock signal list as the
key map file on a Mixed-language/VHDL design to
avoid potential race condition in VCS simulator.
When this environment variable is set, IDX does
not call VerdiLearn to recognize clock signals.

REP_VL_RECOG_CLK_FORCE

When this environment variable is set, IDX calls
VerdiLearn to recognize the clock signal list as the
key map file on a SystemVerilog/Verilog design.

REP_VL_RECOG_CLK_CONCAT_USER_KEY
MAP

By default, IDX does not touch the user-specified
key map file. However, you can still can ask IDX
to append the recognized clock signals to the key
map file by setting this environment variable.

REP_VL_CLK_PRIORITY

By default, the priority of the recognized clock
signal is 2. The default priority can be changed by
setting this environment variable.

Limitations and Known Issues

Limitations and Known Issues
The limitations of IDX are listed as follows:
* Mixed-language/VHDL support in IDX
IDX needs VCS re-elaboration on a pure VHDL design to generate the new simv
executable for waveform replaying. This may take a while but it needs to be done
only once.
IDX cannot apply the stimulus to VHDL physical, time, string, access, and file data
types in the simv executable.
IDX cannot apply the stimulus to VHDL variable in the simv executable.
Replaying the VHDL waveform to the SystemVerilog/Verilog design is not supported
and vice versa. It might raise unexpected behavior due to the value system
mismatch between VHDL and SystemVerilog/Verilog.
Potential race condition issues may arise on a Mixed-language/VHDL design in
VCS simulator.
You must give proper priority for the signals to be replayed, that is, clock/reset
signals, in the key map file to avoid a potential race condition problem.
If the priority is not specified, IDX attempts to recognize the clock signals
and give them the priority. The default priority is 2. The default priority can be
changed by setting the environment variable REP_VL_CLK_PRIORITY.
If the priority is specified, IDX does not touch the user-specified key
map file. However, you still can ask IDX to append the recognized
clock signals to the key map file by setting the environment variable
REP_VL_RECOG_CLK_CONCAT_USER_KEYMAP.
* The IDX simv first usage on a pure VHDL design is not supported.
* The minimum version requirement of Perl for IDX is 5.006. The functionality of the key
map file cannot work with the earlier versions of Perl.
* When using IDX in Verdi/VCS interactive debugging, the command "restart" is not
supported.
* If the time precision is different between the simv executable and waveform, IDX will
give the warning message like below (assume the time precision in simv=ns, and the
waveform=ps).
[IDX_WARN-TPD] Time precision is diff.

Purpose
This document explains how to install the Verdi and Siloti systems, symbol libraries and
memory definition table (MDT) files. The manual should be read from beginning to end,
although you may skip any sections with which you are already familiar.
For detailed descriptions of individual commands, refer to the appropriate chapter of the
Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual. For detailed usage on any of the installed
products, refer to the appropriate user's guide as listed in the Related Publications section
of this chapter.

Audience
The audience for this document includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification such as Verilog, VHDL, and SystemVerilog, and
typically install and set-up tool software.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Verdi and Siloti system runs: UNIX or Linux and that you are knowledgeable
in Verilog or VHDL and digital logic design.

Chapter 1: About This Document
Book Organization

Book Organization
This Installation and System Administration Guide is organized as follows:
* About This Document provides an introduction to this document and explains how to
use it.
* Installing Verdi and Siloti Software explains how to install Verdi and Siloti systems on
the platforms they support.

Conventions Used in This Book
The following conventions are used in this document:
* Italics font is used for emphasis, book titles, section names, design names, file path,
and file names within paragraphs.
* Bold is used to emphasize text, highlight titles, menu items, and other Verdi terms.
* Courier type is used for program listings. It is also used for test messages that the
Verdi platform display on the screen.
* NOTE describes important information, warnings, or unique commands.
* Menu -> Command identifies the path used to select a menu command.
* Left-click or Click means click the left mouse button on the indicated item.
* Middle-click means click the middle mouse button on the indicated item.
* Right-click means click the right mouse button on the indicated item.
* Double-click means click twice consecutively with the left mouse button.
* Shift-left-click means press and hold the <Shift> key then click the left mouse button on
the indicated item.
* Drag-left means press and hold the left mouse button, then move the pointer to the
destination and release the button.
* Drag means press and hold the middle mouse button on the indicated item then move
and drop the item to the other window.

Related Publications
* Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual - provides detailed information on the
Verdi and Siloti command sets.
* Verdi and Siloti Quick Reference Guide - provides a quick reference for using the Verdi
and Siloti systems with typical debug scenarios.
* Linking Novas Files with Simulators and Enabling FSDB Dumping - provides detailed
information on linking Novas object files with supported simulators for FSDB dumping
and the related dumping commands.
* Verdi User Guide and Tutorial - provides detailed information on using the Verdi
platform.
* Siloti User Guide and Tutorial - provides detailed information on using the Siloti system.
* nAnalyzer User Guide and Tutorial - provides detailed information on using the
nAnalyzer Design Analysis module.
* nECO User Guide and Tutorial - provides detailed information on using the nECO
Automated Netlist Modification module.
* Release Notes - provides current information about the latest software version. Refer to
the 'View release notes' link on the product downloads page.
* Language Documentation
Hardware description (Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog, etc.) and verification language
reference materials are not included in this manual. For language related documents,
refer to the appropriate language standards board (www.ieee.org, www.accellera.org)
or vendor (www.synopsys.com, www.cadence.com) websites.

Overview
Workstation Requirements
Before installing Verdi and Siloti systems, verify that you have the following components:
* Software DVD or the software files from the Internet.
* 5.5 GB hard drive space (including downloaded files).
* The license file.

Supported Simulators
Refer to the "Novas Object File Cross Reference Matrix" section in the Linking Novas Files
with Simulators and Enabling FSDB Dumping document for the current list of supported
simulator versions.

Linking Novas Object Files
For complete details on linking the Novas object files for FSDB dumping with various
simulators, see the Linking Novas Files with Simulators and Enabling FSDB Dumping
document.

Supported Platforms
Verdi and Siloti systems support most major Sun and Linux workstations. Refer to the
Release Notes for the current list of platforms and OS versions.
For detailed platform support information, see the Release Specific Support page on
Synopsys Qualified System Configuration website at the following address:
http://www.synopsys.com/qsc
This web page provides release-specific information about supported hardware, operating
systems, and required operating system patches. If the required patch described on this
page is not available from the platform vendor, install the most recent patch instead.
Note:
Solaris platform is no longer supported.

Installing from the Internet
Perform the following steps to install from the Internet:
1. On the Synopsys SolvnetPlus website, enter your User ID and Password, and then
click SIGN IN.
2. On the top bar, click the Downloads link.
3. Under My Product Releases, scroll and click Verdi3.
4. Click the version of interest and then click the Download Here link.
5. Click the YES, I AGREE TO THE ABOVE TERMS button.
6. Select the required files by clicking the appropriate Download button.
Common Files
Executable Files for your specific architecture(s) e.g. 32/64 Bit Linux
7. Invoke the Synopsys Installer by using one of the following commands:
> %installer #To use a text script
> %installer -gui #To use a GUI

You must install the latest release in an empty directory using the latest version of the
Synopsys Installer. Do not install this release over an existing release of a Synopsys
tool.
For information about downloading the Synopsys Installer, see the Synopsys Installer
section at the following address:
http://www.synopsys.com/install
The following directories are created:
bin

The executable programs

license

An empty directory

etc

Software default-setting files

doc

Documentation including online help, release notes,
and so on

share

Symbol libraries, NPI libraries, ovm/uvm libraries, PLI
modules, PLI directory

demo

Demo samples

platform

Platform-dependent data

Setting Up the License Server
Before running Synopsys tools, the Synopsys Common Licensing (SCL) software must
be installed and configured, the license key file must be retrieved, and the license file
environment variable must be defined. For detailed information about SCL installation and
setup, see the Synopsys Licensing Quickstart Guide.
Note:
This release of the product uses the SCL daemon named snpslmd. To use
the product, SCL 11.6 or higher versions of the snpslmd daemon must be
used with the latest license key file. Refer to the SCL 11.6 Release Notes and

Setting Up the Environment and Running the Software
1. If needed, specify the symbol libraries.
2. Confirm Perl (or a link to the executable) is located in /usr/local/bin and that it
exists in your path.
Note:
If Perl is not in this location, some utilities may not work correctly.
3. Set the VERDI_HOME environment variable to the installation directory.
% set VERDI_HOME <VERDI_INST_DIR>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Add the Verdi application (binary) to the search path:
For the C (csh) shell:
% set path = ($VERDI_HOME/bin $path)

For Bourne (sh) and Korn (ksh) shells:
% PATH=$VERDI_HOME/bin:$PATH

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
5. Run the software.
Use the following command to run the Verdi and Siloti system:
> % verdi

Use the following command to run nWave standalone:
> % nWave

Chapter 2: Installing Verdi and Siloti Software
Setting Up the Environment and Running the Software

Refer to the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual for complete details on
executing the Verdi and Siloti platform or nWave (verdi and nWave utility descriptions in
the Utilities chapter).
6. Optionally, run the nCompare software.
Use the following command to run the nCompare module in the batch mode:
> % nCompare [batch mode options]

Use one of the following commands to run nCompare in GUI mode:
> % nCompare -gui [rule file | error report file] or
> % nCompareg [rule file | error report file]

Refer to the nCompare chapter in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual for
details.

Installing Verdi Supplementary Package
In this chapter:
* Overview
* Installing in GUI Mode
* Installing in Batch Mode

Overview
Before installing the Verdi Supplementary package, verify that your workstation meets the
following requirements:
* Software files from the Synopsys SolvnetPlus website.
* 35 GB hard drive space (including downloaded files).
* The license file.
If VCS is installed
You can use Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode by setting VCS_HOME to the VCS
installation directory.
% setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_installed_directory>

If VCS is not installed
You need to install Verdi Supplementary package under path such as:
$VERDI_HOME/platform/

Install Verdi first, if you have not installed it
Note:
The images in this chapter are for reference only. The product version shown in
the images may differ from your release version.

1. Enter the basic information.

2. Select the source directory.

3. Select the target directory.

4. Click Next.

5. Select Product VERDI-The Industry Open Debug Platform.

6. Select all platforms.

7. Check the installation configurations, and then click Accept, Install.

Installation is in progress.

Install the Verdi Supplementary Package
1. Enter the basic information.

2. Select the source directory.

3. Select the target directory <VERDI_HOME>/platform/.

5. Select Product VERDI_SUPP.

6. Retain the default settings.

Introduction
This document provides detailed information about the LCA features and enhancements
that are available in Verdi in the following chapters:

Safety Specification Format
The Safety Specification Format (SSF) is a file format used in Synopsys functional safety
flows.
It defines safety mechanisms for a design.
An SSF file specifies the safety mechanisms to implement in the design.
This file helps ensure that required safety features are inserted and tracked during the
design process.
After implementation, the tool uses the SSF file to compare the RTL and the physically
implemented netlist.
It performs functional safety (FuSa) equivalence checks. These checks confirm that safety
mechanisms are correctly realized in the final design.
The following sections describe SSF support in the various components of Verdi:
* SSF Support in nTrace
* Tcl Command Reference for SSF in nTrace
* SSF Support in Safety Manager
* Tcl Command Reference for SSF in Safety Manager
* SSF Support in nSchema
* Tcl Command Reference for SSF in nSchema
* SSF Support in nWave
* Tcl Command Reference for SSF in nWave
* SSF Support in Temporal Flow View

Limitations of SSF
The following are the limitations of Safety Specification Format (SSF) in Verdi:
* Verdi supports SSF 1.0 only. No syntax highlight or annotation is added on commands
not supported in Verdi.
* Verdi supports SSF only. Support for SSF + UPF will be added in a future release.
* The SSF functionality supports Verilog only.
* The unified find feature is available in the SSF UI.
However, you cannot restore a search result after using unified find.
The selection may have changed or been deleted after the search.
Safety Specification Format (SSF) Support Across Verdi Debug Tools
The Verdi tool supports SSF throughout the debug environment.
Supported components include nTrace, Safety Manager, nSchema, nWave, and Temporal
Flow View.
SSF lets users explore, visualize, and debug safety mechanisms using safety virtual cells
and safety instrumented signals.
With hierarchical views, context-sensitive actions, and synced data panes, you can trace
and validate safety-related logic.
You can quickly locate safety-critical elements and ensure compliance with safety
requirements.
Visual cues and advanced filtering help you identify, analyze, and verify signals impacted
by safety rules.
These features streamline functional safety verification and improve design quality.

Safety Specification Format in nTrace lets users explore, understand, and debug safetyrelated logic.
Users work with safety virtual cells and safety instrumented signals.
Virtual cells are a conceptual entity. They represent safety-related logic or functionality in
multiple designs without RTL code changes.
In Verdi, safety virtual cells are built from SSF safety rules.

These cells appear in a design hierarchy tree as special nodes. Each node matches safety
instrumentation applied to a design.
Safety instrumented signals are inserted or modified in RTL when you apply safety rules or
policies in the Safety Specification Format (SSF).
The following topics describe the interactive nTrace environment. They cover how to view,
navigate, and debug safety virtual cells.
They also describe the user interface for analyzing and handling safety instrumented
signals:
* Safety Virtual Cells in nTrace
* Safety Instrumental Signal in nTrace

Safety Virtual Cells in nTrace
Safety virtual cells are instrumented by the set_safety_core_rule command. Safety
virtual cells, as defined by SSF safety rules, appear as special nodes in a design hierarchy
tree within nTrace. These nodes represent logical groupings of RTL elements affected by
specific safety rules or policies.

and review the underlying RTL even though the RTL itself is unchanged.

Safety Instrumental Signal in nTrace
Safety instrumented signals are automatically generated signals that implement or support
safety mechanisms defined by SSF rules. Verdi displays safety instrumented signals by
scope in the Signal pane.

These signals can be filtered or searched for by using the Safety Inserted option. The
default status is toggle on.

Double-clicking a safety instrumental signal automatically synchronizes the RTL source
code view in nTrace to the original signal declaration. This allows users to quickly locate
and review the underlying RTL, which remains unchanged.
Adding Instrumentation Signals to the Waveform
* To add low-power-related instrumental signals to a waveform by type, choose Add
Instrumented Signals to Waveform > Power.
* To add safety-related signals to a waveform by type, choose Add Instrumented
Signals to Waveform > Safety.
Other than the Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform feature, all general features that
apply to a normal RTL signal also apply to a safety instrumental signal.
If an RTL signal is impacted by a safety rule, the context menus corresponding
to that rule are enabled when you add an instrumented signal to the waveform.
For example, if an RTL signal is impacted by a register rule, the Register

Safety Manager is a comprehensive platform for debugging Safety Specification Format
source designs. This feature provides a visual and interactive environment to analyze
safety policies, models, and their relationships within your design. By leveraging
hierarchical views, context-sensitive actions, and synchronized data panes, you can
efficiently trace, inspect, and validate safety-related logic.

The Safety Specification Format support in nSchema helps users identify, analyze, and
debug safety-related logic in their designs. This is done through safety virtual cells and
safety instrumented signals. These features visually mark cells and signals that are
instrumented for safety. This makes it easier to trace safety mechanisms, understand their
impact, and ensure compliance with safety requirements. By leveraging these features,
users can quickly locate safety-critical elements, view related properties, and add relevant
signals to waveforms for further analysis.

The following topics describe the SSF support available in nSchema:
* Safety Virtual Cells in nSchema
* Safety Instrumental Signals

Utility
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by Utility as part of this
release:
* The tracediff Utility
* Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
* The nCompare Utility
* Utilities for Performance Improvement
* FSDB Utilities

Temporal Flow View (TFV) traces multiple mismatches of signals using the trace
mechanism in batch mode manually. The tracediff utility is provided in Verdi, which
traces mismatches of signals using the trace mechanism in batch mode automatically,
collects the root causes, and provides a trace report. You must import the design
completely, or the utility does not get invoked.
The tracediff utility provides two ways of tracing the mismatches. They are manual
mode and automatic mode as follows:
* Manual mode: A configuration file must be provided which describes the signals to
trace. With -signal_list in the command line, tracediff works in manual mode.
* Automatic mode: A configuration file is not required to be written but can still trace
signal mismatches. All the inputs needed in this mode are design, target waveform
file, and reference waveform file. The tracediff utility invokes nCompare with default
settings and extracts the mismatches from the target waveform file and reference
waveform file. Without -signal_list in the command line, tracediff works in
automatic mode.
After tracing mismatch for the signal list, a report is generated in the tracediffLog/
under the current directory by default. If a report file is not specified while executing the
command, the report is stored in tracediffLog/under the current working directory with
the default name tracediff_report.txt.

* Saving the Traced Path of the Batch Utility in a Database

Syntax for the tracediff utility is as follows:
tracediff -target_waveform <fsdb_file_name> -ref_waveform
<fsdb_file_name> [Verdi option] [tracediff option]

Command Options

-compare_scope
<full_hierarchical_sco
pe>

Specifies the top scope to compare signals. Only signals in
the scope and its sub-scopes are compared. Scope delimiter
must be a slash /.The default value is top scope, which is not
specified.

-compare_x <0|1>

Specifies if the tracediff utility compares X values. The
default value is 1.

-compare_z <0|1>

Specifies if the tracediff utility compares Z values.
The default value is 1, that is by default tracediff utility
compares Z values.

-dut

Checks if the root cause is in the DUT or testbench so that
tracediff utility can annotate a root cause with the accurate
reason. It is optional and need not be specified.

-gen_list

It is provided for running auto mode and stop once the
signal list is dumped. You can revise the file and then reboot
tracediff manual mode with the revised signal list.

-ignore_signal
<signal_list_file_name>

Specifies the location of the file which contains the list of
signals to ignore tracing. Each line contains a signal pattern
and the pattern can be one of the following:
- signal#time: ignore tracing the signal at specified time.
- signal: ignore tracing the signal at any time.
This option can be used if any signal causes tracediff utility
to not function in the auto mode and it is ignored for auto
mode to work. It can also be used in manual mode.
Default is NULL and no signal is ignored.

-jmp_to_earliest

Jumps to the earliest point in time while tracing in the batch
mode.

-auto_max_level <n>

Specifies the hierarchy level limit for the module to be
compared. For example, /top/a is compared but /top/a/b is
not compared if -compare_scope is /top and -max_level is
1 because /top/ais 1 level but /top/a/bis 2 levels from /top.
When n is 0, all signals in the hierarchy starting from the
specified module are compared.
Default value is 0 if not specified.

-auto_max_
sample_per_signal <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches for each
pair of signals, starting from the earliest mismatch until
the maximum number is reached. When the maximum is
reached, the remaining pairs of signals are not compared.
When n is 0, there is still a limit of 2097152 mismatches for
each pair of signals due to the limitation of nCompare.
Default value is 1 if not specified.

-auto_max_
err_cnt_number <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches in a
comparison. When n is 0, there is no limitation on the number
of mismatches.
Default value is 1000 if it is not specified.

-ncompare_opts

Specifies nCompare input options. The format is tracediff
[tracediff options] -ncompare_opts "[nComapre
options]. When -ncompare_opts is used, nCompare

options that are originally supported in tracediff auto mode
are unavailable.Waveform files set up in -ncompare_opts
is ignored. You have to specify what are the target and
reference waveforms for tracediff.
-out_file reportFile.txt Sets the name of the output report file.
-out_format
[plain|smlog]

Sets the format of the output file.If this option is not specified,
the default format of the output file is smlog. If the smlog
option is specified, you can open the output file with Smart
Log to analyze it.

-ref_waveform

The secondary waveform file used to compare signals. This is

Specifies signals that need to be added to the signal list.

Specifies the target waveform. This option imports the

After tracing the mismatch for the signal list, the tracediff_report.txt report is

As illustrated in the following figure, the configuration settings are recorded at the top

Tracediff transforms the given time unit into the time unit used in the target waveform. This

The tracediff utility categorizes signals into the following four types and the meaning of

* Root Cause Not Found
* No Mismatch

Saving the Traced Path of the Batch Utility in a Database
The save/restore trace path feature is supported for traceX/tracediff batch mode. For
traceX/tracediff batch mode, you can use trace utilities in batch mode and get the trace
report. The option -load_trace_report is used to load report in verdi and show the trace
path by invoke traceX/tracediff to trace signal again. However, this behavior might cost a
lot of time to redo Behavior Analysis and tracing.
This project provides mechanism to save the trace path of utility tracing result and restore
them back in GUI mode, therefore, you don't need to redo Behavior Analysis and tracing
while restoring the trace path.
For traceX utility, you need to save the tracing path and traceX result table into the
database. When -load_trace_report option is reported back to Verdi and when you
click on the signal entry, the trace path is restored back to Temporal Flow View.

Figure 62

TraceX Flow

Verdi provides you the capability to open the report file in SmartLog and view the report in
human readable format. You can view or replay the trace path using the SmartLog file.
The -load_trace_report option is supported which opens the SmartLog and
automatically displays the report file provided for tracediff utility. However, this option
should not be used with -target_waveform option and if the signal needs to be traced
again then it takes a lot of time to redo the Behavior Analysis and trace the signal again.
verdi -load_trace_report tracediff_report.txt

Starting with this release, a database is supported which stores the tracing information into
the database and then restores the trace path without tracing the signals again.
Syntax for the database which stores the tracing information is as follows:
tracediff -target_waveform 1.fsdb -ref_waveform 2.fsdb -tdb -tdb_dir
traceDiff.tdb

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
Starting with this release, if there are any failed tests during regression, Verdi finds the bug
and fixes it before allowing any new changes.
Verdi first takes the file to determine the debug entries. Debug entries are monitored
signals in the DUT that have mismatches between the failing and passed waveform. Then
it traces back to find the root causes, and summarizes it in a text file report. This report is
then loaded into Verdi to see the detail trace path from debug entry to root cause.

The following sub-sections provide the details of the use model:
Determining the Bug Entry
The debug entries are read from a .rc file. There are three types of tags in the .rc file:
* Signal: If the tag is Signal, each line must include the full hierarchical name and
a timestamp. These signals are scanned and they become the debug entries if the
values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two waveform files. For
example,
top.memory.nROutstanding#123
top.mySig1#1000
top.mySig2#50

* Scope: If the tag is Scope, each line must include a list of scope names and a
timestamp. Boundary signals within these scopes are scanned and those signals
become the debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different
within the two waveform files. For example,
top,top.myScope1#200
top.myScope2#300
top#100-200

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

* Assertion: If the tag is Assertion, each line must include an Assertion name and a
timestamp. Signals that are associated to that assertion are scanned and become the
debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two
waveform files. For example,
top.memory.eos#160390000

The follow error message is an example on how to specify an assertion failure as debug
entry:
Error: "token.v", 144439:top.memory.eos : at time 160390000
ALL_DONE_EOS: All write transaction addresses must have been
matched with corresponding write response.
nb_cycles: 16040
Executing Axi End Of Simulation checks

here, ALL_DONE_EOS is the name of the assertion and 160390000 is the time.
Analyzing Root Cause
The root cause is analyzed by running the TraceDiff utility in Verdi. The following are the
enhancements to TraceDiff for root cause:
Trace Multiple Root Cause
For root cause, TraceDiff searches all fanins with mismatch on every level.
Trace Database
For root cause, TraceDiff saves the trace results in a trace result database that can be
efficiently and accurately replayed.
Ignore Mismatches on Waveform Time Boundaries
For root cause, TraceDiff does not trace signals with mismatches on the time boundary
only, because the mismatch may be due to inconsistency in the simulation evaluation
order. This helps to filter out false alarms.
Ignore Shifted Sequence
For root cause, TraceDiff ignores mismatches caused by delay shift.
Trace through Design Changes
For root cause, TraceDiff trace through minor design changes.

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
