The following section describes the enhancement to the CRDB utility LCA feature
supported by Verdi as part of this release:
* Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

Enhancement to the CRDB Utility
In the previous releases, the RTL design had encrypted IP blocks because of which CRDB
could not be directly extracted from the FSDB file for the RTL design.
Starting with this release, the -RTL_FSDB option is added in the CRDB utility. This option
can be used to extract the CRDB from the FSDB file for the RTL design. The -RTL_FSDB
option is an alternative option to extract the RTL design.

The flow of CRDB is as follows:
1. Extract the gate level design
2. Extract the RTL design and
3. Perform the correlation.
The syntax for -RTL_FSDB option is:
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name

Here,
RTL_FSDB_name - Specifies the user-defined FSDB file name.
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB -GATE "-f gate.f" -impSVF "block1.svf block2.svf"
-expMap mapping.gz -allreg

Chapter 6: Correlation
Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

The syntax to extract gate level design and RTL design to perform the correlation is as
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name -GATE "<gate level import & BA options>"
-crdb <output CRDB name> <correlation options> [export mapping options]

If you extract RTL CRDB from FSDB more than once, then the previous
database extracted is overwritten with the latest extracted database. -append
option is not supported if you extract CRDB from FSDB. It issues an error
message and aborts the CRDB generation.

The -RTL_FSDB option in the CRDB utility has the following limitations:
* If the FSDB is written by a third party tool instead of FSDB dumper, some information
may be incorrect or missed due to wrong usage of FSDB writer by the third party tool.
The input FSDB requires a module name for each instance. If a module name is not
written into FSDB, then the extraction does not create a model for that instance.
* The following design information which can be extracted from the RTL design may not
be extracted from FSDB.
Register information is not available in FSDB.
Equivalent net or inverted equivalent net is not available in FSDB. That is, if some signals
are originally correlated through an equivalent net, it may not become correlated when
extracting it from FSDB.

The Debug Note feature relies on Verdi session functionality to save or restore a session.
The Verdi session support for SVTB Interactive Mode and HW/SW Debug is as follows:
* SVTB Interactive mode: A Verdi session can restore the breakpoints and simulation
state, with the following usage limitations from simulator (such as VCS) and Verdi.
simv is not movable.
Before saving a session, execute run 0 to ensure that the simulation state is at a
valid point.
Checkpoints and watch lists cannot be restored with the simulation state.

and the executable path of simv (@ session file) are accurate.

automatically. After restoring a Verdi session, execute HW/SW Debug and specify the

cannot be captured due to technical issues. The workaround is to capture the entire

FSDB Command Line, Environment Variable, and Dump
Command Options
The unified FSDB dumper supports three methods for specifying options. The methods
are:
1. Specify an option on the simulator command line. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Line Options section for details on the command-line options.
2. Specify an option using an environment variable. Refer to Appendix A in the Verdi and
Siloti Command Reference Manual for details on the environment variables.
3. Specify an option in an FSDB dumping command. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Option table for details on using options with the dump commands.
If the same option is set using more than one method, the resolution is: Method 1 >
Method 2 > Method 3.
For example, the FSDB dump file name can be set using one of the following methods:
1. Specify the file name on the simulator command line:
> simv +fsdbfile+high.fsdb

2. Specify the file name using an environment variable:
> setenv NOVAS_FSDB_FILE mid_prio.fsdb

3. Specify the file name in an FSDB dumping command:
$fsdbDumpvars("+fsdbfile+low_prio.fsdb");

This means that in this example, the resolved FSDB file name is high.fsdb.

When you set related options through different methods at the same time, the dumper
applies both settings. It does not use the usual priority order (command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command). Instead, it combines the effects:
1. Resolve each option's value using the standard priority: simulator command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command.
2. Apply the union of all resolved settings.
Example 1
1. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

2. Specify the option in an FSDB dumping command to enable dumping all supported
signals:
$fsdbDumpvars("+all");

These options differ, so priority resolution does not apply. The dumper combines both
settings and enables dumping of all supported signals.
Example 2
1. Specify the option on the simulator command line to enable dumping packed MDA
signals:
simv +fsdb+packedmda

2. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

Both +fsdb+mda and +fsdb+packedmda resolve to on. The dumper combines them and
enables dumping of all MDA signals.
Example 3
Specify the options on the simulator command line to filter all dumper messages, warning
messages, and error messages:
simv +fsdb+no_warning +fsdb+no_error +fsdb+no_all_msg

The dumper combines all three options and filters all dumper messages.

The new option is added to the fsdbDumpvars command as follow:
* +msv+isub: Dump the total current that flows into the sub-circuit port. If the dumping
value of signal is positive, then the current flows into the sub-circuit port. If the dumping
value of signal is negative, then the current is flows out of the sub-circuit.
You need to specify the iprobe_wavefore_current option to the XA
configuration file before specifying the +msv+isub option.
* To use these options, the CustomSim version should be 2015.06-SP4 or later versions.
The VCS version must be 2015.09-SP1 and later versions.
* Dumper only supports this option for the VCS simulator.

Dumping Class Objects by Level
You can use the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command to dump the value change in
object to the FSDB file.
Following is the syntax when specified in the design:
$fsdbDumpClassObject( class_name_or_object_name [, option]*)

Following is the syntax when specified on the simulation UCLI command line:
fsdbDumpClassObject class_name_or_object_name [option]*

Where, class_name_or_object_name is the class name or object name in full hierarchy
format that is specified to dump.

Dumping Dynamic Class Objects

When you invoke VCS to compile the design, you must use the -debug_access
+class or -debug_access+ckbd options at the compile command line.
To dump the expandable class pointer signal, set the following environment variable:
setenv FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS 1

Following are the options supported for the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command:
+object_level=depth: Keyword to identify the number of levels of hierarchy to dump for
the subsequent objects. The default value of depth is 1.

Where, depth can have the following value:
N: N level sub-object under the current object or object instantiated from the current class
object.
0: All sub-objects under the current object or objects instantiated from the current class
object.
Note: It is recommended not to set +object_level to 0 as it costs more with a complex
testbench and limited resources.
+fsdbfile+<filename>: Specifies the FSDB file name. If not specified, the default FSDB
file name is novas.fsdb.

Note: An environment variable can be used as part of the filename string argument.
When an environment variable is defined and then embedded into the option, the FSDB
dumper replaces the environment variable with the given definition.
Examples
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class@1");

Dump the first object of class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class@3");

Dump the third object of class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class");

Dump all objects instantiated from class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class", "+fsdbfile+my.fsdb");

Dumps all objects from class simple_class to the specified FSDB file, my.fsdb.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class", "+object_level=3");

Dump objects below the class simple_class up to the depth specified for the depth
variable.

Dumping Queue, Dynamic Array, and Associative Array in HDL
Instance
You can enable the dumping of non-static array (queue, dynamic array, and associative
array) in HDL instance using the following options.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option enables dumping for the non-static arrays in HDL instances, such as dynamic
array, queue, and associative array. As the array size can be big, FSDB dumper only
dumps several array elements in a non-static arrays. The default number is 10 and the
array element starts from index 0.
* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option specifies the different element numbers of non-static arrays. The number must
be 0 ~ 1023.
+fsdb+max_variant_size_array=20

* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.

The following are the limitations of this feature:
* For D, Q, and A array dumping, the following types are not supported:
Event
Hybrid array: For example, int [][0:1]

FSDB Dumping for SystemVerilog in VCS

Multi-dimension variant array: For example, int [][]
Struct non-static array: For example, struct {bit b1; reg r1;} s1[];
Array struct contain variant array or variant array struct contain array:
For example, struct { int a[] } s1[0:1] struct { int a[0:1] } s2[]
* Sequence and region are not supported on a variable that contains D,Q, and A arrays.
* For associative array, index type only supports the integral variables which can map to
a one-dimensional packed array.
* Wildcard index type and user-defined index type are not supported for dumping.
* Variant size array dumping does not support class and string. Both are not supported in
array elements and associated array index.

FSDB Dumping for SystemVerilog in VCS
Verdi supports the following dumping for SystemVerilog only:
* Built-in data type
* Fixed-size array, non-static struct, built-in data type and the combinations
* One-dimensional variant-size array with built-in data type in class, except an event
* Index of the associative array only supports built-in data types which can map to a onedimensional packed array

FSDB dumping has these limitations:
* Dumping does not support class objects that include encrypted code.
* Dumping does not support mailbox, semaphore, or unpacked union.
* Dumping does not support enum with dimension data type in class.
* Dumping does not support combinations of variant size array and/or struct.
* Dumping does not support struct used in module that has a class member.

* For normal class object dumping, if the class definition has protected information, the
FSDB dumper skips that class. For example, the FSDB dumper skips this class:
class protected_class;
int var1;
protected
e&+gZ/]e;67VBR97W+,4SWb^/@]NcEbFc&T>Z_+KY_6KIV_2GcS..)(fD=&+VIYd
/IUcb;.871N#N5eD>>C4)e(c<e^gM3_Dd9gcWYM=-7cKE$
endprotected

* For dynamic, queue, and associative array dumping, these types are not supported:
1. Event
2. Hybrid array
For example, int [][0:1]
3. Multi-dimension variant array
For example, int [][]
4. Array struct that contains a variant array, or a variant array struct that contains an
array
For example,struct { int a[] } s1[0:1]
struct { int a[0:1] } s2[]

* Glitch, sequence, and region are not supported on variables that contain dynamic,
queue, or associative arrays.
* For associative arrays, the index type supports class var, string var, and integral var.
These must map to a one-dimensional packed array.
* Dumping does not support wildcard index types or user-defined index types.
* Verdi applications have these limitations:
* nCompare cannot compare class objects/pointers, or queue and dynamic/associative
arrays.
* Queue and dynamic/associative arrays are supported only in dynamic objects.
Because dynamic objects do not support drag-and-drop between nWave and other
components, queue and dynamic/associative arrays do not support drag-and-drop
between nWave and other components.
* fsdbDumpClassObject does not dump uvm_objects inside uvm_components classes.
Although values change during simulation, these members appear as null in nWave.
They show as solid blue lines with no values.

Encrypted IP
Debugging is complicated when dealing with encrypted IPs due to limited knowledge and
visibility. This leads to time-consuming back-and-forths between SoC and IP teams. To
tackle these challenges, new verification, debug capabilities, and robust methodologies
are required.
An encrypted IP block is a secured version of the RTL source code or its gate-level netlist,
processed through an encryption algorithm. This encryption allows certain tools to operate
on the code, but prevents users from viewing the source. The most versatile encryption
scheme is the IEEE-P1735 standard, widely adopted for interoperability among IP and
EDA vendors.
The objective is to serve IP suppliers and the design teams in the following ways:
* IP Supplier: Protects the security of the IP in the design flow across different EDA
tools.
* IP Users: Ensures the interoperability of the IP across different EDA tools and vendors.

Encrypted IP

The IEEE-P1735 uses the following two levels of encryption to generate an encrypted IP:
1. The first level of encryption creates a random session key that is used to encrypt the
source code into a data_block using a symmetric encryption algorithm such as AES.
2. The second level of encryption uses the public keys of the EDA tool vendor to encrypt
the session key into a key_block using an asymmetric encryption algorithm such as
RSA.
The decryption flow that resides in the EDA tools applies the same process in the reverse
order as follows:
1. The tool scans the key-block searching for its own key; once located, the tool uses its
own private key to decrypt the key-block thus obtaining the symmetric session key.
2. The session key is then used to decrypt the data-block allowing the tool to compile
the original source code.
The following figure illustrates the IEEE-P1735 encryption and decryption flows:
Figure 201

IEEE-P1735 Encryption and Decryption Flows

An encryption envelope is the preamble to the IP block in the source code. An IP supplier
must prepare an encryption envelope containing the public keys for each EDA tool that
is to be given access to the IP block. The encryption envelope consists of pragmas that
provide information such as encryption scheme, encoding type, key owner, key name, and
key method.
The following figure illustrates an encrypted IP containing multiple key-blocks, each
corresponding to a tool or vendor to be given access to the IP. One of the advantages
of the P1735 scheme is that the data block is common to all tools. Therefore, the same

Encrypted IP

encrypted IP block can be delivered to all the IP users and supporting various tools and
flows. The session keys are automatically generated, therefore, they are not known to
anyone and do not need to be safeguarded; only the private decryption keys must be
safeguarded by the respective tools.
Figure 202

An Encrypted IP with three key-blocks

The P1735 standard enables IP reuse across applications, addresses IP security and
interoperability. However, it does not dictate how IP distribution is controlled, what
information a tool can reveal, or how to protect IP contents. Each tool must implement its
own policies to safeguard IP content.

Encrypted IP Policies
The policies that govern Synopsys' simulation and verification tools have been developed
over a period of time to satisfy the needs of IP integrators as well as the security concerns
of IP suppliers. Since the compilers are able to decrypt encrypted IPs, they have access to
the full source code, including the original names of all the objects in the IP. Therefore, the
decryption tools must be carefully devised to avoid mistakenly disclosing any information
deemed proprietary. Specifically, the VCS compiler has been enhanced to safeguard the
private decryption key as well as the data contained in an encrypted IP block.
Error and warning messages issued by the compiler have been carefully designed to
reveal only information known to the IP user but sufficient for the IP supplier to identify the
source of the problem. In particular, any error triggered by an encrypted IP component
includes only three pieces of information: a description of the error or warning, file name,
and the line-number of the offending code - the names of objects in the IP are not
disclosed. The information issued is typically enough for the IP user to report the problem
to the IP supplier.
During simulation or a debug session, all introspection into encrypted IP blocks is
disallowed. This includes actions such as using wildcards through the hierarchy of
encrypted blocks or attempt to use a VPI iterator to traverse the content of the IP, which
would effectively allow IP users to decompile encrypted blocks. Likewise, the simulator
prohibits disclosing the hierarchical names or the values generated by an encrypted
IP block during simulation: The waveforms associated with an encrypted IP cannot be
dumped into an FSDB.

Debugging Standalone IP

There are a few exceptions to the strict IP protection provided to by the tools. An
encrypted IP is allowed to divulge design information. For example, assertions triggered
by an IP block contain the same information as if the assertion was in clear text. Similarly,
if the IP includes statements that print text (for example, $display), the statement is
allowed to execute undisturbed. The rational for this rule is that the IP owner is explicitly
including such code in the IP so it's not the responsibility of the tools to prevent such
actions from divulging internal information. Finally, knowledge of the hierarchical name of
an object inside an encrypted IP block grants an IP user access to that object, to either
examine or change its simulation value or to dump its waveform. The rationale for this rule
is that the only way the IP users knows the name is because the name was disclosed by
the IP owner. This capability is sometimes used by IP suppliers to deploy a workaround

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
ge its simulation value or to dump its waveform. The rationale for this rule
is that the only way the IP users knows the name is because the name was disclosed by
the IP owner. This capability is sometimes used by IP suppliers to deploy a workaround
that changes the behavior of the IP or to issue some information that may help diagnose a
problem while running at the IP user site.
Although the simulator does allow IP users to manipulate the behavior of a
signal internal to an encrypted IP block by specifying its hierarchical name,
this type of external manipulation of the behavior of the IP block is highly
discouraged and should be used rarely and in extreme cases. Instead, all
interactions between the design and an encrypted IP component should occur
through the IP's hardware interface, that is, top-level ports. Forcing signals in
lieu of a proper hardware reset or an initialization or configuration sequence can
cause the IP to malfunction and create problem that is difficult to debug.

Debugging Standalone IP
Debugging a potential IP problem while running a full chip test is challenging not just
due to lack of IP visibility; SoC or system-level simulations are large and compile and
run much slower than standalone IP tests. This situation is exacerbated when IP owners
incrementally request additional data from IP users to analyze a problem; the IP user must
typically recompile and rerun a lengthy simulation to generate the additional information.
To enable effective IP reuse, the debug problems associated with encrypted IP need to be
addressed.
Encrypted FSDB, is a proposal enabled by an asymmetric encryption scheme to protect
not just the source code (as enabled by P1735) but also the simulated waveforms.

Encrypted IP Waveform
When an encrypted IP includes unpredictable constructs or its internals are manipulated
beyond its I/O ports, IDX may not replicate a system level issue at the IP level. For
debugging, the IP supplier requires waveforms of all signals, which can be done using
Verdi alone. However, due to encrypted IP policies, an IP user cannot dump the internal
waveforms unless the IP supplier discloses all internal names, which is impractical. To

Debugging Standalone IP

solve this, the IP supplier can allow the dumping of waveforms during system level testing,
which are then encrypted for confidentiality. The IP user can generate the encrypted FSDB
but can't view the waveforms unless given the decryption key.
The Encrypted IP Waveform is a mechanism for securely exporting encrypted FSDB
files that can only be decrypted by IP suppliers using their private decryption key. The
Encrypted IP Waveform feature changes several aspects of the IP creation as well as the
simulation and debug flows. The Encrypted IP Waveform feature proceeds in the following
IP Supplier
1. Obtains an asymmetric RSA key pair.
2. Adds the public key to the IP and encrypts the IP.
IP User
1. Compiles the design with the new IP, which contain the public key.
2. Runs the system level simulation with a new option.
3. Specifies the design instances whose waveforms are to be dumped.
4. Ships the resulting FSDB to the IP supplier.
Finally, the IP owner uses the private key to load the FSDB waveforms into Verdi and
begin the IP debug session.
The encrypted IP waveform overall flow is illustrated in Figure 203. Each of the steps are
covered in detail in the next sections.

text:
Although the Encrypted IP Waveform capability introduces changes to the IP preparation
and encryption flow, these changes are required to safeguard the IP. Other options such
as a post-encryption option to add the public key would give someone other than the IP
owner the ability to tamper with the IP. Encrypting the public key with the rest of the source
code ensures that no one other than the simulation tool use the key. It thus provides the
same security as the encrypted IP flow itself.
IP users are responsible for safeguarding their own data. VCS honors a request by an IP
user to dump the waveforms of nonencrypted design blocks - albeit all the waveforms
are encrypted using the IP owner's public key. Therefore, the IP owner can view all the
waveforms in the encrypted FSDB, even those that are not part of the IP. To avoid this, IP

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
Debugging Standalone IP

users must be careful to only dump non-proprietary data or limit the waveform dump to
only the IP of interest.
VCS protects the encrypted IPs that have different public keys. If instructed to dump
the waveforms of IP blocks with different public keys, VCS issues an error and does not
generate the FSDB. This means that if different IP owners need to debug a failure, multiple
simulation runs are needed; one run for each IP owner - or one for each public key.
1. Obtaining RSA Keys
There are many ways to obtain an RSA private/public key pair. You can use
fsdbEncKeyGen to generate RSA key pair or use official RSA website to generate it.
2. Adding the Public Key and Encrypting the IP
IP owners can use the new option -fsdb_public_key to have the -ipprotect
option of the VCS compiler to automatically add the public key attribute as part of the
encryption. The fsdb_key attribute is only relevant for the top-level module of the IP,
VCS automatically extends it to encompass the full hierarchy of the IP. The fsdb_key is
disregarded if specified anywhere else in the hierarchy of the IP block. In addition, only
one fsdb_key attribute should be specified in the IP.
vcs -full64 -sverilog -ipopt=noincludeprotect -ipprotect
encryption_header -fsdb_public_key public.pem ip.v

Specifying the fsdb_key to all the files causes VCS to add the fsdb_key
attribute to every module, which, as stated above is functionally immaterial
and increases the size of the encrypted data.
3. Compiling the Design
To enable the waveform dumping capabilities, the IP user must specify the
-debug_access and -debug_region=encrypt options to the VCS compile command
vcs top.v ip.vp -debug_access -debug_region=encrypt

This command generates a simv executable that is capable of generating an encrypted
FSDB.
4. Running the Simulation
To enable Encrypted IP Waveform for a simulation run, IP users need to add the +fsdb

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
+public_key_ip simv option when running the executable, as follows:
simv +fsdb+public_key_ip

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
5. Specifying Instances to be Dumped

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow Summary

IP users designate the design instances to be dumped using the $fsdbdumpvar task.
If any of the design instances specified to $fsdbdumpvars is an encrypted block that
includes a fsdb public key then the entire FSDB is encrypted using the public key.
As noted earlier, attempting to dump waveforms for encrypted IPs with different fsdb
keys result in an error and the dump is aborted. Similarly, adding instances in multiple
$fsdbdumpvars commands and any of the instances have a different public key results
in an error and the dump is aborted, even if a dump has already started.
6. Loading an Encrypted FSDB
The IP owner can load an encrypted FSDB into Verdi by specifying the private key
through the environment variable FSDB_DECRYPT before running Verdi.
setenv FSDB_DECRYPT private.pem
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb

If the private key is incorrect or it is not specified the FSDB fails to load. An encrypted
FSDB is rendered useless to anyone without the private decryption key. One of the
advantages of the Encrypted IP Waveform flow is that the IP owner does not need to
run the simulation. The encrypted FSDB contains all the simulation data as it executed
in the system level test.

Encrypted IP Waveform Limitations
Encrypted IP Waveform feature has the following limitations:
* Top-level scope of the system-level test must be non-encrypted.
* Only works with P1735 encryption. The protect or protect128 flows are not supported
(No support for +/-autoprotect, +auto2protect, auto3protect129, )
* Encrypted module with public key inside, the following hierarchy is not dumped.
Non-Verilog scope : under VHDL, SystemC, Spice, AMS and so on.
Protected Verilog without public key.
Protected Verilog with different public key.
* The following items are not dumped inside encrypted module with public key:
Encrypted module without public key or with different public key
Non-encrypted module
Other language
SVA
Interface port
Global parameter
Class object
* Supports only $fsdbdumpvars, and all the options inside the task are ignored for the
dumping of encrypted IP part, that is, it is treated as full dump. Note that the options
still take effect for normal part.
* Selecting dumping individual items inside encrypted blocks is disallowed. Only a full
instance of an encrypted hierarchies is supported.
* Only one public key per encrypted IP is supported.
* Partial protection/encryption is not supported. that is, a whole module must be in the
envelope.
* Addition of the public key attribute changes the number of lines in the IP.

* Uses a new FSDB version. Only supported starting with VCS/Verdi 2023.12.

PyVerdi Python Package
Verdi provides a Python package PyVerdi, which supports the following two APIs:
* callCommand
* addCallback
Before you execute Python inside Verdi, Verdi automatically imports both APIs, letting you
to directly write callCommand and addCallback inside your Python script without the need
for from PyVerdi import *.
PyVerdi.callCommand
The callCommand API is used to run Tcl commands. This API returns both Tcl return value
(integer) and the result (string) as a tuple.
Syntax: callCommand(tclString: str) -> tuple[int, str]
PyVerdi.addCallback
The addCallback API is used to register the Python function as an event callback
function, like addEventCallback in Tcl. This API returns true if the callback is registered
successfully; otherwise, it returns false. If you register both the Python callback and the Tcl
callback for the same event reason, only the Python callback gets triggered.
Syntax: addCallback(callbackReason: str, callbackFunc: callable[[str],
any]) -> bool

EDR (Electronic Debug Record) is a feature that allows you to create, save, and load a
Verdi session, which may contain texts, screenshots, Tcl scripts that are used to reproduce
or solve an issue in Verdi. A common usage scenario would be that an R&D wants
to share his Verdi debug session with another R&D. He can create and save an EDR
session that contains the necessary steps to reproduce an issue. Then the other R&D can
reproduce the Verdi debug session quickly with a single click.

Prerequisites for Installing the EDR Server
This section lists the system and software requirements that must be met before starting
the EDR Server installation.
To ensure stable operation of the EDR server, verify that the machine meets the minimum
hardware requirements:
* CPU: A modern processor with at least 1 GHz clock speed
* RAM: Minimum of 8GB
* Disk: Minimum of 20GB

Environment Setup for the EDR Server
This section explains how to prepare the system environment, such as setting required
environment variables, user permissions, and directory paths.
Before running the installation script, set up the required environment variables:
# Required : Set VERDI_HOME
setenv VERDI_HOME /path/to/verdi
# Optional: Set EDR project directory
setenv EDR_PRJ /path/to/edr/project
# Run the installation script (recommended for first-time installation)
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/install.csh --use_template_config

* For first-time installation, it is recommended to use -use_template_config option which creates a template configuration file
with default values and directly uses it for installation.
* If EDR_PRJ is not set, the installer prompts you to specify it.

Command-Line Options
This section provides details about the commandline options available for installing and
managing the EDR Server.
The EDR server installation script supports the following options:

--help

Display help information

--create_config

Generate edr_config.yaml without installing

--create_template_config

Generate a template configuration file

--use_config

Use existing edr_config.yaml for installation

--use_template_config

Create template config and use it for installation (recom-mended for
first-time installation)

--restart_server

Restart EDR server based on previous installation

--terminate_server

Terminate running EDR server

--check_server

Check if EDR server is running

--start_mongo

Start MongoDB server only (no EDR installation)

--shutdown_mongo

Shutdown MongoDB server

--check_mongo

Saving EDR
Before invoking Verdi, set the VCS_HOME and VERDI_HOME environment variables using the
following commands respectively:

Once Verdi is opened, navigate to Tools -> Save to EDR to save the EDR.
The Save EDR dialog opens as shown in the following example figure:
Figure 213

Save EDR Form

* Run_Mode: This field supports Session mode and TCL mode. Session mode saves
a Verdi session skipping the reproduced steps, and TCL mode saves the command
history and enable you to see how the debug record is reproduced.
* Title: This field automatically set the string as <user>_<app>_<date> to help users
distinguish different records. The app can be Verdi or formal or static. You may add
more app names later.
* Category: A predefined list of error characteristics. The default value is Unknown
Issue.

* Category: A predefined list of error characteristics. The default value is Unknown
Issue.
* Tags: You may add one or more Tags (separate by comma) to the record.
* Permission: The permission drop-down list contains Public and all Linux groups
of the current users. The default value is public. Once permission is set to group,
enable_case_extration is disabled. If an EDR has public permission, all users can
access it. If an EDR has group permission, only users who have the corresponding
Linux group permission can access it.
* Description: You may add the description of the debug record to capture the main
purpose of the session.
* Other Setting:
Environment Setting: The environment setting does not add all user environments
to the record; however, only the important ones are added. The users can add other
environment settings to the record as needed.
Data Preparation: This tab enables you to set the batch mode commands to
prepare the data for Verdi debug. Default Commands are the pre-defined batch
mode commands by EDR. You may change it if needed. Once you write your own
data preparation commands, Enable Case Extraction check box is disabled.

Figure 214

Save EDR - Data Preparation

Data Path: FSDB or KDB or simulation logs are collected by default. You can also
add customized data paths.
Figure 215

Data Path

For simulation logs, EDR automatically gathers files that are opened with the
viaLogViewerOpenLog SmartLog Tcl command.
For FSDB, EDR automatically gathers files that are opened with the wvOpenFile or
debLoadSimResult nWave Tcl commands.
* Advanced: This field shows the advanced features that enables you to set multiple
checkpoints in the record, and Case Extraction. You may click "+" to add the
checkpoint. A checkpoint contains the command history executed so far (from last
saved checkpoint or from beginning) with a snapshot and checkpoint notes. You may
also use Update Snapshot to update from the current active window. If multiple views
are selectable, you may choose which individual view to save. (The feature is based

on standard Capture Window feature of Verdi.) If there is no new command between
the new checkpoint and last one, a warning message is issued to let you know that the
current checkpoint is discarded.
Figure 216

Save EDR - Advanced Setup

* Enable Case Extraction: If this field is enabled, EDR tries to collect the data needed
to run the session. For Verdi run (post process and interactive debug), KDB/FSDB is
collected. The collected data is saved in a centralized location to avoid dependency
data being overwritten by users, so that the EDR replay can work independently.
* Enable Debug Telemetry: If this field is enabled, EDR tries to run Debug Telemetry
Analysis after the EDR is saved. Then the telemetry results get uploaded to the
database as part of EDR.
After the record is ready, click Save to upload the EDR record to Web Server. Click Copy
Link to copy the link string. You may also use the Reset to reset the debug session to
beginning or last checkpoint and keep operating to save the new debug records.

edrSearch
The edrSearch utility allows you to search through EDRs.
Input
A search string that follows the rules below.
Supported Search key:
"session_name"
"session_description"
"session_sig_catg"
"session_creator"
"session_id"
"session_workmode"
"session_group"
"time_range"
"path.KDB"
"path.FSDB"
"path.simulation_log"

Supported Logical Operators
"AND"
"OR"

Supported Match Operators
"="
"~"

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
For example, the following string queries the EDRs whose session_name contains verdi
and session_creator is jack.
edrSearch "session_name ~ verdi AND session_creator = jack"

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
Note that time_range is a special key and it only supports three value: week, month,
quarter.
For example, the following string queries the EDRs that are created in last seven days and
session_description contains debug.
edrSearch "time_range = week AND session_description ~ debug"

Output:
One or more matched EDR session IDs, if not found, the output is "No matched records in
database."
edrReplay
The edrReplay utility allows you to replay the EDRs.
Input
* EDR session ID
* Work directory (optional)
Replay Verdi is invoked if session ID is valid. Else, print an error message.
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrReplay -session_id
6c47cb1b3a2d483ab408f0171211ee90 -work_dir /remote/vgemanits/yuesenlu/edr

edrUtil
The edrUtil utility allows you to configure your personal EDR setup.
Input
One or more combination of the options supported by the script.
Successful configuration of the EDR.
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrUtil -display abcodcvde0xxx7:1
-replay_dir /u/abc/my03/edr
abc's display is set to abcodcvde0xxx7:1.
abc's replay dir is set to /u/abc/my03/edr.

EDR Replay Dialog
The EDR Replay dialog can be opened using Tools -> EDR Replay.

After a session is replayed either from the web server or directly from Record URL, Verdi
launches with an EDR Replay dialog.
The EDR Replay dialog lists the checkpoint list of the record, and a snapshot of each
checkpoint. By default, checkpoint 1 is executed. And you can select other checkpoints
by clicking on "Go to Checkpoint". (For example, go to checkpoint 3 from checkpoint 1).
The checkpoints in between are executed in the order if it is a TCL-based checkpoint;
otherwise, it restores the session for the selected checkpoint directly.
Figure 226

EDR Replay

Debug Telemetry
Debug Telemetry is a utility integrated with EDR. It collects information about user
activities during the debugging process.
Examples include modules, scopes, and signals.
The VERDI_ENABLE_ELECTRONIC_DEBUG_RECORD environment variable must be
set to 1 to use the Debug Telemetry feature.
You need to click Advanced<< to view the Enable Debug Telemetry field.

Figure 227

Debug Telemetry

After the EDR is saved successfully, the data extraction flow takes place. You can click
Settings to view the status.

Figure 228

Debug Telemetry Status

You can switch to the EDR web page to view Debug Telemetry information. This view
summarizes the number of modules and signals accessed during debugging.
For example, in the following figure, 3 modules and 10 signals were accessed in total.

You can click this link and navigate to the summary page of Debug Telemetry for more
details.

EDR Serverless Mode
EDR Serverless Mode lets you save and replay Electronic Debug Record (EDR) sessions
locally without connecting to a server. Use this mode to keep debug data on your own
machine or when server access is limited.
* Saving EDR in Serverless Mode
* Replaying EDR in Serverless Mode
EDR runs in serverless mode if the environment variable

SNPS_VERDI_INTERNAL_ELECTRONIC_DEBUG_RECORD_WEB_SERVER_URI is not set.

Saving EDR in Serverless Mode
When saving an EDR session, Verdi displays a warning indicating serverless mode is
active.

* The Save EDR dialog box shows the storage path and lets you choose where to save
the EDR session.
* After saving, Verdi displays the local path of the saved EDR session.

Replaying EDR in Serverless Mode
Using the Command Line Utility
1. Run the following command to replay a saved EDR session:
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrReplay -session_dir <path_of_saved_EDR>

2. Replace <path_of_saved_EDR> with the actual path where your EDR session is
saved.
Using Verdi EDR Browser
1. Open the EDR Browser in Verdi.
2. Enter the local path to search for EDR records on your disk.
The search is recursive with a default maximum depth of 3.
If the search takes too long, click Stop to end the search.

3. After the search finishes, results are displayed in the EDR Browser.
4. Click Replay to replay the selected EDR session.

Upgrading the server means updating the server software to a newer version, typically

The following sections describe the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer (Cache Mode)
LCA feature supported by Verdi as part of this release:
* Overview
* Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer (Cache Mode)

Overview
Synopsys Memory VIPs are based on Synopsys SystemVerilog Technology (SVT)
infrastructure. The infrastructure includes SystemVerilog classes and Memory Server.
The Memory Server is one of the key elements of SVT Memory VIP infrastructure. Actual
memory values are stored in the Memory Server, rather than in a SystemVerilog array.
The primary advantage of this approach is performance independence. The Memory
VIP does not rely on each simulator's sparse array server implementation. For multi-GB
memories, the simulation typically accesses only a small portion of the overall address
space. In addition, this approach supports virtual patterns. These patterns enable memory
initialization without significant memory or performance overhead.
In a Memory VIP, protocol-level transactions and memory actions are stored in an FSDB
file. The Memory Server can be configured to record all memory actions to the same
FSDB file. You can then view the memory-related data in the Verdi Memory Protocol
Analyzer. With the information recorded by the Memory Server, you can determine any
memory address value at any time during simulation.
The SVT Memory Server has been enhanced to store the memory actions associated with
the server in an FSDB file as transactions. The streams of these transactions are tagged
with hidden attributes. The Verdi environment recognizes the memory instances and

Overview

displays them in the new Memory Array browser. In addition, you can view the memory
actions of the Memory Server in Transaction Table View or Transaction and Protocol
Analyzer windows.
For performance considerations, each instance of a Synopsys Memory VIP must be
configured to dump data to the FSDB file. By default, this capability is not enabled.
Synopsys Memory VIPs provide controls for dumping protocol-level transactions. They
also dump the status of internal state machines and the memory actions performed by the
Memory Server.

To enable and use the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer(Cache mode) in Verdi, it is

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer (Cache Mode)
Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer also provides debug capability for cache line data
for designs that utilize the AMBA ACE protocol. The AMBA ACE Verification IPs are also
enabled to capture cache related data and store the data within an FSDB file.
It offers the following capabilities for cache visualization and debug:
* Recognize, load, and display the data related to cache memory.
* Provide synchronization between the Cache and Memory Protocol AnalyzerCache
view, Transaction and Protocol Analyzer, and other transaction views.
* Search the data related to cache memory.

Viewing Cache Related Data in Verdi
Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzerdisplays data related to cache memory to help you
to analyze and debug the design efficiently, as it provides visualization and analysis of one
or more cache memories at a specific simulation time.
You can invoke the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer window using any of the
following methods:
* In the Verdi main window, click the Tools -> Transaction Debug -> Cache and Memory
Protocol Analyzer command.
* In the Protocol Analyzerwindow, click the Tools ->New Cache and Memory Protocol
Analyzer command.
* In the Protocol Analyzerwindow, select a coherent/snoop transaction and click the
Show Cache Operations right-click option to open either a filtered (single address) or
an unfiltered view. This view occupies the bottom half portion of the available area, but
can be rearranged or moved (if required).

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview
The cache debug view window comprises of the following panes:
* Hierarchy Tree pane
* Cache pane
* History pane
* Details pane
The following figure illustrates the cache debug view window:
Figure 231

Cache Debug View

Hierarchy Tree Pane
The Hierarchy Tree pane displays scopes and streams that have associated cache or
memory data and each scope/stream has a corresponding check box. You can select a
stream/scope check box to view its associated cache or memory data.
If you select a cache scope or stream, the cache data is opened with the cache view.
If you select a memory scope or stream, the cache data is opened with the memory view.
The check box is mutually exclusive. In a given memory browser at a given
time, you can view either memory data or cache data, but not memory and
cache data together. To view both memory data and cache data simultaneously,
you need to open two memory browser windows.

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

The following figure illustrates the Hierarchy Tree pane:
Figure 232

Hierarchy Tree Pane

All the possible actions and the resultant behaviors are as follows:
* If no items are checked in the Hierarchy Tree pane,
Checking a memory instance loads the memory data.
Checking a cache instance loads the cache data.
* If a memory instance is already loaded,
Checking a memory instance loads new memory data in the current view (only one
memory instance can be selected at a time).
Checking a cache instance loads the cache data in the current view.
* If a cache instance is already loaded,
Checking a memory instance loads the memory data in the current view (replacing
the cache data).
Checking/unchecking a cache instance adds/removes the cache data in the current
view.
The memory data can now be opened using the Hierarchy Tree, instead of the
Select Memory option used in previous releases. You can open and view the
memory data by checking the associated check box for a scope or stream.
Right-click to access options such as: Expand All, Collapse All, and Open in
Memory Browser. Clicking the Open in Memory Browser option opens the

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

selected scope/stream data in a new window (with cache view/memory view
based on the selected scope/stream data).

Cache Pane
The Cache pane displays the contents of one or more cache memories at a particular
simulation time. The following figure illustrates the general layout of the Cache pane and
shows the selected instances in the Hierarchy Tree pane:
Figure 233

Cache Pane

The following widgets are present in the Cache Pane:
* Timeline Cursor is present at the top of the Cache pane and indicates the current
time being displayed. This time value is also shown in the toolbar. You can display the
contents of the caches for a different simulation time by clicking the desired time.
* The table present under the timeline cursor shows the contents of the caches for the
selected instances. In the preceding figure, the contents of master_0 and master_1
instances are being displayed. Instances with cache data can be added to or removed
from the view using the check boxes in the Hierarchy Tree pane.
The rows in the table are sorted by the address value. You can specify a single address
value or an address range to filter the displayed data using the filter available in the
toolbar.
The contents of each column in this table are described below.
Column

Address

Specifies the address for all cache lines in a row.

Type

Specifies the coherent transaction type.

State

Specifies the cache line state (UD, SD, UC, SC).

Data

Specifies the cache line data.

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

The cell background color for the cells is displayed as specified in the following figure:
Figure 234

Cell Background Color Coding for State Cells

A cache line operation may be empty for a particular cache, if there is no data in that
cache for a specific address row. For example, if the caches for master_0 and master_1
have data for address 0x100, but the cache for master_2 does not contain any data for
that address, the area for the cache line operation for master_2 for address 0x100 is
empty.
Since cache line data can be large, the data values are displayed in a modified
hexadecimal format, that is, an underscore character ('_') is inserted every fourth byte in
the hexadecimal data.

History Pane
The History pane shows the history for an item that has been selected in the Cache pane.
The history includes all the related items that are recorded for the entire simulation for a
specified address where cache instance or address is selected. For example, the Cache
pane shows cache data at the current time.
However, the History pane shows data for the following:
* All the selected cache instances.
* All the cache transactions that occurred in the simulation history based on the address
of the selected cache in the Cache pane.
Once the history table is loaded, it can also be used for navigation. Double-click an item in
the History pane to make that item the current selection. The item is moved to the Cache
pane and the other panes are updated accordingly.
If you select a cache operation in the Cache pane, the Details table is updated with the
cache operation attributes and the History table is updated with previous cache operations
(with same address and instance of the selected cache operation). This selection also
shows value change navigation for the next/previous cache operation (for the same

address and cache instance of the selected cache operation). You can select a cache
operation by clicking on a cell in one of Type, State, or Data columns.
The complete history of all the ports for the selected cell address is displayed
irrespective of the selection on address or on a particular cache operation.

Address Filter in the Cache Pane
The Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer provides you the capability to filter and display
data for the desired address range.

Synchronization With Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer

To filter and display data in the Cache pane for a specified address range, perform the
following steps:
1. Enter the address range (starting address and end address) in the fields next to the
Enable/Disable Address Filter icon as follows:

2. Click the Enable/Disable Address Filter

icon present in the toolbar.

On disabling the Address Filter, the Cache pane gets reset to the original
view and displays all the addresses.

Synchronization With Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer
Verdi provides the capability that lets you synchronize the Cache pane with Verdi
Transaction and Protocol Analyzer and other transaction views, which provides a better
debug experience.
In addition to creating a cache operation transaction, relationships are established
between various transactions, which are used to display appropriate information in the
cache view and aid in the debug process. The predecessor/successor relationship is
illustrated as follows:

The VIP captures information related to the cache memory into a separate scope called
cache. This scope is present inside the same hierarchy as the master instance. The scope
contains a scope attribute, which indicates that this scope contains cache related data.
This data can be read by and displayed in the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer:
Cache view.
The following two scopes are created below the cache scope:
* The info scope, which is used to store general information about the cache, such as the
width of each cache line and the number of lines in the cache.
* The operations scope, which is used to store the cache operation transactions.
When a cache operation is recorded, a predecessor/successor relationship
is established between each coherent transaction and the associated

Synchronization With Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer

snoop transactions. If appropriate, this relationship is also established with
the slave transaction. Additionally, a predecessor/successor relationship
is established between each snoop transaction and the cache operation
transaction.

When a coherent transaction is selected in Transaction and Protocol Analyzer,
the time in the Cache pane is set to the end of the coherent transaction. This is

setenv VERDI_SCALABLE_SHELLDB

The performance of wildcard searching and filtering in Instance Tree with Scalable

text:
Filter by Scope and Patterns
It can be displayed by the right-click Menu "Show Filter" or short cut (Ctrl+Shift+F).
* Filter String Combo box: allows you to edit, support wild-card, and scope with
delimiter ".". In Support Drop, the drop type is DND_STRING.
* Case-Sensitive button: It matches strings whether it is case-sensitive or not. The case
insensitive is the default value.
Filter supports the following two filter modes:
* Filter in Expanded Tree
* Filter in Whole Design
This can be switched by Preferences -> Source Code -> Design Tree -> Search and
Filter Tree Nodes
When "Search and Filter in Expanded Tree" is checked, the filter only shows match tree
nodes that are already expanded/traversed by the user. By default, it is on. After that,
"Filter Dynamically" check-box gets enabled.
When "Search and Filter in Expanded Tree" is unchecked, the filter shows all matched tree
nodes. It supports non-blocking.
If the count of match tree nodes is more than "Maximum Filter Results to Display", a
warning message box pops up.
To restore filtered tree to its original status:
* Use right-click Menu "Restore to Original Instance"
* "Type "*" or empty string in the "Filter String Combo box"
Filter by Type
Click on filter button
to open the filter by type form. Check/un-check filter buttons to
show/hide the specified kind.
Navigation
You need to input the completed hierarchy, then select the corresponding tree node. It
supports drop and drag with DND_STRING.
Drawing for Preload Flow
Grays out all Non-loaded scope.

Preload Icons:
* Icon at bottom left corner. Example, Include loaded scope
* Icon at bottom right corner. Example, Exclude scope
* Drawing for power design: Instances that belong to the same power domain shows
the same color.
Tip
It shows the following information in tip:
* Full name
* Preload status: "Include Loaded Instance.", "Exclude Module", "Non-loaded Instance".
* Power domain name
The short cut "Shift" can copy all tip content in clipboard.
Tip can be hidden by un-checking "Show tip" in the right-click menu.
Expand/Collapse Node
You can click "+" to expand node. It supports non-blocking. You can expand tree nodes or
collapse tree nodes.
You can have a maximum total tree node limit of 20 million. If the generated tree nodes
exceeds it, the following warning message is displayed:
"Failed to expand the tree node, because the maximum limit %d has been reached."
Reload
Reload designs regenerates Instance Tree. All filtered or expanded status is cleared. Once
the rebuilt is done, Instance tree automatically restores active scope to the previous active
scope before reloading.
Save/Restore Session
Save/restore flow restores the current active scope.

nWave Enhancement
The following section describes the nWave LCA features supported by Verdi as part of this
release:
* Unified Transaction and Signal Waveform Debugging in nWave
* Dynamic Object Signal Enhancements in nWave
* Improved Waveform Drawing Performance for FSDB-GATE Signals

This feature enables you to add both transactions and signals into nWave. Thus, the
integrated nWave window helps you get the maximum benefit of the screen size and other
features to debug an error using both transactions and waveforms on a single application
For more information about this feature, refer to the Transaction Debug chapter.

After loading a waveform file into Verdi which stores the dumped dynamic objects, you can
review the waveforms in the nWave with following enhancements:
* Support for UVM Component and Register Objects
* Viewing UVM Hierarchy Name for Class Object Signal in nWave Signal Pane
* Support to Expand Class Object
* Support Filtering of Internal Attributes for Expanded Class Object/Pointer
* Support for Queue, Dynamic Array, Associative Array in Class Object
* Adding Class Handle to Waveform

text:
Support for UVM Component and Register Objects
To enable the following enhancements,
perform the following:
* Set the environment variable VERDI_ENHANCE_DYNAMIC_OBJECT.
* To dump UVM component object, you must specify +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE
option at simulation runtime.
* To dump UVM register object, you must specify +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE option at
simulation runtime.
* To specify dumping level for UVM component object, you must specify
+UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N option at simulation runtime. The default value of N is 1. If N
is specified as 0, all level of objects are dumped.
Or,
* You can also use the Object Level preference option (Tools -> Preferences ->
Interactive Debug->Dynamical Dumping page) in Verdi interactive mode, as shown in
the following figure, to specify dumping level for UVM component object. The default
value is "1".
Figure 246

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
New Object Level Option in Preferences Dialog

If +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE or +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE is not specified, the
object dumping level is determined by the Object Level preference option.
If +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE or +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE is specified, the object
dumping level is determined by the largest number between +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N
and Object Level Options. For example, if +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N is specified and

Object Level is set to M, the object dumping level is determined by the largest number
between N and M.

Perform the simulation for the demanded debugging features using the corresponding
runtime options:
./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+UVM_AWARE+COMPWAVE +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=2

Set the environment variables for nWave features introduced in this section, using the
following command:
setenv VERDI_ENHANCE_DYNAMIC_OBJECT

Viewing UVM Hierarchy Name for Class Object Signal in nWave
Signal Pane
If a class object signal belongs to uvm component, Verdi displays UVM hierarchy name as
the signal's name in the nWave Signal Pane.
* Use either the drag-and-drop operation or the Add to Waveform right-click option on a
class object signal in the following views:
Object View
Member View
Source View
Local View
Watch View
The feature is available in the above views in Interactive mode.

* Use the Add to Waveform right-click option on a class object signal in the OVM/UVM
Hierarchy tree.
Figure 247

Adding Class Object Signal to nWave Signal Pane

Click View -> Hierarchical Name to view the UVM hierarchical name as the class object
signal's name in the nWave Signal Pane, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 248

Viewing UVM Hierarchical Name as the Signal's Name

Note: Verdi displays the dumping hierarchy instead of UVM hierarchy when you perform
runtime operation for this signal (like shift, invert, rename, and so on).
* Copying and pasting a signal (using the copy/paste right-click options) with UVM
hierarchy name in nWave Signal Pane displays the UVM hierarchy directly for the
added signal also, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 249

Displaying UVM Hierarchy of the Pasted Signal

Note: Verdi displays the dumping hierarchy instead of UVM hierarchy when you perform
drag-and-drop operation (using the drag/drop right-click options) for the signal in nWave
Signal Pane.
* If a signal is added to the nWave Signal Pane from the Get Signals dialog, Verdi
displays the dumping hierarchy on the Signal Pane, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 250

Viewing Signal Added From Get Signals Dialog

Support to Expand Class Object
You can double-click a class object/pointer signal to view its member attributes once the
FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS environment variable is set while dumping the waveform.

Support Filtering of Internal Attributes for Expanded Class
Object/Pointer
Verdi supports filtering internal attributes when expanding class object/pointer by
default. You can use Filter Internal Attribute for Class Object preference option (Tools >
Preferences > Waveform > View Options > Miscellaneous > Filter Internal Attribute
for Class Object) to disable it.

Figure 251

Preferences-Filter Internal Attribute for Class Object

While an object is expanding, if only one super exists, super is shown. If there are more
than one, it shows super_<n>. If its corresponding class is UVM class type, this feature
filters out super, super_<n>.*, super_<n+m>.* (m = 1, 2, 3, ).
All the signals with leaf name as rspor req is retained.
While expanding an object, which is one of the uvm base class type, all the
members of the object are retained. That is, the filtering feature has no effect.

Support for Queue, Dynamic Array, Associative Array in Class
Object
Verdi displays queue, dynamic array, and associative array for a class object in the nWave
Signal Pane when they were dumped into the loaded waveform. See Dumping Class
Objects by Level for usage of dumping non-static array in class object. You can also
double-click a queue, dynamic array, or associative array to expand it and view its member
data.
The following table shows the icons displayed for queue, dynamic array, and associative
array in the nWave Signal Pane:

Element Name
Queue
Dynamic Array
Associative Array

* For queue, the parent signal shows the number in the queue and expanded member
shows the member in the queue, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 252

Queue Support for Class Object

* For dynamic array, the parent signal shows the number in the array and expanded
member shows the member in the array, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 253

Dynamic Array Support for Class Object

* For associative array, the parent signal shows the number in the array and expanded
member shows the member in the array. The member is a composite signal with
key,value as its value, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 254

Associative Array Support for Class Object

You can define the maximum dumping element size using the setenv
FSDB_MAX_DYNAMIC_ARRAY_SIZE environment variable. For example, if max
element size in design is 1000 and you have set the max element size in
dumping option to 100 (setenv FSDB_MAX_DYNAMIC_ARRAY_SIZE 100), and
after simulation run for a while, the current max dumping element size is 50.
Then, nWave max expanded number of queue, dynamic array, associative
array is 50.
In Interactive mode, nWave generates the following message when max size
of queue/array is increased: Maximum number of available item increased,
collapse and expand to see its new member(s)

Viewing Maximum Dumping Element Size
The maximum expanded number of queue, dynamic array, and associative
array is decided by the maximum dumping element size, which can be specified
by FSDB_MAX_VARIANT_SIZE_ARRAY environment variable or the +fsdb
+max_variant_size_array simulation option. However, the real maximum dumping
element size depends on the simulation time. For example, after simulation run, if the
current maximum dumping element size is 50, then nWave maximum expanded number of
queue, dynamic array, and associative array is 50.
* The save/restore commands are supported in the signal.rc file.
* Since the size of queue/array may change during simulation, new members can be
added to queue/array at runtime. nWave cannot add new members to the expanded

queue/array automatically. Verdi issues the following message for nWave when
maximum size of queue/array is increased in interactive mode.
Maximum number of available items increased, collapse and expand to
see its new member(s).

* Supported waveform file: normal FSDB file and virtual file in "switch" type.

Adding Class Handle to Waveform
You can drag-and-drop class object handles to waveform from the Source, Local, and
Watch views during Verdi Interactive mode, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 255

FSDB file and virtual file in "switch" type.

Adding Class Handle to Waveform
You can drag-and-drop class object handles to waveform from the Source, Local, and
Watch views during Verdi Interactive mode, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 255

Drag-and-Drop Class Object Handles to Waveform

As shown in the figure, when drag-and-drop is performed on dvr signal from the Source/
Local/Watch to waveform, Verdi adds it as a class object handle and displays UVM
hierarchy name as signal's name (for example: /uvm_test_top/top/e/dvr). You can
also use the Add to Waveform right-click option on a class object handle in the Source,
Local, and Watch views to add it to waveform.

Improved Waveform Drawing Performance for FSDB-GATE
Signals
Describes nWave performance enhancements for FSDB-GATE signals: pixel-based
drawing (SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER), multitasking dense drawing, optional
red X highlighting (Waveform > View Options > Waveform Pane > Show X Color in
Multitasking Dense Drawing), docked/undocked progress display, default vs NeedX mode,
and limitations (unfinished files, auto-update, virtual files, anyall/real signal).
This feature improves the speed of drawing waveforms in nWave when working with
FSDB-GATE signals. FSDB files can contain many signals that are marked as secondary,
meaning their value changes are not dumped directly but reconstructed during reading.

This reconstruction can slow down nWave operations, especially for gate-level FSDBs with
many value changes. The new solution speeds up waveform drawing and makes the user
interface more responsive.
* Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
* Enabling and Using X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense Drawing
* Limitations of Multitasking Dense Drawing and Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave

Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
The pixel-based drawing feature in nWave improves how waveform data is displayed,
especially when handling large datasets. This feature changes how dense pixels and
'X' (unknown) values appear in the waveform view.
Setting Environment Variables
To activate the pixel-based drawer feature, set the following environment variable before
launching Verdi and nWave:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER 1

Using the Feature
* Open nWave as usual after setting the environment variables.
* nWave polls the FSDB reader and update the waveform incrementally.

* The interface remains responsive; you can scroll, click, and view signal tips even while
data is loading.
* Unfinished waveform data appears as blue pixels. These pixels update as more data
loads.

nWave now draws green pixels to represent areas with enough value changes, instead of
checking each value change one by one. This speeds up rendering for large datasets. The

Enabling and Using X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense
Drawing
The X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense Drawing is a feature that helps users
quickly identify unknown (X) values in waveforms when working with large FSDB (Fast
Signal Database) files. This feature is especially useful when debugging gate-level
simulations, as it visually highlights X values in dense waveform regions, making it easier
to spot issues without zooming in on every signal.
When you load a large FSDB file in nWave, the tool uses a dense drawing mode to speed
up waveform rendering. In this mode, nWave summarizes many value changes (vc) into
a single pixel. By default, X values might not be shown in red unless you zoom in. The
"NeedX" mode allows you to display X values in red even in dense drawing, but might
impact performance.

* Default Mode: Fast drawing, X values might not appear in red unless zoomed in.
* NeedX Mode: Precise X detection, X values appear in red in dense drawing, but might
slow down performance.

Enabling X Color Display (NeedX Mode)
Follow these steps to enable the X Color Display in nWave:
1. Go to Waveform > View Options > Waveform Pane > Show X Color in Multitasking
Dense Drawing in the nWave preferences.
2. Set the option to On.
When enabled, dense drawing shows "X" values in red for more accuracy.
When disabled (default), "X" values are not shown in dense mode, but appears
when you zoom in.
Viewing Progress and Status
* Undocked nWave Window: The progress bar appears in the toolbar when data is
loading. Hover over the bar to see tips.

* Docked nWave Window: The progress bar appears in the banner area, and a busy
status is shown in the tab area.

Limitations of Multitasking Dense Drawing and Pixel-Based
Drawer for nWave
* The "Show X Color in Multitasking Dense Drawing" option applies only to GATE FSDB
dense drawing.
* Enabling NeedX mode might impact performance, especially with large files.
* In default mode, "X" values might not be shown in red unless you zoom in.
* In default mode, "X" values are not shown in dense drawing unless NeedX mode is
enabled.
* Only the smallest range of value changes per pixel is reconstructed, which might affect
accuracy for some signals unless zoomed in or NeedX mode is enabled.
* This feature is not supported with unfinished files.
* Not supported with auto-update feature.
* Does not support virtual file (except auto-switch).
* Does not support anyall-related feature and real signal.

Support Tracing Capability for Low Power Bind Checker Module
The tracing capability of the low power checker module is enhanced to trace the port
connection of the checker module bound with the bind_checker command. This feature
allows you to view the signals connected to the bind-checker module and gets the driver/
load information when debugging the checker module. This feature is supported only for
the checkers bound to the retention/isolation cell.
You must use the following command to enable this feature:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_XML_ENABLE_BINDCHECKER_HIGHCONN

With the support, when you trace a signal inside the bind-checker module, or trace a
signal whose driver/load is inside bind-checker module, Verdi displays the highconn of the
checker module port with a statement beginning with LP Bind Checker message. To view
this message, you must enable the Show Passthroughs option in the Preferences dialog.
For example, consider a checker module with four ports SAVE_SIGNAL, RESTORE_SIGNAL,
RETPN, and RETGN, where highconns of these ports are tb.top_unit.restore,
tb.top_unit.restore, tb/top_unit/VDD_ret, and tb/top_unit/VSS respectively.

Support for New Instrumentation Methodology for SystemVerilog
Interfaces
VCS supports a new instrumentation methodology for SystemVerilog interfaces using the
-power=upfim compile option. For example:
% vcs test.v -upf demo.upf -kdb -lca -power=upfim
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidr

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
Starting with this release, Verdi supports this methodology by default. It supports all
existing low power debugging features based on this new instrumentation methodology.

The following are the limitations of this feature:
* This feature supports only the modport port name same as the signal name. That is,
this feature only works based on the signal names inside modport/interface.
* Nested modport is not supported.
* All instrumented signals in interface are not supported in FSDB.

Support Verdi Low Power XML Functionality for VHDL
VCS Plato supports the UPF Information Model (UPFIM). The UPFIM flow preserves all
existing Verdi GUI behavior. That is, there is no behavior change between the Verdi low

Verdi Low Power Import Performance Improvement

power XML (lp_xml) flow and the Verdi UPFIM flow. You must use the -power=upfim
compile option on the vcs command line to enable UPFIM flow. For example:
% vcs test.v -upf demo.upf -kdb -lca -power=upfim

Verdi Low Power Import Performance Improvement
Profiling shows that Verdi low power import takes a long time to traverse all UPF
commands from the power database. To resolve this issue, run a batch mode executable,
lpcom, in parallel with VCS compilation.
lpcom processes the power database and serializes it into an archive. During Verdi bring

text:
up, Verdi automatically picks up the archive and transforms it into the Verdi database.
This support is now enabled at compilation using the -kdb=lpcom compile option.
Following is the usage example:
% vcs design.v -sverilog -upf file.upf -lca -kdb=lpcom
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidir

When you use this option, Verdi imports resolved power KDB (PW-KDB) directly instead of
building Verdi Power Model.
You can use the following environment variable to disable -kdb=lpcom:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_DISABLE_LPCOM 1

UVM Aware Debug
The following section describe the UVM-Aware Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as
part of this release:
* Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug
* Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features
* Native UVM Dumping Support

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug
When you debug a UVM error or fatal event in Verdi interactive mode, you need to rerun
the simulation to reach the error point after starting Verdi.
The Verdi Instant Recall feature lets you save the error point as a debug session during
batch-mode simulation. The UVM error message report helps you find error types, group
them, and plan your next steps for debugging with Instant Recall.
After you save the simulation session for a UVM error or fatal event, you can use Verdi to
restore the session in interactive mode. This saves time because you do not need to rerun
the simulation.
To enable the Instant Recall flow, use the -instantRecall VCS runtime option. The
Instant Recall flow enables the following:
* Record the simulation session at the first UVM error or fatal, and then use Verdi to start
debugging from the point where the simulation session was recorded.
* Stop the simulation at the first UVM error or fatal, print out the error message, create
checkpoint information of debug point, save the session, and then exit the simulation.
You can know at which UVM_ERROR is the checkpoint saved and identify that the test failed
with UVM_ERROR.
UVM error message report helps you to identify error types, group them, and perform the
next step for debugging with Instant Recall.
You can continue to perform debugging by using the -i -cprestore [saved_session]
Verdi command line option to restore the simulation session to Verdi in interactive mode.

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* You can enable Instant Recall flow in VCS using the -instantRecall runtime option.
For example, simv -instantRecall.
For compilation, you must specify the -kdb and -debug_acc+reverse options to
enable this feature.
* The -instantRecall option auto-generates a default instant recall script named
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl under the run directory. The following are the
key points to note:
The instant recall script enables reverse debug (config reversedebug on), saves
debug point on the first UVM error or fatal, and then saves the session.
The saved session is the simulation session, not the Verdi session.
Simulation sources this Tcl script before sourcing your -do/-i script.
By default, .synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl is overwritten for every instant
recall run.
To modify this script, you can add a header in this Tcl file to keep the current Tcl
version by adding/removing comment, so that your modification can take effect in
later instant recall runs.
The session can be overwritten if it exists.
Provide default session name. You can also define session names in the
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl file.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits.
Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
* The session is saved under the run directory. You can execute from the Verdi
command line as follows to restore the session from the time point where the first UVM
error or fatal happened.
% verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore [checkpoint_session]

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
You can specify the simulation session name to restore. If no file is specified, the
default session file is restored.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits and Verdi closes the interactive debug mode.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features

* From the Verdi command line, the restore session should not be used with -do/-i.
Example: verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore sess -do myScript
Verdi issues a warning message and skips -do/-i.
The following is the limitation of this feature:
* When Verdi is invoked with the -i -cprestore option, it may not consider some
runtime options of the Restart simulation command. This can happen as the Verdi
behavior is the same as the restore mechanism. That is, Verdi may not extract some of
the runtime options applied to simv.
You can use one of the following workarounds to avoid this limitation:
1. If an FSDB file is dumped for the simulation with the -instantRecall option, you
can invoke Verdi using both the -i -cprestore option and the FSDB file together.
The simulation options are saved in the FSDB file and can be reused while invoking
Verdi.
Example:%> verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -i -cprestore
2. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options manually in the Verdi
command line as follows:
Example:%> verdi -dbdir simv.daidir -i cprestore -simDelim
+UVM_TEST_NAME=test_2m_4s // runtime options are used in the simulation
3. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options after invoking Verdi and
before performing Restart.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features
By default, UVM data is dumped into the default FSDB file. You can use the
+uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> runtime option to specify the FSDB

file for the UVM debug features enabled by the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE runtime options.

The following options can be specified with the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE:
UVM_AWARE, HIER, TLM, TLM2, IMP, RAL, FAC, COMPWAVE, RALWAVE, or MSG.

If filename.fsdb is not specified, then the file name is set to uvm.fsdb

Native UVM Dumping Support

automatically. If only filename is specified without .fsdb, then .fsdb is appended to the
file name automatically.
When the +uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> option is specified, the +UVM_VERDI_TRACE
related dumping option dumps UVM components into the specified FSDB file, similarly, the
+UVM_TR_RECORD related transactions are recorded into the specified FSDB file.
If the +fsdbfile+<high.fsdb> and +uvm_fsdbfile=<uvm.fsdb> options are
used together, the resolution is +fsdbfile > +uvm_fsdbfile. That is, the
resolved FSDB file name is high.fsdb.
If the +uvm_fsdbfile=<uvm.fsdb> option is specified and $fsdbDumpvars
is called without specifying fsdb_name, uvm.fsdb only includes uvm items
as described in this section. The $fsdbDumpvars system task still generates
novas.fsdb as the default FSDB file for the specified scope in the function call.

Native UVM Dumping Support
VCS dumps the transactions and messages natively, thereby allowing seamless
integration without requiring modifications to customer libraries. It helps avoid unexpected
compile-time errors, ensures backward compatibility, and facilitates debugging using the
Fast Signal Database (FSDB).
To enable the native UVM dumping support feature, use the following compile-time and
runtime options. You can also use the compile-time options in the command file and
compile the design using the -f, -F, or -file option.
Compile-Time Options (vlogan and vcs)
-native_uvm_dumping uvm-1.1|uvm-1.2|uvm-ieee|uvm-ieee2020: Enables native

transaction dumping for specified UVM versions.
Runtime Option (simv)

-native_uvm_dumping: Enables +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+TLM

automatically.
